# A dashboard and control API for Celery

<p class="cm-tagline">See what every task is doing, act on it, and pause a single
future occurrence of a periodic task — without touching your beat schedule or
restarting anything. Works with any Django, Flask or FastAPI project that already
uses Celery.</p>

[Get started](quickstart.md){ .md-button .md-button--primary }
[View on GitHub](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/celery-manager){ .md-button }

</div>


!!! warning "Beta — `0.3.0b1`"

    Working and tested, with roles, audit logging and a documented
    [stability policy](stability.md). Anything outside that policy may still
    move before 1.0, so pin the exact version. The [changelog](changelog.md) records what breaks between
    development builds.

## Sixty seconds

```bash
pip install --pre celery-manager
```

Then mount the dashboard into your existing app and start the events listener next
to your workers. For a plain-language tour of everything it does, see
[Features](features.md). The [Quickstart](quickstart.md) walks through install, the required
Celery settings, creating the first user and signing in.

## How it works

celery-manager is three cooperating pieces, all pointed at the same database:

1. **The REST API and dashboard** — a FastAPI app serving the JSON API under `/api`
   and the dashboard at `/`. Mount it into your own ASGI app or run it standalone.
2. **The events listener** — `celery-manager events`, a long-running process that
   records every task's status transitions from Celery's event bus, whether or not
   the task uses `@track`.
3. **The `@track` decorator** — optional, per task. It adds log capture, enables
   per-occurrence pause and cancel, and records the run as started before the task
   body runs.

Because they share one SQLAlchemy-backed store, any combination can run in separate
processes or containers. See [Configuration](configuration.md) for `db_url` and the
rest.

## Requirements

Python 3.10+ and an existing Celery project. See the
[Quickstart](quickstart.md#install) for extras.

## Licence

celery-manager is open source under the
[MIT licence](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/celery-manager/blob/main/LICENSE),
copyright &copy; 2026 Mahmoud Ahmed.


## Observe host-owned work

The 0.3 candidate also observes synchronous/async application jobs without a
Celery app. [Real-world operations](real-world-operations.md) covers RunObserver,
health/outbox probes, first-due scheduler expectations, correlation, duplicate
visibility, preflight, annotations and operator safeguards. For customer-facing
history, [tenant-scoped read-only mode](tenancy.md) enforces a narrower HTTP
boundary than ordinary manager roles.


<!-- docs/features.md -->

# Features

Everything celery-manager does, in plain words. Each feature says what it is
for, how you use it, and where to read the details.

Two pieces do most of the work, so it helps to know them first:

- **The events listener** (`celery-manager events`) watches Celery and
  records every task run. Most of what you see in the dashboard comes from
  it, with no change to your tasks.
- **The `@track` decorator** is optional, per task. Add it when you want
  log capture, live progress, or the ability to skip and pause scheduled
  runs. Without it, a scheduled task always runs.

## See what your tasks are doing

**Task list.** Every run of every task, newest first, with its status,
runtime and start time. Filter by status, search by task name, ID or
arguments, pick a date range, or group runs by task.
In the dashboard: **Tasks**. [Read more](dashboard.md#task-list)

**Task detail.** One run in full: arguments, worker, queue, timings, and for
a failure, the exception and traceback first. Retries link back to the run
they came from.
In the dashboard: click any run. [Read more](dashboard.md#task-detail)

**Log capture.** Log lines your task writes while it runs are saved with
that run and shown on its page. Needs `@track`.
[Read more](decorator.md#what-log-capture-actually-captures)

**Live progress.** Call `report_progress(current, total, message)` inside a
long task and watch a progress bar, elapsed time and an estimated finish
while it runs. Needs `@track`.
[Read more](progress.md)

**Workflows.** When a run is part of a chain, group or chord, its page shows
the whole workflow as a tree, so you can see which step failed.
In the dashboard: the **Workflow** card on a run's page.
[Read more](dashboard.md#workflow-card)

**Live updates.** The task list and run pages update by themselves within
about a second. The **Live** badge in the header shows the connection is up.
Nothing to set up. [Read more](dashboard.md#live-updates)

## Act on tasks

**Start a task.** Pick any registered task, fill in its arguments (defaults
are prefilled from the function), and optionally choose a queue or a delay.
In the dashboard: **Start task** on the task list.
[Read more](dashboard.md#start-task)

**Cancel or terminate.** Cancel stops a run that hasn't started yet.
Terminate also kills one that is already running.
In the dashboard: the buttons on a run's page.

**Retry.** Run a failed task again with the same arguments, or use
**Retry with changes** to edit them first. Select several failed runs to
retry them together.

**Dead letters.** Runs that failed after their last retry, in one list,
grouped by task and exception. Fix the arguments and run one or many again.
[Read more](dead-letters.md)

**Bulk cancel.** Cancel the runs you've selected, or every waiting or
running task that matches your current filters. You see the count before
you confirm. [Read more](queues.md#bulk-cancel)

## Control periodic tasks (beat schedules)

All of these need `@track` on the task. celery-manager doesn't change your
beat schedule: beat still sends the task, and `@track` makes it skip. Run
beat with `-S celery_manager.beat:Scheduler` so each firing carries its
scheduled time and a skip applies only to that firing.

**Skip one upcoming run.** Open a schedule to see its next runs, and skip or
cancel just one of them. The rest of the schedule carries on as normal.
This is what celery-manager was built for.
In the dashboard: **Schedules**, then a schedule's name.
[Read more](dashboard.md#schedule-occurrences-future-schedule-view)

**Pause a whole schedule.** Stop a schedule from running until you resume
it, or until a time you choose (1 hour, tomorrow 9:00, or a custom time).
Resuming picks up from now: it doesn't catch up on the runs it missed.
In the dashboard: **Pause schedule** on the Schedules page.
[Read more](dashboard.md#pausing-a-whole-schedule)

**Edit a schedule.** Change a schedule's crontab or interval from the
dashboard, see its next five runs before you save, and revert to the
schedule in your code at any time. Needs beat to run
`celery_manager.beat:DatabaseScheduler` and `schedule_editing=True`.
In the dashboard: **Edit schedule** on a schedule's page.
[Read more](schedules.md)

**Maintenance windows.** Skip chosen schedules, or all of them, on a
recurring window such as every Sunday from 02:00 for two hours, in any
timezone. Runs inside the window are recorded as skipped with the reason;
there is nothing to resume afterwards.
In the dashboard: **Schedules**, under the schedule list.
[Read more](schedules.md#maintenance-windows)

**Missed runs.** A scheduled run that was due but never arrived (beat was
down, the message was lost) is listed on the schedule's page and counted on
the schedule list, instead of going unnoticed.
In the dashboard: **Schedules**, then a schedule's name.
[Read more](decorator.md#missed-run-detection)

## Understand trends and failures

**Insights.** How many runs, how many succeeded, and how long they take
(median and p95), over the last hour, day, week or month.
In the dashboard: **Insights**. [Read more](insights.md)

**A page per task.** The same numbers and charts for one task, plus its
recent runs and most common errors.
In the dashboard: click a task name in Insights or on a run's page.
[Read more](insights.md#task-page)

**Grouped failures.** Failures with the same cause are grouped together,
even when the messages differ slightly (an ID or a number), so a flood of
errors shows up as one problem. Retry a whole group at once.
In the dashboard: **Insights**, then **Failures**.
[Read more](insights.md#failures)

## Run your workers and queues

**Workers.** Every worker that is online: what it's running now, how many
tasks it has processed, and which queues it reads from. From here you can
shut a worker down, add or remove a pool process, and start or stop
reading from a queue.
In the dashboard: **Workers**. [Read more](workers.md)

**Rate limits.** Change how often a task may start, on the running workers,
without a deploy. The change lasts until a worker restarts.
In the dashboard: the **Rate limits** table on the Workers page.
[Read more](workers.md#runtime-rate-limits)

**Queues.** How many messages are waiting in each queue right now, and how
many workers read from it.
In the dashboard: **Queues**. [Read more](queues.md)

**Purge a queue.** Delete every waiting message in one queue. You type the
queue name to confirm. [Read more](queues.md#purging-a-queue)

**Data retention.** Delete runs and their logs after a number of days you
choose, per task, so the database does not grow forever. Off until you set
it. In the dashboard: **Settings**. [Read more](retention.md)

**Metrics.** A `/metrics` endpoint in the Prometheus format, with run counts,
runtimes, failure ratios, queue depth, workers online and missed runs, plus an
optional OpenTelemetry export. Protected by a token you choose.
[Read more](metrics.md)
## Know when something goes wrong

**Alerts.** A message to Slack, a webhook or email when a task's failure
rate jumps, a queue backs up, a worker goes offline, or a periodic task
misses its run. Rules are set per task, queue, worker or schedule (or a
pattern), with a quiet period so one incident sends one message, and a
"resolved" message when it's over.
In the dashboard: **Alerts**. [Read more](alerts.md)

## Share and keep what you find

**Links to a view.** Your filters are part of the page address, so
**Copy link** gives a teammate exactly what you're looking at.

**Saved views.** Save a set of filters under a name and come back to it
later. Saved in your browser. [Read more](dashboard.md#saved-views)

**Export.** Download every run that matches your filters as CSV or JSON.
[Read more](dashboard.md#export)

**Audit log.** Every action taken from the dashboard (cancel, retry, pause,
purge, start, and so on) with who did it and when.
In the dashboard: **Audit log**. [Read more](dashboard.md#audit-log)

## Set it up your way

**Works with your framework.** Mount the dashboard into a FastAPI, Flask or
Django project, or run it on its own. [Read more](integrations.md)

**Any database.** SQLite by default, or PostgreSQL, MySQL and anything else
SQLAlchemy supports, through `db_url`.
[Read more](configuration.md#db_url-backend-notes)

**Upgrades handle themselves.** When a new version changes the database,
it updates the tables when it starts. If you'd rather do that as a deploy
step, run `celery-manager migrate`.
[Read more](configuration.md#schema-and-upgrades)

**Sign-in.** Dashboard users with hashed passwords and session cookies.
There is no default account: you create the first one yourself.
[Read more](quickstart.md#create-your-first-dashboard-user)

**Sign in with your app's users.** Mounted in Django, Flask or FastAPI, the
dashboard can let your app's own users in and take their role from your app
(Django staff and superusers out of the box), with no second set of accounts.
[Read more](integrations.md#sign-in-with-your-apps-users)

**Roles.** Give each account `viewer` (look, don't touch), `operator`
(retry, cancel, pause, worker controls) or `admin` (also purge queues,
shut down workers, change branding). The server enforces it; the dashboard
hides what you can't use.
[Read more](roles.md)

**Manage users in the dashboard.** Admins add accounts, change roles, reset
passwords and delete accounts from the **Users** page; everyone can change
their own password. A password change signs that account out everywhere
else. [Read more](roles.md#from-the-dashboard)

**Themes and branding.** Light, dark or follow the system, chosen per
browser. Set the product name, accent colour and logo once for everyone.
In the dashboard: **Settings**.
[Read more](dashboard.md#appearance-and-branding)

**A REST API for everything.** Every action in the dashboard is also an API
call, so you can script it. [Read more](rest-api.md)


<!-- docs/choosing.md -->

# Is celery-manager the right tool?

## Decision guide

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| A live view of workers and tasks, nothing stored, no accounts | **Flower**. celery-manager can replace it, but Flower is lighter for that alone. |
| Durable run history, failure inbox, retry from a UI, audit log, roles, SSO | **celery-manager** |
| Pause or skip *one* future occurrence of a periodic task without editing beat | **celery-manager** (no other Celery tool does this) |
| Edit beat schedules from a UI | django-celery-beat admin, RedBeat tooling, or celery-manager (which wraps those backends and adds audit, preview and pause) |
| Know when a scheduled job did not run, without self-hosting | **Sentry Crons / Healthchecks.io / Cronitor**. celery-manager detects missed runs and beat outages itself, and can also ping one of those services as an [external dead-man's switch](beat-liveness.md). |
| Graphs, long-term metrics, paging | **Prometheus + Grafana** fed by celery-manager's [`/metrics`](metrics.md) and the shipped [dashboard and alert rules](metrics.md#grafana-dashboard-and-alert-rules). |
| Orchestrate DAGs, data pipelines, long workflows | **Airflow, Prefect, Temporal**. Different category. |
| Job history for arq, Dramatiq, Taskiq or a hand-written loop | celery-manager's [other-runner adapters](other-runners.md) (history, failures and alerts; Celery-only controls do not apply) |

celery-manager is a poor fit when you do not run Celery and only need a cron
log (a small table in your own app is cheaper), or when Flower plus Grafana
already answers every question your team asks.

## Quickstarts

Each recipe assumes `celery_app` is your Celery instance and `SECRET` a
private random string. Run `celery-manager create-user admin --role admin
--db-url sqlite:///cm.db` once to get a login. Workers call
`celery_manager.setup(config)` with the same `db_url` (see
[Integrating with your app](integrations.md#the-worker-beat-and-events-listener)).

### FastAPI

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from celery_manager import CeleryManagerConfig
from celery_manager.api.app import create_app

from myproject.celery import celery_app

config = CeleryManagerConfig(celery_app=celery_app, db_url="sqlite:///cm.db", secret_key=SECRET)
dashboard, _ = create_app(config)
app = FastAPI()
app.mount("/celery-manager", dashboard)   # uvicorn main:app
```

### Flask

```python
from a2wsgi import ASGIMiddleware            # pip install "celery-manager[flask]"
from flask import Flask
from werkzeug.middleware.dispatcher import DispatcherMiddleware
from celery_manager import CeleryManagerConfig
from celery_manager.api.app import create_app

config = CeleryManagerConfig(celery_app=celery_app, db_url="sqlite:///cm.db", secret_key=SECRET, live_stream="poll")
dashboard, _ = create_app(config)
app = Flask(__name__)
app.wsgi_app = DispatcherMiddleware(app.wsgi_app, {"/celery-manager": ASGIMiddleware(dashboard)})
```

### Django (separate process)

```python
# dashboard.py - run with: uvicorn dashboard:app --port 8001
import django, os
os.environ.setdefault("DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE", "mysite.settings")
django.setup()
from celery_manager import CeleryManagerConfig
from celery_manager.api.app import create_app
from celery_manager.integrations.django import django_authenticator
from mysite.celery import app as celery_app

config = CeleryManagerConfig(celery_app=celery_app, db_url="sqlite:///cm.db", secret_key=SECRET,
                             authenticate_request=django_authenticator())
app, _ = create_app(config)
```

### Observe-only (no Celery)

```python
from celery_manager import CeleryManagerConfig, RunObserver

observer = RunObserver(CeleryManagerConfig(celery_app=None, db_url="sqlite:///cm.db"))

@observer.observe("reports.nightly")
async def nightly_report():
    ...
```

### Try it without any of that

```shell
pip install "celery-manager[standalone]"
celery-manager demo          # SQLite + seeded runs, opens http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```


<!-- docs/quickstart.md -->

# Quickstart

## Try it in one minute

```bash
pip install --pre "celery-manager[standalone]"
celery-manager demo
```

`demo` creates a SQLite database in a new temporary directory, seeds a week of
sample history (grouped failures with tracebacks, a slow task, skipped
occurrences, a running task with progress) and four periodic schedules, creates
an admin account with a random password, and serves the dashboard on
`http://127.0.0.1:8765/`. It prints the password and the directory; delete the
directory to remove everything. No broker or worker is involved, so actions that
need one (retry, revoke, purge) answer with the broker's error. Flags:
`--dir`, `--host`, `--port`, `--no-browser`.

Not sure celery-manager is what you need? See
[Is celery-manager the right tool?](choosing.md), which also has a short
quickstart per framework.

## Install

celery-manager is in beta (a pre-release on PyPI), so pass `--pre` to pip:

```bash
pip install --pre celery-manager
```

With extras:

```bash
pip install --pre "celery-manager[standalone]"   # adds uvicorn
pip install --pre "celery-manager[flask]"        # adds Flask and a2wsgi
```

Alternatively, install a tagged release straight from git (`v0.1.0a1` is a
GitHub-only pre-release; PyPI starts at `0.1.0a2`):

```bash
pip install "git+https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/celery-manager.git@v0.1.0a5"
```

(Extras with git: `"celery-manager[standalone] @
git+https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/celery-manager.git@v0.1.0a5"`.)

`uvicorn` is **not** a core dependency — celery-manager is an ASGI app, and
mounting it into a server you already run needs no server of its own. If you
want to serve the dashboard standalone (`uvicorn your_module:app`, or the
bundled demo's `run_dashboard.py`), install the `standalone` extra
(`celery-manager[standalone]`). To mount it in a Flask app, install the `flask`
extra (`celery-manager[flask]`, which adds Flask and `a2wsgi`) — see
[Integrating with your app](integrations.md#flask-wsgi).

## Wire it into your app

```python
import os

from celery_manager.config import CeleryManagerConfig
from celery_manager.api.app import create_app

config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=your_celery_app,
    db_url="sqlite:///celery_manager.db",  # or any SQLAlchemy URL
    secret_key=os.environ["CELERY_MANAGER_SECRET_KEY"],  # private + random
)
app, _ = create_app(config)
```

`secret_key` signs every session cookie, so it must be private and random —
generate one with
`python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"` and load it
from your secrets store. `create_app` raises `ValueError` and refuses to
start if it is empty or left at the `"change-me"` default.

`create_app` returns `(app, session_factory)`. The FastAPI `app` serves the
JSON API under `/api/*` and — once the frontend has been built and copied
into `src/celery_manager/dashboard/static/` — the dashboard SPA at `/` (or at
whatever prefix you [mount it under](integrations.md); the SPA uses relative
URLs).
`create_app` also runs a one-time sync of `celery_app.conf.beat_schedule`
into the `periodic_schedules` table on startup, so the dashboard's schedule
list reflects whatever periodic tasks your app has configured.

Run it with any ASGI server, e.g. `uvicorn your_module:app` (installing
the `standalone` extra above if you don't already have uvicorn).

!!! warning "Running on plain HTTP? You need `cookie_secure=False`"
    This is the single most likely thing to stop you on your first run. The
    session cookie is `Secure` by default, and a browser will accept a
    `Secure` cookie over plain HTTP but **refuse to send it back** — so you
    log in successfully and then immediately appear logged out, with nothing
    in any log to explain it.

    If you are developing against `http://localhost`, add
    `cookie_secure=False` to the config above. Leave the default alone
    anywhere reachable over anything else — see
    [Configuration](configuration.md#cookie_secure-and-why-it-defaults-to-true).

## Run the events listener

```bash
celery-manager events --celery-app your_module:your_celery_app --db-url sqlite:///celery_manager.db
```

This is a separate long-running process (alongside your worker and beat) —
it's what gives the dashboard visibility into every task, decorated or not.
It subscribes to Celery's event bus directly (no broker polling) and
upserts each task's status (`queued`, `started`, `succeeded`, `failed`,
`retried`, `revoked`) into the same database the API reads from.

`--db-url` must point at the same database as the one you pass to
`CeleryManagerConfig` in the app process. The listener takes no secret
key: it doesn't serve HTTP or sign sessions.

### Required Celery settings

The events listener only records what Celery *emits*, and Celery emits task
events only when asked. Set both of these on your Celery app (the publishing
side needs the second one, so put them in the config shared by web, worker and
beat):

```python
app.conf.worker_send_task_events = True   # same as running the worker with -E
app.conf.task_send_sent_event = True      # publisher emits task-sent (carries the queue)
```

Alternatively start the worker with `celery -A yourapp worker -E`, but
`task_send_sent_event` has no CLI flag, so it must be in the config.

Without them:

- No `-E` / `worker_send_task_events`: the listener receives nothing from the
  worker, so `worker` stays `null` and the listener contributes no
  queued/started/finished transitions or runtimes.
- No `task_send_sent_event`: `queue` stays `null` (it comes only from the
  `task-sent` event).
- Tasks decorated with [`@track`](decorator.md) still record status, timings,
  exceptions and logs from the worker process, but never `worker` or `queue`,
  and undecorated tasks are not recorded at all.

!!! warning "macOS: prefork workers"
    On macOS, a prefork worker can fail every task with
    `ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 3, got 0)`. The cause is
    an upstream Celery 5.6 / billiard 4.3 bug: billiard spawns pool children
    instead of forking them, and Celery only initialises a spawned child when
    `FORKED_BY_MULTIPROCESSING` is set. This is not caused by celery-manager.
    Workarounds: start the worker with `FORKED_BY_MULTIPROCESSING=1 celery -A yourapp worker ...`,
    or, for local development, use `--pool=threads` or `--pool=solo`.

The listener (`celery-manager events`) must run as its own long-lived process,
next to the worker and beat.

## Create your first dashboard user

```bash
celery-manager create-user admin --role admin --db-url sqlite:///celery_manager.db
```

It asks for the password twice. Use the same `--db-url` as your config.
Make the first account an `admin`: `create-user` makes `viewer` (read-only)
accounts unless you pass `--role`. See [Roles](roles.md) for what `viewer`,
`operator` and `admin` can each do.

Or from Python, with your `config` in scope:

```python
from celery_manager.auth.users import create_user
from celery_manager.db.session import init_db, get_session_factory

Session = get_session_factory(init_db(config))
create_user(Session(), "admin", "a-real-password")  # role defaults to "admin" here
```

Passwords are hashed with bcrypt before being stored; there's no
plaintext-password path anywhere in the auth code. A password must be 1 to 72
bytes when UTF-8 encoded (bcrypt's limit): `create_user` raises `ValueError` for
an empty one or a longer one rather than silently truncating it.

There is no default account and no first-run setup screen, so **the
dashboard is unusable until you run this** — it is the second thing that
stops people on a first run. The users table lives in the same `db_url` as
everything else.

Then sign in at the dashboard URL.

## Opt a task into full tracking (optional)

Every task shows up in the dashboard automatically once the events listener
is running — no code changes required. If you also want per-occurrence
schedule control (pause/cancel one future run of a periodic task) and log
capture on the task's detail page, apply `@track` above
`@app.task` — **and wire the worker process with `celery_manager.setup()`**:

```python
# myproject/tasks.py — imported by the Celery worker
import celery_manager
from celery_manager.config import CeleryManagerConfig

from myproject.celery import app

# Required: this runs in the WORKER process, which is where tracked tasks
# execute. create_app() wires the dashboard process only — without this call
# the worker's @track decorators silently do nothing.
celery_manager.setup(CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=app,
    db_url="sqlite:///celery_manager.db",  # the same DB the dashboard uses
    secret_key="a-real-secret-in-production",
))


@app.task(bind=True)
@celery_manager.track(schedule_name="send-report-every-2-hours")
def send_report(self):
    ...
```

`setup()` is idempotent, so it's safe for several task modules to call it.
See [The `@track` decorator](decorator.md) for details.

## Report live progress (optional)

Once the worker is wired, a task can publish its own progress to the
dashboard while it is still running:

```python
from celery_manager import report_progress


@app.task(bind=True)
@celery_manager.track()
def import_customers(self, rows):
    for i, row in enumerate(rows):
        handle(row)
        report_progress(i + 1, len(rows), f"row {i + 1}")
```

Database writes are throttled to one every 0.5 seconds per run, so this is
safe inside a tight loop, and the call never raises into your task. Omit
`total` for open-ended work. See [Live progress](progress.md).


<!-- docs/integrations.md -->

# Integrating with your app

`create_app(config)` returns a self-contained ASGI application (a FastAPI app)
that serves the dashboard at `/`, the REST API at `/api/*` and the live-update
stream at `/api/stream`. You can run it on its own, or **mount it under a
prefix** (say `/celery-manager`) inside the web app you already have. The
dashboard's URLs are all relative, so the same build works at the root and under
any prefix.

Runnable projects for each framework live in the repository:
[`examples/fastapi_demo`](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/celery-manager/tree/main/examples/fastapi_demo),
[`examples/flask_demo`](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/celery-manager/tree/main/examples/flask_demo) and
[`examples/django_demo`](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/celery-manager/tree/main/examples/django_demo).

!!! note "Always use the trailing slash"
    Open the dashboard at `/celery-manager/`. Its asset and API URLs are relative
    to the page, so without the slash they would resolve against the host's
    root. Starlette (so FastAPI) redirects `/celery-manager` to
    `/celery-manager/` for you; check that your own proxy or framework does too.

## FastAPI

Mount it like any other ASGI sub-application:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

from celery_manager.api.app import create_app
from celery_manager.config import CeleryManagerConfig

dashboard, _session_factory = create_app(CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=celery_app,
    db_url="sqlite:///celery_manager.db",
    secret_key=SECRET,   # a private random value, not "change-me"
))

app = FastAPI()
# ... your own routes ...
app.mount("/celery-manager", dashboard)
```

Run with `uvicorn main:app` and open `http://localhost:8000/celery-manager/`.
Your routes keep working; the mount only claims its own prefix.

`create_app()` does all of its setup immediately and registers no
startup/lifespan handlers, so it doesn't matter that a mounted sub-app's
lifespan never runs.

## Flask (WSGI)

Flask is WSGI and the dashboard is ASGI. Adapt it with
[`a2wsgi`](https://github.com/abersheeran/a2wsgi) and route the prefix with
werkzeug's `DispatcherMiddleware`:

Install the extra with `celery-manager[flask]` (see the
[Quickstart](quickstart.md#install)); it adds Flask and `a2wsgi`.

```python
from a2wsgi import ASGIMiddleware
from flask import Flask
from werkzeug.middleware.dispatcher import DispatcherMiddleware

from celery_manager.api.app import create_app

app = Flask(__name__)
dashboard, _ = create_app(config)

app.wsgi_app = DispatcherMiddleware(app.wsgi_app, {
    "/celery-manager": ASGIMiddleware(dashboard),
})
```

Serve `app` with any WSGI server (`flask run`, gunicorn, waitress). Login,
the task list and every other REST call work through the adapter.

!!! warning "Use polling through WSGI/a2wsgi"
    Set `config.live_stream = "poll"` before `create_app(config)`. The API omits
    `/api/stream` and the SPA uses polling without repeatedly opening EventSource
    connections. Long-lived SSE connections consume WSGI workers and adapters may
    not promptly notice disconnects. Keep `"sse"` for an ASGI deployment that
    supports streaming. Older demos' `without_sse` wrapper is no longer necessary
    when this option is set.

For OIDC, bridge sessions, trusted origins, frame ancestors, immediate task links
and external schedule adapters, see the [production adoption guide](production.md).

## Django

Django's WSGI `urlpatterns` can't serve an ASGI app directly. Two options:

- **Standalone process (recommended).** Run the dashboard with uvicorn next to
  your Django server, the way the bundled demo does:
  `examples/django_demo/run_dashboard.py` builds the `create_app(...)` app and
  runs it on its own port. Put it under a path of your main domain with a
  reverse proxy (below) if you don't want a second hostname.
- **In-process.** If your project serves itself over ASGI, wrap Django's ASGI
  application and the dashboard in a small dispatcher (for example a Starlette
  `Mount("/celery-manager", dashboard)` next to `Mount("/", django_asgi_app)`).
  On plain WSGI the Flask recipe above (`a2wsgi` + `DispatcherMiddleware`) works
  with the same SSE caveat.

## The worker, beat and events listener

Mounting only affects the web process. The rest of the setup is unchanged
and each process must use the **same `db_url`**:

| Process | Command | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Web | `uvicorn main:app` / `flask run` | Calls `create_app()`; needs the real `secret_key`. |
| Worker | `celery -A yourapp worker` | Must call `celery_manager.setup(config)` at import time of the module that defines your tasks, or `@track` silently does nothing. Needs no `secret_key`. |
| Beat | `celery -A yourapp beat -S celery_manager.beat:Scheduler` | Only if you have periodic tasks. The scheduler stamps each firing so a skip applies to exactly that run; see [How the skip/cancel check works](decorator.md#how-the-skipcancel-check-works). |
| Events listener | `celery-manager events --celery-app yourapp:app --db-url sqlite:///celery_manager.db` | Records every task, including undecorated ones, and the queued/started transitions. |

```python
# tasks.py (imported by the worker)
import celery_manager
from celery_manager.config import CeleryManagerConfig

celery_manager.setup(CeleryManagerConfig(celery_app=app, db_url=DB_URL))
```

The events listener needs Celery task events switched on; see
[Required Celery settings](quickstart.md#required-celery-settings).

Create a dashboard user with `celery-manager create-user NAME --role admin --db-url ...`
or `celery_manager.auth.users.create_user`; both demos include a `create_user.py`
script. Or skip separate accounts altogether and let people sign in with your app's
own users: see the next section.

## Sign in with your app's users

Instead of keeping a second set of accounts, the dashboard can ask your Django,
Flask or FastAPI app who a request belongs to, and which [role](roles.md) they get.
Set `authenticate_request` on the config to a function that takes the Starlette
`Request` and returns an `ExternalUser(username, role)`, or `None` when the request
isn't signed in to your app:

```python
from celery_manager.integrations import ExternalUser

def authenticate(request) -> ExternalUser | None:
    user = my_app_user_from(request)          # your cookie or token, your user table
    if user is None:
        return None                           # not signed in to my app
    return ExternalUser(username=user.email, role=role_for(user))

config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    ...,
    authenticate_request=authenticate,
    login_url="/login?next={next}",           # where "Sign in with ..." goes
    logout_url="/logout",                     # where "Sign out" goes
    login_provider_name="Acme",               # "Sign in with Acme"
    local_login_enabled=False,                # optional: no dashboard passwords at all
)
```

Ready-made authenticators for Django and Flask are below. For FastAPI you write the
function yourself, usually a few lines around the code you already use to check a
user.

### How a request is signed in

On **every** request, in this order:

1. **Your app is asked first.** If it returns an `ExternalUser`, that is who the
   request belongs to, even if the browser also has an older dashboard session for a
   local account.
    - `role` is `"viewer"`, `"operator"` or `"admin"`: signed in with that role.
    - `role` is `None`: a real user of your app who may not use the dashboard. Every
      request gets `403` and the dashboard shows a "No access" page naming the
      account. There is no fallback to a local account in the same browser.
2. **It returned `None`** (not signed in to your app): the dashboard's own accounts
   and `cm_session` cookie are tried, as before. With `local_login_enabled=False`
   that step is skipped and the request is a `401`.

Because the role comes from your app on each request, demoting someone, removing
their access or deactivating them in your app applies on their next request.

**It fails closed.** A role that isn't one of the three (a typo such as `"Admin"`,
a role from your own app such as `"superuser"`), anything that isn't an
`ExternalUser`, an empty or over-long username, or an exception from your function
is a `500` with the reason in the server log ("authenticate_request returned role
'superuser' for 'dana' ..."). It is never turned into access, and never into "not
signed in", which would hide the bug behind the login page. An `HTTPException`
raised by your function (say, a dependency that raises its own `401`) is passed
through unchanged.

Your function runs in FastAPI's worker threadpool, so it may block: a database query
or an ORM call is fine. An `async def` function works too. It is called once per
request, so keep it as cheap as your app's own per-request user lookup.

The dashboard reports where the account came from: `GET /api/whoami` returns
`"source": "external"` for your app's users and `"local"` for its own accounts.

### Django

```python
from celery_manager.integrations.django import django_authenticator

config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=celery_app,
    db_url=settings.CELERY_MANAGER_DB_URL,
    secret_key=settings.CELERY_MANAGER_SECRET_KEY,
    authenticate_request=django_authenticator(),
    login_url="/admin/login/?next={next}",
    login_provider_name="the Django admin",
)
```

It reads Django's session cookie (`SESSION_COOKIE_NAME`, `sessionid` by default),
loads the session with your `SESSION_ENGINE` and the user with the backend that
signed them in, and checks the session's auth hash the way `django.contrib.auth`
does, so changing a password in Django ends their dashboard access too. Inactive
users get no access. It only ever reads the session: it never re-keys or flushes it,
since a changed session cookie can't be delivered from the dashboard's response and
would sign the person out of your Django site.

Requirements:

- **Django must be set up in the dashboard's process** with the same settings
  (database, `SECRET_KEY`, session engine): mount the dashboard in your ASGI
  application, or call `django.setup()` before `create_app()` the way
  `examples/django_demo/run_dashboard.py` does.
- **The browser must send Django's cookie to the dashboard**, which it does when
  both are served under the same host name: mounted in the same app, or behind one
  reverse proxy. Cookies don't depend on the port, so `localhost:8000` (Django) and
  `localhost:8001` (the dashboard) share them in development.

**Roles.** By default superusers are `admin`, other staff (`is_staff`) are `operator`,
and everyone else has no access. To use permissions instead, define them on any
model of yours and use `permission_roles`; each user gets the highest role they hold
a permission for, directly or through a group:

```python
from celery_manager.integrations.django import django_authenticator, permission_roles

class OpsSettings(models.Model):          # any model works; this one can be empty
    class Meta:
        permissions = [
            ("celery_manager_admin", "Can administer celery-manager"),
            ("celery_manager_operate", "Can operate celery-manager"),
            ("celery_manager_view", "Can view celery-manager"),
        ]

authenticate_request = django_authenticator(
    role_for=permission_roles(
        admin="ops.celery_manager_admin",
        operator="ops.celery_manager_operate",
        viewer="ops.celery_manager_view",
    ),
)
```

Active superusers hold every permission, so they are always admins under this
mapping. Any other rule is a function of the user, for example by group:

```python
def role_for(user):
    groups = set(user.groups.values_list("name", flat=True))
    if "SRE" in groups:
        return "admin"
    if "Support" in groups:
        return "viewer"
    return None

authenticate_request = django_authenticator(role_for=role_for, username_for=lambda u: u.email)
```

**Signing out.** Django's `LogoutView` accepts only `POST` (since Django 5.0), and the
dashboard's sign-out is a plain link, so point `logout_url` at a page of yours that
has a sign-out button, or at a small view that logs out on `GET`. Without a
`logout_url`, people signed in through Django get no sign-out item in the dashboard.

### Flask

For the dashboard mounted in your Flask process (a2wsgi + `DispatcherMiddleware`, as
in [Flask (WSGI)](#flask-wsgi)), where the browser sends Flask's session cookie with
every dashboard request:

```python
from celery_manager.integrations.flask import flask_authenticator

app = Flask(__name__)
app.config["SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE"] = "Lax"

@login_manager.user_loader
def load_user(user_id):
    return db.session.get(User, int(user_id))

dashboard, _ = create_app(CeleryManagerConfig(
    ...,
    authenticate_request=flask_authenticator(
        app,
        load_user=load_user,
        role_for=lambda user: {"sre": "admin", "dev": "operator"}.get(user.team),
    ),
    login_url="/login?next={next}",
    logout_url="/logout",
))
app.wsgi_app = DispatcherMiddleware(app.wsgi_app, {"/celery-manager": ASGIMiddleware(dashboard)})
```

It opens Flask's session through your app's own session interface (so the cookie's
signature is checked with your `SECRET_KEY`, and a server-side session extension
works the same way), takes the user id from `session["_user_id"]` (where Flask-Login
keeps it; change it with `user_id_key=`), and calls your `load_user` inside a request
context of your app, so `db.session` and other extensions work there. `role_for` is
required, since Flask has no built-in notion of staff. The username shown and
audited is the user's `username`, else `email`, else `get_id()`; pass
`username_for=` to choose. Users with `is_active = False` get no access.

Flask-Login's "remember me" cookie is not used: restoring a session from it means
writing a new session cookie, which only your app's response can do. Someone signed
in only by that cookie is sent to `login_url` and comes back with a session.

Flask doesn't set `SameSite` on its session cookie unless you do. The helper logs a
warning if `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` is unset; see [Security notes](#security-notes)
for why the dashboard is still protected and why you should set it anyway.

### FastAPI and Starlette

There is no single way FastAPI apps sign people in, so you write the function. Reuse
whatever your own routes use to find the user:

```python
from celery_manager.integrations import ExternalUser

def authenticate(request):
    token = request.cookies.get("access_token")
    if not token:
        return None
    claims = verify_jwt(token)                 # your own verification
    if claims is None:
        return None
    role = {"platform": "admin", "oncall": "operator"}.get(claims.get("team"))
    return ExternalUser(username=claims["sub"], role=role)

dashboard, _ = create_app(CeleryManagerConfig(
    ...,
    authenticate_request=authenticate,
    login_url="/login?next={next}",
))
app.mount("/celery-manager", dashboard)
```

An `async def` function is fine, for an async database or token service. Reading an
`Authorization: Bearer ...` header works too, for scripts calling the
[REST API](rest-api.md); a bearer header isn't sent by the browser on its own, so it
can't be used for cross-site request forgery.

### Sign-in screen and sign-out

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `login_url` | `None` | Where "Sign in with ..." links to. `{next}` is replaced with the dashboard's own address (URL-encoded), so your login page can send people back. A path (`/accounts/login/`) or an `http(s)` URL; anything else (`javascript:`, `//other-host`) makes `create_app()` refuse to start. Without it, the login screen asks people to sign in to your app and come back. |
| `logout_url` | `None` | Where "Sign out" goes for people signed in through your app (a plain link, so a `GET`). The dashboard clears its own cookie first. Without it they get no sign-out item: clearing only the dashboard's cookie would not sign them out of your app. |
| `login_provider_name` | `"your app"` | What the screens call your app: "Sign in with Acme". |
| `local_login_enabled` | `True` | `False` makes your app the only way in: the password form is replaced by the "Sign in with ..." link, `POST /api/auth/login` is refused with `403`, and existing dashboard sessions stop working. `create_app()` refuses `False` without an `authenticate_request`. |

With local login on, the login screen shows the password form and, if `login_url` is
set, a "Sign in with ..." link under it. Keeping one local admin account is a good
break-glass for when your app's sign-in is down.

People signed in through your app have no password here: the dashboard hides
**Change password** for them and `POST /api/me/password` answers `409`. The
[Users page](roles.md#managing-accounts) still manages local accounts and is titled
**Local accounts** while an authenticator is configured. Your app's users are not
listed there, because their roles live in your app.

### Security notes

- **Cross-site request forgery is still blocked.** The dashboard's CSRF defence is the
  `Origin` check on every `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` (see
  [REST API: auth](rest-api.md#auth)). It runs before any sign-in check and doesn't
  depend on which cookie would have signed the request in, so a request from another
  site, or from a sibling subdomain, is refused with `403` before your authenticator
  is even called. That matters because your app's cookie may be weaker than the
  dashboard's own: `cm_session` is always `SameSite=Lax`, Django's `sessionid` is `Lax`
  by default, but Flask's session cookie has no `SameSite` unless you set
  `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE`. Every current browser sends `Origin` on cross-origin
  writes, so the check holds regardless; set `SameSite=Lax` on your own cookie anyway,
  as the second layer `cm_session` has. Your app's own CSRF middleware (Django's
  `CsrfViewMiddleware`, Flask-WTF) does not cover the mounted dashboard, and doesn't
  need to.
- **Your app's session is now a dashboard credential.** Anything that can steal or
  ride your app's session (an XSS hole anywhere on the same host) can use the
  dashboard with that user's role. Give dashboard roles to the accounts you would trust
  with them, not to every signed-in customer: the default Django mapping admits staff
  only, and `None` is always "no access".
- **The audit log records the username your function returns**, as is, the same as
  for a local account. Choose a username people recognise (an email address is
  unambiguous). If you keep local accounts too, don't give them names your app's
  users have, or the audit log can't tell the two apart.
- **The dashboard never writes to your app's session.** The helpers only read it, so
  signing in to the dashboard can't sign anyone out of your app or extend their
  session.

## Cookies, `cookie_secure` and the mount prefix

The session cookie is named `cm_session` (not `session`, so it doesn't collide
with Flask's or Starlette's own) and is scoped to the mount prefix: its `Path`
is the ASGI `root_path`, so the browser doesn't send it to the rest of your app.

`cookie_secure=True` (the default) marks the cookie `Secure`, so the browser only
sends it over HTTPS. Behind TLS, leave it alone. For local plain-HTTP
development, set `cookie_secure=False` (see
[Configuration](configuration.md#cookie_secure-and-why-it-defaults-to-true)),
otherwise login appears to succeed and the next request is unauthenticated.

## Behind a reverse proxy

To serve the dashboard from its own process under a path of your main site,
have the proxy strip the prefix and tell uvicorn what it was:

```bash
uvicorn yourmodule:dashboard --port 8001 --root-path /celery-manager
```

```nginx
location = /celery-manager { return 308 /celery-manager/; }
location /celery-manager/ {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8001/;   # trailing slash strips the prefix
    proxy_set_header Host $http_host;              # $host would drop a non-default port
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $http_host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    # SSE: don't buffer the stream, and allow long-lived connections
    proxy_buffering off;
    proxy_read_timeout 1h;
}
```

`--root-path` is what scopes the session cookie to `/celery-manager`. State-changing
requests carry a CSRF `Origin` check against the request's host: make sure the
proxy passes the original public `host:port` in `Host` and/or `X-Forwarded-Host`
(as above). Use `$http_host`, not `$host`: nginx's `$host` drops the port, so on
a public URL such as `https://ops.example.com:8443` the browser's `Origin` would
no longer match.

!!! warning "Troubleshooting: login returns 403 `cross-origin request refused`"
    The proxy is rewriting `Host` (to the upstream address, or to a name
    without the port). Make `Host` or `X-Forwarded-Host` carry the public
    `host:port` the browser used, as in the config above.


<!-- docs/deployment.md -->

# Deployment

celery-manager is several small processes that share one database and one
configuration. This page is the checklist; the details live in the pages it
links to.

## Process layout

| Process | Command | Count |
|---|---|---|
| Dashboard and API | `uvicorn your_module:app` (or mounted in your ASGI/WSGI app) | one or more |
| Celery worker | `celery -A your_module worker -E` | as many as you need |
| Beat | `celery -A your_module beat -S celery_manager.beat:Scheduler` | exactly one |
| Events listener | `celery-manager events --celery-app your_module:app --db-url ...` | one |
| Migrate (deploy step) | `celery-manager migrate --db-url ...` | once per release |

Every process must build the same `CeleryManagerConfig` (same `db_url`, same
`db_schema`). Only the dashboard process needs `secret_key`.

A complete Compose file with all of these, PostgreSQL and Redis is in
[`examples/docker/`](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/celery-manager/tree/main/examples/docker).

## Checklist

1. **Database.** Use PostgreSQL or MySQL for anything beyond a single machine.
   SQLite is for development and the demo.
2. **Migrations.** Run `celery-manager migrate` as a deploy step and start the
   long-running processes with `auto_migrate=False`. See
   [Schema and upgrades](configuration.md#schema-and-upgrades).
3. **Secrets.** Set a long random `secret_key` from your secret store. See
   [`secret_key` in production](configuration.md#secret_key-in-production).
4. **HTTPS.** Serve the dashboard over HTTPS and keep `cookie_secure=True`.
5. **Accounts.** There is no default account: run
   `celery-manager create-user admin --role admin --db-url ...`.
6. **Celery settings.** Enable task events (`worker_send_task_events`,
   `task_send_sent_event`). `celery-manager doctor` is a read-only preflight
   that reports what is missing.
7. **One beat.** Run exactly one beat with the celery-manager scheduler.
8. **Retention.** Set retention rules and run `celery-manager prune` on a
   schedule; see [Data retention](retention.md).
9. **Network.** Keep the dashboard on a private network or behind your
   identity-aware proxy; see [Security](security.md).

## Health and monitoring

Run `celery-manager doctor` after each deploy. For metrics and alerting, see
[Metrics](metrics.md), [Alerts](alerts.md) and [Beat liveness](beat-liveness.md).
Production specifics (external schedulers, OIDC, storage isolation) are in
[Production adoption](production.md).


<!-- docs/upgrading.md -->

# Upgrading

celery-manager is in beta (a pre-release on PyPI), so pass `--pre` to pip and read the
[Changelog](changelog.md) before moving between versions. APIs may still change
before 1.0; the [stability policy](stability.md) says what is covered.

## Standard upgrade

1. **Back up** the celery-manager database if its history matters to you.
2. **Install** the new version in every environment that runs it (dashboard,
   workers, beat, events listener):

    ```bash
    pip install --pre --upgrade celery-manager
    ```

3. **Migrate.** By default `init_db()` upgrades the schema when the first
   process starts, so a restart is enough. If you run with
   `auto_migrate=False`, run the migration as a deploy step first:

    ```bash
    celery-manager migrate --db-url "$CELERY_MANAGER_DB_URL" --check   # exit 1 if behind
    celery-manager migrate --db-url "$CELERY_MANAGER_DB_URL"
    ```

4. **Restart** all processes, then run `celery-manager doctor`.

The database user needs DDL permission when a release adds a schema revision.
Full details, including the adoption of databases created by early alphas, are in
[Schema and upgrades](configuration.md#schema-and-upgrades).

## Rolling back

Downgrades are not wrapped in a command, and an older release against a newer
schema is unsupported. Restore the backup you took in step 1 and reinstall the
previous version.

## Version notes

- **0.3:** see the [0.3 release guide](release-0.3.md). Browser sessions are
  server-side now; rotate `secret_key` on upgrade to invalidate old cookies
  (see [Browser sessions](auth-sessions.md#upgrade-compatibility)).
- Every release lists schema changes and breaking changes in the
  [Changelog](changelog.md).


<!-- docs/production.md -->

# Production adoption

The 0.2 release combines the production foundations and external scheduler
work needed to run celery-manager beside an existing deployment. Optional adapters remain opt-in. Database
and adapter CI jobs are release gates; local SQL compilation is not evidence of a
successful SQL Server deployment.

## Multiple codebases

Use a distinct database or schema for each codebase/environment. Task UUIDs,
schedule names, worker identities, retention settings and local accounts share a
storage namespace; two unrelated applications must not share that namespace.
Configure the API, workers, producers, listener and beat consistently for each app.

Several Celery apps can be configured in one Python process. Tracking, log/result
policies and progress select the owning task app's runtime using task-local context;
an unconfigured app does not inherit another app's storage. Install a producer hook
for each app. Independent services should still use separate listener deployments
and storage namespaces. Test this topology with the optional adapters and live
services before rollout.

## Safe dispatch

```python
config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=celery,
    db_url=database_url,
    secret_key=secret,
    startable_tasks={"imports.preview", "reports.generate"},
    allow_queue_override=False,
    retry_edit_args=False,
)
```

`None` permits registered user tasks; an empty collection disables dispatch through
the dashboard and API. A callable receives `(task_name, principal)` and may make a
per-user decision. Unknown names return 422; policy refusals return 403 and are
audited. Start, retries, bulk retries, failed-run reruns and schedule run-now share
the policy. A per-task Pydantic model in `args_schemas` validates bound task
arguments strictly before publication. The same model drives the **Run now**
dialog: when its fields are strings, numbers, booleans or string enums
(optionally nullable), the dialog shows a form for them, and
`GET /api/tasks/registered` returns the model's JSON Schema as `args_schema`.
Other shapes keep the JSON editor. Queue overrides require explicit opt-in;
failed-run reruns preserve the original queue. Manager retries and failed-run
reruns preserve the original tenant, correlation ID, operation key and approved
metadata under the current metadata policy, while recording the acting operator
as initiator. Invalid stored context fails before publication; bulk requests
validate every selected row before dispatch.

Single cancellation of an unknown task ID returns 404. An admin may deliberately
use `?force=true`. Bulk and broker-held-message controls keep their existing
semantics.

## Bounded history

Logs default to 256,000 UTF-8 bytes, including a truncation marker between the
beginning and end. Capture retains bounded buffer memory. `log_capture_level`,
`log_capture_loggers` (logger-name prefixes), `log_redactor`, and `log_capture`
control collection. The capture level filters records already emitted by the
host loggers; it does not lower their effective levels. A failed redactor withholds
the raw output. Capture is scoped
to the task's execution context and thread; logs in newly spawned threads are not
attributed to the parent task. `log_view_role` controls API access to captured logs.

Results default to 64,000 bytes (`result_max_bytes`) and can be disabled with
`store_results=False` in both workers and listener. JSON-compatible returns are
encoded as JSON; other values use a representation. Truncation is explicit and
truncated results are display text, not a JSON round-trip format. The decorator's
result takes precedence over the listener's event representation. Existing
[retention rules](retention.md) prune these fields with their task runs.

## External identity

Existing `authenticate_request` integrations continue to work. `ExternalUser` can
also carry a stable `subject`, recorded separately from display names in audits.
Providers in `principal_providers` run first, followed by `authenticate_request`,
then local cookies if local login is enabled. Only a provider returning `None`
falls through; a rejected bearer token cannot fall back to another identity.

```python
from celery_manager.auth.providers import OIDCBearerProvider

provider = OIDCBearerProvider(
    issuer="https://identity.example/tenant/v2.0",
    audience="your-application-id",
    role_map={"Celery.Admin": "admin", "Celery.Read": "viewer"},
)
config.principal_providers = (provider,)
config.local_login_enabled = False
```

Install `celery-manager[oidc]`. Issuer, audience, expiration and signatures are
validated with an explicit asymmetric algorithm allowlist. Roles require an
explicit mapping or `role_mapper(claims)`; unknown permissions grant no access.
The adapter uses cached JWKS and refreshes for a rotated key ID. It validates
bearer tokens; it does not implement an interactive OIDC redirect flow. Use the
host application's existing login flow.

For link-outs into the SPA, opt in to `session_bridge_enabled=True`. A freshly
authenticated `POST /api/auth/bridge` sets a signed dashboard cookie for
`bridge_max_age_seconds` (300 by default). It cannot renew itself. Permission
changes take effect when that short session expires; deployments requiring
immediate revocation should use the host request authenticator on every request.
`session_max_age_seconds` controls local-account sessions.

`trusted_origins` enables credentialed CORS for explicit origins. Cross-origin
cookie writes from other origins remain refused. `frame_ancestors` permits
embedding from explicit origins and removes the conflicting deny-frame header.
These are separate controls: allowing CORS does not allow framing.

## Broker dependencies

For Redis brokers, install `celery-manager[redis]` so Celery's compatible Redis
transport dependencies are installed. RabbitMQ deployments do not need that extra.
The development extra includes Redis because the broker regression tests import
its transport even when no live Redis server is configured.

## Immediate task links and WSGI

```python
from celery_manager import install_publish_hook, task_url

celery_manager.setup(config)
install_publish_hook(celery, initiator=current_person_id)
result = import_task.apply_async(kwargs={"source": "example"})
link = task_url("https://ops.example/celery-manager/", result.id)
```

The optional producer hook stamps the initiator before publication and records a
queued row after successful publication. It is process-local; install it in each
producer process. One installation per Celery app replaces its previous hook.
The hook scopes signals by the current Celery app; multi-app producers should
ensure the publishing app is current. It returns an uninstall callable. Storage
failures do not fail the host's task publication. A link that opens before a row
exists says it is waiting for a record and retries; it does not claim a nonexistent
ID is definitely queued.

Use `live_stream="poll"` with WSGI/a2wsgi. The server omits `/api/stream` and the
SPA polls without repeatedly opening EventSource connections. ASGI deployments
can keep `live_stream="sse"`.

`celery-manager events` enables worker events at startup and every 60 seconds.
Use `--no-enable-events` to opt out. The listener warns after two minutes without
a worker heartbeat. Event enabling does not turn on producer `task-sent` events;
set `task_send_sent_event=True` in producer applications for queue-wait metrics.

## External schedulers

```python
from celery_manager.schedulers import RedBeatBackend
config.scheduler_backend = RedBeatBackend(celery)
```

Install `[redbeat]` or `[django-beat]` for the corresponding backend. Static
`beat_schedule` remains the default, with read-only definitions and the existing
opt-in timing editor. `RedBeatBackend(celery)` and
`DjangoCeleryBeatBackend(celery)` own their definitions in their existing stores.
They preserve entry names and per-entry identity. Missing entries become disabled
history rows; overrides are kept.

Schedule API requests refresh a backend snapshot at most once per
`schedule_sync_interval_seconds` (30 by default). A dashboard refresh discovers
runtime changes without a restart. A backend outage returns 503 and keeps the
stored snapshot; it never disables everything as if the backend were empty.

Use the matching stamping scheduler:

| Backend | Beat scheduler |
|---|---|
| Static | `celery_manager.beat:Scheduler` |
| Static with package timing edits | `celery_manager.beat:DatabaseScheduler` |
| RedBeat | `celery_manager.beat:RedBeatScheduler` |
| Django Celery Beat | `celery_manager.beat:DjangoDatabaseScheduler` |

The existing `DatabaseScheduler` name retains its meaning. During a host migration,
`@track(schedule_from=lambda args, kw: kw.get("schedule_name"),
consume_kwargs=("schedule_name",))` can read a legacy identity kwarg and remove it
before the body runs. Stamped occurrence headers remain authoritative.

Writable backends support:

| Route | Minimum role |
|---|---|
| `POST /api/schedules` | admin |
| `PATCH /api/schedules/{name}` | operator |
| `DELETE /api/schedules/{name}` | admin |
| `POST /api/schedules/preview` | viewer |
| `POST /api/schedules/{name}/skip-next` | operator |
| `POST /api/schedules/{name}/run-now` | operator |

CRUD is audited with before/after definitions. Static-backend CRUD returns 409.
`GET /api/schedules/backend` reports capabilities; `/api/schedules/health` reports
unregistered task references. Schedule run-now is manual and carries no occurrence
stamp, so it does not consume a scheduled skip. Create requires a registered task;
schedule dispatch options reject reserved `cm_` headers.

The backend remains the source of truth. A second package-owned schedule authority,
automatic reconciliation and restoration after Redis data loss are intentionally
not enabled by this release.

## Natural-language schedules

The default parser accepts a limited, deterministic grammar: `every N seconds`,
`every N minutes/hours/days`, `daily at HH:MM`, `weekdays at HH:MM`,
`weekends at HH:MM`, and raw five-field cron. Unsupported or impossible schedules
are rejected. The create form previews ten upcoming runs in the application
timezone before enabling save. Existing schedule edits retain their preview.

For broader language, supply a custom parser or `LLMParser(provider)`, where the
host's provider implements `complete(system, user) -> str`. Rules handle recognized
phrases first; otherwise the AI must return a JSON schedule spec. Its result goes
through the same validation. No SDK, API key or vendor is built into the package.
One expression per entry is supported. Holiday calendars and multi-expression
requests require a future scheduling model. Preview is still needed: syntax
validation cannot prove that a model understood the user's intent.

## Storage isolation and deployment

Set `db_schema="celery_manager"` on databases supporting schemas and provision that
schema before migrating. `engine_options` are passed to SQLAlchemy without mutating
shared model metadata. SQLite uses a separate database file; arbitrary SQLite
attached schemas and table prefixes are not supported. Keep API, worker, listener
and beat storage settings identical.

For deployments with multiple processes:

```sh
celery-manager migrate --db-url "$CELERY_MANAGER_DB_URL" --db-schema celery_manager
```

Then run application processes with `auto_migrate=False`. User-management and prune
commands also accept `--db-schema`. Long-running commands should load the complete
config with `--config myproject.cm:config`.

SQL Server adds a transaction-owned migration application lock and update/range
locks around task-run creation and merging. Server timestamps use UTC defaults.
SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server have dedicated CI contracts for migrations,
concurrent writers and pruning. SQL Server additionally needs ODBC Driver 18,
installed outside Python; `[mssql]` installs its Python driver only.

## Operational health

The listener persists worker online/heartbeat/offline observations. Read
`GET /api/health/workers` for last-seen status and `/api/health/runs` for possibly
stuck runs or runs associated with a lost worker. These are advisory findings;
worker loss does not prove execution stopped, so task status is never rewritten.
The initial stuck threshold is configurable through the request's `stuck_seconds`.

For beat liveness, set `app.conf.celery_manager_db_url` and, where needed,
`app.conf.celery_manager_db_schema` on a stamping scheduler. It writes a heartbeat
at most every 30 seconds and bounds sleep accordingly. It does not migrate the
database. `/api/health/beat` reports healthy, stale, or unknown when no heartbeat
has ever been recorded. This assumes one beat owner per storage namespace.

Microsoft Teams channels use Workflows webhooks with Adaptive Cards and the
existing alert incident/dedup/delivery machinery. Webhook URLs remain write-only.
Existing failure-rate, missed-run and worker-offline alerts remain available;
new health findings do not yet introduce separate alert rule kinds.


## Host-owned execution and native operations

The same 0.3 candidate also supports observation-only deployments without a
Celery application. See [real-world operations](real-world-operations.md) for
RunObserver, custom probes/outbox metrics, independent scheduler expectations,
correlation/duplicate visibility, doctor, annotations and action safeguards.
[Tenant history mode](tenancy.md) is a stricter read-only HTTP boundary, separate
from initiator filters and ordinary manager-wide roles. Monitoring storage must
still be provisioned and migrated deliberately when runtime DDL is disabled.


<!-- docs/release-0.3.md -->

# 0.3.0b1: real-codebase operations

This release focuses on SQL schedule authority, exclusion locks, individual
failure handling and operational history: the pieces that matter most when an
existing Celery deployment replaces hand-built operations code.

The interrupted implementation contained a release plan and partial grammar,
description and timezone changes. Review found that windowed hourly expressions
ignored the requested step and the initial timezone implementation did not
become due correctly. The corrected implementation has regression coverage for
actual beat due checks, UTC projection, daylight-saving transitions and pickle
round trips.

## Scheduling language and descriptions

The deterministic parser accepts weekday lists and ranges (`Mon and Thu at
06:30`, `Mon-Fri at 09:00`), reversed phrasing (`at 06:30 on Mon and Thu`), and
several daily times sharing one minute (`daily at 09:00 and 17:00`). It accepts
`every day` and the existing numbered intervals and raw five-field crons.
It refuses unsupported or ambiguous phrases rather than guessing.

Timezone names can be supplied with a crontab spec or in a phrase such as
`Mon at 06:30 in Europe/Berlin`. They must be IANA names; intervals are elapsed
durations and do not carry a timezone. The preview displays its authoritative
zone. Text requests can pass `timezone` separately. The schedule editor retains
per-entry zones; SQL-backed schedules preserve them on reload and export.
Celery remains responsible for cron's behavior at repeated or missing local
times; this release does not add holiday calendars or a custom DST policy.

An hourly window preserves its starting minute and actual hour step:
`every 2 hours between 09:30 and 17:30` runs at 09:30, 11:30, 13:30, 15:30
and 17:30. Minute windows must fit within one hour: `every 15 minutes between
09:10 and 09:40` runs at 09:10, 09:25 and 09:40. Other window shapes require
separate schedules because one cron cannot express their exact inclusive
boundaries. Several times with different minutes also need separate entries.
Always review the upcoming runs before saving.

Install `celery-manager[schedule-descriptions]` for cron-descriptor descriptions.
Without it, common times/weekday lists have deterministic descriptions and
complex expressions are displayed as cron text. The existing optional host
AI provider remains available and uses the same schedule validation.

## Durable schedules, locks and alerts

- [SQL schedules](sql-schedules.md) describes the optional SQLAlchemy scheduler,
  explicit initialization, SQL authority, dry-run adoption/repair, snapshot
  conflicts and lossless exports. No reconciliation plan deletes extra entries.
- [Singleton execution](singleton.md) documents Redis leases, key selection,
  conflicts, renewal, inspection and conditional administrative release.
  Lease loss cannot stop already-running Python side effects; idempotency
  and downstream constraints remain necessary.
- [Alert rules](alerts.md) adds individual/consecutive failures, stuck/lost,
  stale beat, SLA, runtime regression and a daily digest, including minimum
  samples and unknown-data behavior.
- [Failure inbox](dead-letters.md) adds acknowledge/ignore/reopen and review
  history. These actions never rewrite the task's execution result.
- [Beat liveness](beat-liveness.md) covers multiple owners and an external
  dead-man's-switch URL, so monitoring need not share beat's failure domain.
- [Worker history](workers.md) records deduplicated minute observations with
  bounded retention; gaps remain gaps rather than implied zero activity.
- [Browser sessions](auth-sessions.md) covers shared-database login backoff,
  individual session revocation and upgrade behavior for older cookies.
- [Embedding](embedding.md) covers `/api/v1`, OpenAPI and the status widget.

## Initiator filtering and propagation

`GET /api/tasks?started_by_me=true` matches the authenticated subject when the
host supplies one, otherwise the local username. `initiator=...` permits an
explicit exact filter. Counts, export and matching bulk cancellation share the
same filter. This is a convenience filter, not row-level access control: viewer
access still permits viewing all runs. The dashboard's filter persists in the
URL and saved views.

Dashboard dispatches and operator retries stamp their acting identity in the
message and seed it in history. With `install_publish_hook`, tasks published
inside a worker inherit that request's initiator, including ordinary chains
and group publications. Explicit message identity takes precedence; another
Celery app's current task never supplies a fallback identity. Host-side workflow
roots need the producer hook/initiator callback. The package does not infer
identity for messages published by uninstrumented code.

## Legacy pause CSV import

The CSV schema is exactly `schedule_name,paused_until`; a blank end means an
indefinite pause. Timestamps must include a timezone offset and be in the
future. All schedules must already exist. Names cannot repeat. Imports are
limited to 5,000 rows and 1 MB, validate every row before writing, and commit
all pauses and one audit entry together.

```csv
schedule_name,paused_until
nightly-import,
weekly-summary,2099-01-01T12:00:00+02:00
```

```shell
celery-manager import-pauses pauses.csv --config myproject.cm:config --actor migration-admin
# Review the dry-run output, then apply the same file:
celery-manager import-pauses pauses.csv --config myproject.cm:config --actor migration-admin --apply
```

Administrators can also POST `/api/schedules/pause-import` with
`{"csv":"schedule_name,paused_until\nnightly-import,\n","dry_run":true}`.
Only `dry_run:false` writes. This imports decorator-enforced pauses; tasks must
use `@track` and the stamping scheduler for those pauses to stop their bodies.
It does not change the scheduler backend's enabled flag.

## Drift diagnostics

`GET /api/schedules/health` reports unregistered task references, historical
entries missing from the current backend, and differences between code and
backend definitions. A backend-only definition may be intentional when SQL is
authoritative. Unsupported custom schedules make the comparison unknown.

Add `inspect_consumers=true` to request a bounded live queue-consumer broadcast.
`no_observed_consumer` means no responding worker reported that schedule's queue;
it does not prove there is no worker. A timeout or empty reply is unknown.
These diagnostics never scan arbitrary Redis keys or delete backend data.
Reconciliation plans and audit history provide the reviewable change path.

## Deliberately remaining work

The broad interrupted plan included compatibility projects that require separate
acceptance criteria. This release does not claim them as completed:

- Configurable monitoring table prefixes. Separate database schemas remain the
  supported isolation mechanism; SQLite uses separate files.
- Arbitrary orphan Redis-key discovery/deletion or transactional cross-backend
  reconciliation recovery. No automatic keyspace wipe is introduced.
- Generated SDKs, unrestricted English grammar, multiple cron expressions in
  one entry, holiday calendars or a custom repeated/missing-time policy.
- Domain-specific failure summaries. Host applications still own business
  context and downstream side-effect safety.

Database migrations now reach **0020**. 0015–0017 add failure review,
authentication state and worker samples; 0018 adds source/tenant/context and
operation/correlation identifiers; 0019 adds custom health and independent
scheduler expectations; 0020 adds operation annotations. Back up monitoring
storage and run explicit deployment migrations with a DDL credential, then
`celery-manager migrate --db-url ... --check`. `auto_migrate=False` prevents
runtime DDL; it does not provision tables. The optional SQL scheduler has its
own initialization/upgrade procedure.

## Ten native operability additions in this same release

This candidate also adds the following without changing a host application's
runner:

1. `RunObserver` records synchronous/async host jobs without a Celery app.
2. Trusted tenant resolution restricts HTTP to read-only SQL-scoped history,
   with no admin bypass for global views, events or writes.
3. Queued/started/terminal lifecycle observations expose durable background-work
   diagnostics; explicit interruption and fail-open telemetry health preserve
   host execution semantics.
4. Host-collected custom numeric probes and an outbox aggregate helper report
   depth, oldest age, exhausted retries and delivery latency.
5. Independent scheduler registrations monitor liveness and expected commands
   from the first due occurrence, without waiting for a completed historical run.
6. Tenant/request/business identifiers and bounded metadata connect observations
   and instrumented Celery publications to the host.
7. Operation-key and correlation matching reveal related attempts without
   preventing duplicates or claiming exactly-once side effects.
8. Read-only doctor/preflight checks storage and configuration, with explicit
   CLI/Python opt-ins for outbound broker/worker checks.
9. Environment-scoped deployment and planned-maintenance annotations provide
   context without automatically pausing jobs or suppressing alerts.
10. Sensitive HTTP actions can require audited reasons and exact environment
    confirmation in addition to the existing role/task policies.

See [real-world operations](real-world-operations.md) for exact signatures,
configuration, lifecycle/privacy contracts and examples, and
[tenant security](tenancy.md) for the restricted-mode boundary. The Operations
page displays stored probe/scheduler health, annotation history and admin
preflight. Task detail shows observation source/context, same-tenant related
attempts, and the deployment/maintenance context at the run's start or send time
outside tenant mode. External observations cannot be retried or cancelled through Celery
controls. These are package-native features; no host application's execution,
outbox schema or migration policy is silently rewritten.

## Verification status for the expanded candidate

Local verification for the expanded candidate on 2026-10-30:

- The final broad Python regression sweep passed **1,542 tests**. Thirty optional/service
  tests skipped locally; four socket-server notification tests and the
  socket-server RabbitMQ module were excluded because this environment cannot
  bind local test servers. The 19 RabbitMQ cases that do not require a server
  passed separately.
- All 13 frontend behavior tests passed. Frontend lint and production build
  passed, and the packaged static assets match the generated bundle exactly.
- Ruff, whitespace checks and the strict documentation build passed.
- Wheel and source distributions built successfully and passed strict Twine
  metadata checks. An isolated installation of the built wheel passed native
  lifecycle/concurrency, exact Unicode identity, health/scheduler, tenant API,
  dashboard assets, doctor and migration 0014→0020→0014→0020 smoke checks.
- A final 16-test native-observation regression run also covers refusing a
  database collation alias of an existing external attempt ID.

These are local test results, not a certification of a live host deployment.

Live PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQL Server storage, optional scheduler contracts, real
broker/Redis behavior, supported Python interpreter runs and a host-application
trial remain acceptance gates unless explicitly recorded as executed. A
configured CI service is not evidence of a passing live test; mocked browser
checks do not establish end-to-end backend behavior. Publishing remains downstream of successful main CI; a local merge does not
publish a package.


<!-- docs/real-world-operations.md -->

# Observe real application work

This guide covers ten operating capabilities added to the same 0.3.0b1 release:
non-Celery observations, tenant isolation, durable lifecycle diagnostics, custom
probes/outbox measurements, independent scheduler expectations, correlation,
duplicate visibility, preflight, operational annotations and sensitive-action
preconditions. They observe and protect existing execution paths. They do not
install a new executor, delivery engine or business workflow.

## Observe host-owned work

`RunObserver` works without a Celery application. The host keeps its current
async job runner, queue consumer or scheduler and wraps the work it already calls.

```python
from celery_manager import CeleryManagerConfig, RunObserver, current_run

config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=None,
    db_url="postgresql+psycopg://monitor:...@db/observations",
    db_schema="job_monitoring",
    auto_migrate=False,
    secret_key="load-a-private-dashboard-key-from-the-environment",
)
observer = RunObserver(config)

@observer.observe("import.customers")
async def import_customers(batch):
    # This function is still invoked and scheduled by the host application.
    await existing_import(batch)

async def handle_request(batch, tenant_id, request_id):
    async with observer.context(
        tenant_id=tenant_id,
        correlation_id=request_id,
        metadata={"integration": "crm", "request_id": request_id},
    ):
        await import_customers(batch)
```

Provision the monitoring schema and deploy its migrations with a separate DDL
credential before running this example. `auto_migrate=False` prevents runtime
migration attempts; it does not create missing tables. Omitting it retains the
package's normal automatic-migration behavior. `RunObserver` construction performs
no database work; persistence initializes lazily on the first operation. A
monitoring-only dashboard uses the same `config` with
`create_app(config)` imported from `celery_manager.api.app`.
It presents observations and supported monitoring/operations views, while Celery
broker, worker and scheduling controls are unavailable.

`observer.observe(name, *, run_id=None, tenant_id=..., context=None,
operation_key=None, correlation_id=..., outcome=None)` returns a handle that is
both a context manager and a decorator. Synchronous and asynchronous functions,
`with` and `async with` are supported. `observer.context(...)` is also synchronous
or asynchronous; nested contexts merge metadata and restore previous context on
exit. `current_run()` returns the active handle in the current thread/async task,
or `None` outside an observed body. It does not create a new execution.

A reusable decorator creates a new run identity on every invocation, including
concurrent calls. It rejects an explicit `run_id`; use a context manager or manual
handle when the host already has an attempt ID:

```python
async with observer.observe(
```
