An invalid spec raises `celery_manager.schedule_specs.ScheduleSpecError`.
For the schedule in force (edit or code), use
`celery_manager.control.schedules.effective_schedule(session, name, entry)`.

## Maintenance windows

A maintenance window skips chosen schedules on a weekly recurrence, for
example every Sunday from 02:00 to 04:00, and ends by itself: nothing is
paused, so there is nothing to resume. Beat keeps sending; each firing due
inside an enabled window is recorded as `skipped` and the task body does not
run, exactly like a [pause](rest-api.md#pausing-a-whole-schedule). The run's
detail shows why: `Skipped: maintenance window: Sunday patching`.

Manage windows on the **Schedules** page, under the table. Anyone signed in can
see them; operators can create, edit and delete them (each change is in the
audit log). A window has:

- **Days** of the week, a **start time** and a **duration**. It can cross
  midnight (Saturday 23:00 for 3 hours covers early Sunday), and can last up
  to a week.
- A **timezone**, an IANA name such as `Europe/Berlin`. It defaults to the
  Celery app's `timezone` setting, or `UTC` if that is unset.
- **Applies to**: all schedules, or the ones you pick.
- **Enabled**: a disabled window is kept but ignored.

The dialog previews the next five windows as you type.

How a firing is judged:

- By the time it was *due*, not when a worker picked it up. With beat running
  `celery_manager.beat:Scheduler` that is the stamped occurrence time; without
  it, the time the task starts.
- The start is inclusive and the end exclusive, so a run due exactly at 04:00
  runs under a window that ends at 04:00.
- Windows follow their timezone's daylight saving changes. The duration is real
  elapsed time, so a window that spans a clock change is an hour longer or
  shorter on the wall clock. A start time that does not exist on a
  spring-forward day (02:30 when the clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00) begins
  when the clocks reach it; an ambiguous one on a fall-back day uses the first.
- Edits and deletions apply from the next firing. Firings already skipped stay
  skipped; nothing is caught up afterwards.
- If the schedule is also paused, or the occurrence was skipped by an operator,
  that reason is the one recorded.

Upcoming runs on a schedule's page are marked **Maintenance window: name**
before they happen, and the schedule list shows a chip with the window's name
(highlighted while it is in progress). [Missed-run
detection](decorator.md#missed-run-detection) is unaffected: a run skipped by a
window counts as arrived, because the decorator still records it.

The decorator must be configured in the worker process (`celery_manager.setup`),
as for pausing; windows are read from the same database.

```python
from celery_manager.control.maintenance import active_windows, create_window

with session_factory() as session:
    create_window(session, {
        "name": "Sunday patching", "days_of_week": [6], "start_time": "02:00",
        "duration_minutes": 120, "timezone": "Europe/Berlin", "applies_to": "*",
    }, "alice")
    active_windows(session, "nightly", datetime.now(timezone.utc))
```


## Dashboard definition controls

On **Schedules**, administrators using a writable scheduler backend can choose
**New schedule**, enter its unique name and registered task name, then describe
when it runs. The description is parsed by the deterministic grammar described
above. Enter an optional IANA timezone such as `Europe/Berlin` for calendar
schedules; leave it blank to use the app timezone. Intervals are elapsed durations
and do not need a timezone. **Preview next runs** returns the normalized definition
and renders occurrences in its reported timezone. Changing the description or
zone invalidates that preview, so creation always uses the reviewed definition.

Creation accepts positional arguments as a JSON array, keyword arguments as a JSON
object, and delivery options as a JSON object. For example, arguments `[42]`,
keyword arguments `{"format":"csv"}`, and options `{"queue":"reports","priority":5}`.
Supported delivery options are `queue`, `exchange`, `routing_key`, `priority`,
`expires`, and `headers`; the server rejects unsupported keys and reserved
`cm_` headers. These values are part of the schedule definition and affect future
scheduled messages.

Operators can expand **Edit arguments and delivery options** on a writable
schedule. Saving replaces those three complete fields; omitted old keys are
removed. If a refresh discovers changed backend arguments or options, saving is
blocked until **Reload current definition** is chosen; reloading discards unsaved
form edits. This guards against an already observed stale form, not concurrent
writes that happen after the last refresh. Existing runs retain their recorded inputs. The normal **Edit schedule**
sheet supports an explicit timezone on crontabs as well as interval and cron
fields. Preview errors block saving. Static code-owned backends remain read-only
for argument and delivery-option changes.

Administrators also see **Schedule backup and reconciliation**. This provides
export, adoption, and repair with a reviewed before/after plan and explicit apply
approval. See [durable SQL schedules and ownership](sql-schedules.md) for the
workflow, supported schedules, and concurrency limits.


<!-- docs/progress.md -->

# Live progress

Celery's event stream carries lifecycle transitions — sent, started,
succeeded, failed — and nothing else. It cannot tell the dashboard that a
task is on row 412 of 10,000, because only the task itself knows that. So
celery-manager gives you one function to say it:

```python
from celery_manager import report_progress

report_progress(current, total=None, message=None)
```

Call it from *inside* your task body, as often as is natural. It writes to
the `task_runs` row for the run that is currently executing, so the number
shows up while the task is still in flight.

`celery_manager.progress.report_progress` is the same function —
`celery_manager.report_progress` is the documented public alias.

## A basic loop

```python
import celery_manager
from celery_manager import report_progress


@app.task(bind=True)
@celery_manager.track()
def import_customers(self, row_count: int = 60):
    for row in range(1, row_count + 1):
        handle_row(row)
        report_progress(row, row_count, f"row {row} of {row_count}")
    return f"imported {row_count} rows"
```

That is the whole API. There is nothing to initialize, no context object to
thread through your helpers, and no state to clean up — `@track` binds the
current run for the duration of the task body and unbinds it afterwards.

The same task exists, runnable, in the bundled Django demo as
`tasks_app.tasks.import_customers`.

## Open-ended progress: no total

Some work genuinely has no denominator — draining a queue, following a
stream, scanning until exhausted. Omit `total`:

```python
@app.task(bind=True)
@celery_manager.track()
def tail_event_stream(self, seconds: int = 30):
    seen = 0
    for _ in range(seconds):
        seen += poll_once()
        report_progress(seen, message=f"{seen} events seen")
```

`progress_total` is then stored as `null`, and there is no percentage to
compute. The dashboard shows the running count and the message rather than
inventing a progress bar it cannot honestly fill.

A `total` of `0`, a negative number, or anything that isn't int-able is
treated exactly like `None` — open-ended. celery-manager never invents a
denominator.

## The write throttle

`report_progress()` is meant to be safe inside a tight loop, and a naive
implementation inside a 100,000-row loop is 100,000 commits. So actual
database writes are throttled to **at most one per 0.5 seconds per run**;
calls that arrive inside that window are dropped, not queued.

The throttle interval is the module-level constant
`celery_manager.progress.MIN_WRITE_INTERVAL_SECONDS`. It is a plain module
attribute, **not** a field on
[`CeleryManagerConfig`](configuration.md) — an operator with an unusually
loaded database can raise it by assigning to it before tasks start:

```python
from celery_manager import progress

progress.MIN_WRITE_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 2.0
```

Two consequences worth knowing:

- **The completing call always writes.** A call where `total` is known and
  `current >= total` bypasses the throttle, because the final
  `10000 / 10000` is the update people actually look for and dropping it
  would leave every finished task displaying 99%.
- **An open-ended loop's last update can be lost.** The throttle is a
  pre-write check that never queues anything, and a `total=None` loop has no
  "completing" call to force through, so the very last
  `report_progress(seen)` before the task returns may simply be dropped. The
  row then shows a count that is a fraction of a second stale, forever. This
  is accepted: the run's terminal status is what tells you it finished.

The throttle uses a monotonic clock, so an NTP step or a DST change on a
misconfigured host can neither freeze progress for hours nor defeat the
throttle.

## Messages are sticky

Passing `message=None` — the default — leaves whatever message is already on
the row **untouched**. That is deliberate: the common shape is a caller who
sets a phase label once and then just counts.

```python
report_progress(0, len(rows), "fetching")   # message set
for i, row in enumerate(rows):
    handle(row)
    report_progress(i + 1, len(rows))       # still says "fetching"
```

To clear a message, pass an empty string — `""` is written through and
renders as no message:

```python
report_progress(i + 1, len(rows), "")
```

Messages are a one-line UI label ("row 412", "compressing"), not a log line.
Anything longer than 500 characters
(`celery_manager.progress.MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS`) is truncated rather than
rejected — a clipped label is still useful, and rejecting it would throw away
the progress numbers along with it. A non-string is coerced with `str()`.

## It never raises into your task

celery-manager is an observability layer wrapped around someone else's work,
so a progress call must never change a task's outcome. `report_progress()`
swallows everything:

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| No running task at all (called from a shell, a test, or a helper used both inside and outside a task) | Nothing recorded. One `WARNING` per process on the `celery_manager.progress` logger, then silence. |
| The process never called `celery_manager.setup(config)` | Nothing recorded, and a *separate* one-off `WARNING` that names `setup()` — this is the one you will hit on a misconfigured worker. |
| `current` is negative, or not convertible to `int` | The call is ignored silently. |
| `total` is `0`, negative, or not convertible to `int` | Treated as `None` (open-ended). |
| A database write fails | Logged by the decorator's `_persist_run`; the task's own result and exception are untouched. |

Both warnings are logged **once per process**, so a task looping a hundred
thousand times cannot flood your worker log.

!!! tip "If progress never appears, check the worker log first"
    The most common cause is the same one that silently disables `@track`:
    the **worker** process never called `celery_manager.setup(config)`. The
    dashboard process calling `create_app()` does not help — that is not
    where your tasks run. See
    [Wiring](decorator.md#wiring--the-worker-process-must-call-celery_managersetup).

## Where the progress goes

Four nullable columns on `task_runs` (`celery_manager.db.models`):

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `progress_current` | The count the task last reported. |
| `progress_total` | The denominator, or `null` for open-ended progress. |
| `progress_message` | The last message, or `null` if none was ever set. |
| `progress_updated_at` | When that write happened (UTC). |

All four are served raw — no percentage, no ETA — by both
[`GET /api/tasks`](rest-api.md#tasks) and `GET /api/tasks/{task_id}`, so the
client can decide how to render them in whatever space it has. Progress is
opt-in, so for tasks that never call `report_progress()` they are simply
`null`, which is different from `0`.

## Tasks without `@track`

`@track` is the normal path, and it is the one to prefer: it creates the
run's row up front (see
[the `started` row](decorator.md#the-started-row-written-before-your-task-body))
and knows the run's effective id even when Celery gave it none.

But `report_progress()` also works in an undecorated task. If there is no
`@track` context it falls back to `celery.current_task.request.id`, and
progress lands on whatever row exists for that uuid — or on a row it inserts
itself, seeded with the task name Celery reports and `status="started"`, if
nothing has created one yet (which is what happens when the events listener
isn't running either). Those seed values are only ever used on insert; they
can never restate a status the decorator or the listener has established.

The whole Celery lookup is guarded, so a task running outside a real Celery
context degrades to "no progress recorded", never to an exception.


<!-- docs/dashboard.md -->

# Dashboard walkthrough

The dashboard is a single-page React app served by the same FastAPI app as
the REST API — once built, its static files live at
`src/celery_manager/dashboard/static/` and are mounted at the app's root (`/` standalone, or the prefix you mount it
under; every API and asset URL is relative, so either works). It uses
`HashRouter` rather than browser history routing (the server has no
catch-all fallback route, so a real GET for e.g. `/tasks/abc` would 404
before React ever loads — routing on the URL fragment keeps every deep
link resolving to the same `/` request the server actually serves).

Every screen calls the [REST API](rest-api.md) with `credentials:
"include"` so the session cookie set at login is sent automatically (the
SSE subscription uses `withCredentials: true` for the same reason).

**There is no global `401` interceptor.** `App.tsx` calls `whoami()` exactly
once, on mount, to decide between the login screen and the app; nothing
re-checks after that. So if your session expires while a tab is open, the
next call fails *in place* — the task list shows "Couldn't load tasks.", the
settings screen shows "Your session has expired. Sign in again to save
settings." — and you stay on the screen you were on until you reload. That
is a rough edge, not a design: reloading takes you to the login screen.

## Login

The entry screen, shown when the mount-time `GET /api/whoami` comes back
unauthenticated. A simple username/password form:

- Inputs are locked (`disabled`) while a login request is in flight, so a
  slow network can't produce a double-submit.
- A failed login shows an inline error (`role="alert"`) without leaking
  whether the username or the password was wrong — both `401` cases are a
  single generic message.
- If the mount-time check fails at the network level (server unreachable,
  DNS/CORS issue), you get a distinct **"Connection problem"** screen with a
  **Retry** button *instead of* the login form — a server that isn't
  answering is a different problem from a bad password, and showing a login
  form you cannot possibly submit would be a lie. A network failure during
  an actual login attempt is likewise kept out of the "invalid credentials"
  message.

When your app signs people in (`authenticate_request`, see
[Sign in with your app's users](integrations.md#sign-in-with-your-apps-users)),
the screen adds a **Sign in with <your app>** link under the form, going to
`login_url`; with `local_login_enabled=False` that link is all it shows. Someone
your app signed in but gave no role sees a **No access** screen naming the
account instead of the form, with **Sign out of <your app>** when `logout_url`
is set. For them, the sidebar has no **Change password**, and **Sign out**
goes to `logout_url` (or is absent without one).

On success, the app switches straight to the task list; there's no
separate "remember me" control — the session cookie lasts 7 days by
default (see [Configuration](configuration.md#secret_key-in-production)).

## Navigation

A thin persistent nav bar sits above every authenticated screen: the
brand mark and wordmark on the left, then **Tasks** / **Schedules** /
**Audit Log** / **Workers** / **Settings** (`NavLink`, so the active screen is
highlighted), and a three-way **Auto / Light / Dark** theme control on the
right, and a **Sign out** button. Sign out calls `POST /api/auth/logout`,
which clears the `cm_session` cookie, and returns you to the login screen; while
the request is in flight the button reads "Signing out…", and if it fails an
error message is shown and you stay signed in. Each screen underneath still owns its own page header — the nav bar
deliberately doesn't duplicate per-screen titles or actions.

The brand mark and wordmark are whatever the deployment has been branded
with; see [Appearance and branding](#appearance-and-branding) below.

## Task list


The default screen after login (`/`), and the one that gets the most
attention. Filters live in a panel down the left; results, and everything
that describes them, live to the right.

### Filter panel

- **Search** — matches task name, task ID, and argument values, debounced
  so a re-query doesn't fire on every keystroke. It is a substring match
  over the JSON text of `args`/`kwargs`, so searching `alice` finds a run
  whose kwargs contain it; there is no way to express `kwargs.user ==
  "alice"`. See [REST API](rest-api.md#tasks).
- **Status** — `all` plus every status
  (`queued`/`started`/`succeeded`/`failed`/`retried`/`skipped`/`revoked`).
- **Group by** — nothing / status / task name / date. Grouping is done in
  the browser over the rows currently loaded, not across the whole
  history, and the group headers say so ("3 loaded" rather than a total).
- **Date range** — folded away by default, since it is the least-reached
  control. Dates are sent as UTC instants; a picked end date is widened to
  the end of that local day, so your own last day doesn't silently drop
  out of the results.
- **Active filters** appear as removable chips with a **Clear all**, and
  the same list is repeated in the "no matches" empty state — so an empty
  table tells you which filter emptied it instead of leaving you guessing.

Below roughly 1024px the panel collapses behind a **Filters** toggle
carrying a count of what's active. The collapse is `display: none` on the
rail (the markup stays mounted, so your typed filter state survives a
toggle), which is the one hiding technique that also takes the inputs out
of the tab order — a collapsed panel never leaves focusable controls
sitting invisibly behind the table.

### Results

- **"Showing 50 of 1,308 runs"** — the total reflects the filters, so it
  answers "how much is there of *this*", not "how big is the table".
- **Runtime** shows a live-ticking elapsed time for a running task and a
  final duration for a finished one.
- **Progress** — a running task that reports a *known total* via
  [`report_progress()`](progress.md) gets a bar, a percentage, its own
  message, and a projected time remaining. A task that never reports
  progress gets none of that and shows elapsed time only: a bar sitting at
  0% would read as a stuck task, so "not instrumented" never renders as 0%.
  If such a task stops reporting for a while, the row says how long it has
  been quiet and drops the estimate — extrapolating a rate that has visibly
  stopped would keep counting down as if nothing were wrong.

    **Open-ended progress is thinner here than on the detail page.** With no
    total there is no percentage and no bar, and the row shows only the
    task's `progress_message` — the raw count is not rendered in the list,
    and the "no update for …" stalled note is gated on there being a
    percentage, so it doesn't appear either. An open-ended reporter that
    passes no `message` is therefore indistinguishable in the list from one
    reporting nothing at all. The [task detail](#task-detail) page shows the
    count and the quiet time in both cases; use it when you are watching one
    open-ended run.

    A running task's percentage is capped at **99%** until it genuinely
    reports completion — rounding 0.998 up reads as a finished task that is
    somehow still working. The list and the detail page share one derivation
    (`lib/taskProgress`) so they can never quote two different percentages
    for the same run.
- **Bulk retry** — available while the `failed` filter is active. The
  selection is dropped whenever the filter, search, dates, page or mode
  change, and is separately pruned against the visible rows on every
  refresh, so a bulk retry can never act on a row you can no longer see.
- Each row links to that task's detail page.

### Filters live in the URL

The status tab, search, group-by, date range and history-mode page are all
part of the address (`#/?status=failed&q=smtp&from=2026-08-01&group=name`;
history pages add `offset=50`). Reload, back/forward and a link pasted into a
fresh tab all restore the same view. Choosing a tab, date, grouping or page
adds a history entry, so Back undoes it; typing in the search box replaces the
current entry instead, so Back is not a per-keystroke undo. Defaults are left
out of the URL, and unknown values in a hand-edited link are ignored.

**Copy link** copies the current address (it falls back to a hidden-textarea
copy where the clipboard API is unavailable) and confirms with "Link copied".

### Saved views

**Views** in the toolbar saves the current status, search, date range and
grouping under a name; picking one applies it as a single history entry.
Views can be renamed and deleted (deleting asks for confirmation). They are
stored in this browser's `localStorage` only, so they do not follow you to
another browser or profile and are not shared. If the browser refuses to store
them, the menu says so.

### Export

**Export** downloads every run matching the current filters (not just the
loaded page) as CSV or JSON, using `GET /api/tasks/export`. If the result hit
the server's row cap, the page tells you it exported the newest N of M runs.

### Live mode and history mode

The list has two modes, and it always says which one it is in.

**Live** is the default: it updates as runs change (see
[Live updates](#live-updates) below), and **Load more** widens the page up
to the API's 500-row ceiling. Every refresh re-requests the whole span you
have open rather than just the newest page, so a background refresh can
never collapse your loaded rows back to page one.

**History** is for reading further back. You get into it from **Browse all
N runs by page** under the table, or from **Browse older runs** when a live
page has hit the 500-row ceiling. It pages explicitly through the full
filtered total: a ledger above the table reads `Runs 501–550 of 1,308`, and
a pager below it reads `Page 11 of 28` between **← Newer** and **Older →**
buttons (each move scrolls you back to the top of the table). The poll is
switched off while you are in history — which is what makes offset paging
trustworthy, since rows can't shift under you between clicks; SSE events are
ignored in this mode too. The header indicator changes from a pulsing
**Live** dot to a still **Paused** one, and a bar above the table offers
**Back to live**.

### Live updates

The screen opens an SSE connection (`GET /api/stream`) on mount and
refetches when a task event arrives (in live mode only — see above), rather
than patching individual rows from the event payload. A burst of events
becomes at most one refetch a second. Events come from the database, so
writes by the separate events listener and by workers reach the list
within about a second. See
[REST API: how changes reach the stream](rest-api.md#how-changes-reach-the-stream).

The header indicator tells you whether that connection is up. **Live**
(pulsing) means it is. **Connecting** or **Reconnecting** (still) means it
isn't, and while it isn't, the list falls back to polling every 5 seconds;
it also polls while the last refresh failed. When the stream comes back the
list refetches once to catch up and the poll stops. A run's detail page
works the same way for that one run, with a 2-second fallback poll.

A refetch never replaces the rows with a spinner: only the first load shows
a full "Loading tasks…" state. A refetch you *caused* — changing a filter,
or an SSE event arriving — dims the table briefly while the new data is in
flight. The 5-second poll deliberately does not dim, since a table that
flickered every five seconds on its own would be worse than a table that
quietly updates. A failed *background* refresh shows a banner above the
still-visible rows; a failure with no rows behind it shows an error state
with **Try again**.

### Start task


The **Start task** button in the page header opens a side sheet (Escape or
**Cancel** closes it and returns focus to the button):

- A searchable picker of the tasks registered on the Celery app
  (`GET /api/tasks/registered`), each with its docstring's first line. If the
  web process hasn't imported your task modules the list may be empty or
  short; type any task name and choose **Use "name"** to dispatch it anyway.
- **Args** (JSON array) and **Kwargs** (JSON object) editors, with the task's
  signature shown and kwargs prefilled from its defaults. Invalid JSON, or the
  wrong shape (an object in Args, an array in Kwargs), shows an error under
  the field and disables the button.
- An optional **Queue**, and **Run** now, after a delay (countdown seconds) or
  at a specific time (ETA, your local time).

Submitting calls `POST /api/tasks/start` (audited) and opens the new run's
page. You can also start tasks over the [REST API](rest-api.md).

## Task detail


`/tasks/:taskId`. Shows one task run in full:

- Status badge, and a **Retry** button shown only when `status ===
  "failed"` — calls `POST /api/tasks/{task_id}/retry` and, on success,
  shows a link to the newly created run (`new_task_id`) rather than
  navigating away, so the user can compare old and new runs side by side
  if they want.
- **Retry with changes**, next to Retry on a failed run: opens the same
  editor as Start task, fixed to this run's task and prefilled with its args
  and kwargs. Submitting sends them in the body of `POST
  /api/tasks/{task_id}/retry`, records the usual retry lineage, notes the
  edit in the audit log (with the new arguments), and opens the new run. If a
  stored value can't be parsed as JSON (older listener-recorded runs keep a
  Python repr) the editor shows it as-is so you can rewrite it.
- Args and kwargs, pretty-printed as JSON (the API returns them as raw
  JSON strings; the page re-parses and re-serializes with indentation for
  display, falling back to the raw string if parsing fails).
- A **"Why it failed"** panel — exception message plus full traceback —
  shown only when the run has a recorded exception.
- A **log output** panel showing everything captured via `@track`'s log
  capture during the run (see [The decorator](decorator.md)), or an empty
  state if the task wasn't decorated or produced no output.
- A **Run** panel: for a running task, the progress bar, percentage,
  message, live elapsed time and an estimated finish; for a finished one,
  the total duration and the start/finish times. The estimate is labelled
  and prefixed as an estimate, and its projected clock time deliberately
  omits seconds — second-level precision on an extrapolation would claim
  accuracy it doesn't have. As on the task list, open-ended progress shows
  a count with no bar, and a run that has gone quiet says so and drops the
  estimate.
- An **Execution** panel: worker, queue, ETA, started, finished, runtime.
  A value that isn't recorded reads as `—` with the reason — "Still
  running", "Hasn't started yet", "No ETA set", or a plain "Not recorded"
  where nothing more specific is knowable — never as a blank cell you have
  to interpret. In practice **ETA always reads "No ETA set"**, because
  nothing in celery-manager currently writes that column; see
  [the REST API note](rest-api.md#datetimes-in-task-responses). Worker and
  queue read "Not recorded" whenever the events listener wasn't running.
- A **Retry lineage** panel, shown only when there is lineage to show: the
  run this one was retried from, and every run retried from it (there can
  be several — retrying a failed run repeatedly is normal). Each is a link,
  so the chain can be walked in both directions.

Panels are ordered for someone debugging at 2am: what broke, how far it
got and how long it took, which worker and queue, whether anyone has
already retried it, then the log, then args/kwargs as the recipe to
reproduce it.

While the run is still *active* — `queued`, `started` or `retried`, not
just running — the page listens on the live stream and refreshes itself
whenever the run changes (progress included). It stops the moment the run
reaches a terminal status, so a finished run's page isn't left listening
forever. While the stream is down it polls every 2 seconds instead. If one of those refreshes fails the page keeps the
data it has and says so ("Live updates paused… Still retrying every 2s.")
rather than blanking.


### Workflow card


When a run belongs to a chain, group or chord, the detail page shows a
**Workflow** card between the run summary and the log. It lays out every run
that shares the same root as an indented tree, exactly as Celery's
`parent_id` links them: each row has a status, the task name (a link to its
own page), and its runtime, and the run you are on is highlighted. Members of
a group are gathered under a **Group** row, and a chord's callback appears
under the parent that Celery recorded for it. A summary line counts tasks by
status ("7 tasks: 5 succeeded, 1 failed, 1 started").

Rows with children have a disclosure button (keyboard operable), and the card
has **Expand all** / **Collapse all**. Trees of more than 30 tasks start
collapsed except for the path to the current run. Very large workflows show
the first 500 runs and say so. Runs that stand alone show no card. The
lineage is captured from Celery events (`task-sent`/`task-received`) and by
`@track`, so it appears for runs seen by either.

## Schedules list


`/schedules`, and where the **Schedules** nav link lands. A card per
configured periodic schedule, backed by `GET /api/schedules`: the schedule's
name (a link into its occurrences view), the task it runs, and its
`schedule_spec` as Celery renders it (`<freq: 2.00 hours>`). A schedule with
`enabled: false` carries a **disabled** badge — though nothing sets that flag
today, so in practice every card is enabled.

The list is a pure read of the `periodic_schedules` table, which
`create_app()` syncs from `celery_app.conf.beat_schedule` **once at
startup**. A schedule added to your beat config while the dashboard process
is running will not appear until it restarts. Empty state: "No periodic
schedules configured yet."

A schedule edited from the dashboard shows the edited timing with
"Edited by *user*, *time*" beside it (hover for what the code says). See
[Editing schedules](schedules.md).

## Schedule occurrences (future-schedule view)


`/schedules/:name`. Lists the schedule's next 10 computed occurrences
(`GET /api/schedules/{name}/occurrences`) and lets a user pause one:

- Each row is in one of three states, computed client-side from the API
  response: **pending** (no override yet), **paused** (an override with
  action `skip` or `cancel` exists — both read as "a human has already
  decided this occurrence's fate"), or **resolved** (`consumed: true`,
  meaning the occurrence's scheduled time has actually passed — in
  practice every row this screen shows is still in the future, so this
  state only appears defensively, if the API were to ever return a
  consumed row).
- A **← All schedules** back link returns to the [schedules
  list](#schedules-list), which is where you arrived from.
- **Skip this run** / **Cancel this run** buttons on each non-resolved
  row call `POST /api/schedules/{name}/occurrences/pause` with that row's
  `target_time` and the chosen action. A button already matching the
  row's current action shows as pressed/labeled accordingly (e.g. "Skipped")
  rather than being hidden, so re-clicking the same action or switching to
  the other one both work as an update in place — matching the pause
  endpoint's own update-in-place idempotency (see
  [REST API: occurrence-matching nuances](rest-api.md#occurrence-matching-nuances-worth-knowing)).
  There is no "reschedule" control in the UI, and the API no longer accepts
  that action value either (it returns `422`) — the data model still has the
  column, but no reschedule behavior is implemented.
- A per-row busy/error state means one occurrence's pause request failing
  doesn't block or hide the others; a page-level success notice
  auto-dismisses after 6 seconds.

### Pausing a whole schedule

The **Schedules** list has a **Pause schedule** button on every row, and the
occurrences page has one in its header. It opens a small menu: **Pause
indefinitely**, **For 1 hour**, **Until tomorrow 9:00** (your local time), or
**Until…** with a date and time picker that must be in the future (Escape or a
click outside closes it). **Resume schedule** acts immediately. The list shows
a **Paused indefinitely** or **Paused until \<local time\>** badge with who
paused it and when, and the occurrences page shows a banner with a Resume
button and marks each upcoming run **Will be skipped**, but only the runs
before the end time of a timed pause; later ones run normally. When the time
passes the schedule resumes by itself, and the audit log records an automatic
resume. Per-occurrence skips and cancels keep their own badges and still work.

While paused, every firing is recorded as `skipped`. Limits: resuming does
not run anything immediately and does not catch up on missed firings, since
the next regular beat firing simply runs; and only `@track`-decorated tasks
are enforced. See [REST API: pausing a whole schedule](rest-api.md#pausing-a-whole-schedule).

### Interval schedules

**Interval schedules (`schedule(run_every=…)` / bare seconds / `timedelta`).** Celery beat fires these at "previous fire + interval", and beat's own record of the previous fire isn't visible to the dashboard. celery-manager therefore anchors upcoming occurrences to the schedule's most recent observed run and projects forward by the interval. With beat running `celery_manager.beat:Scheduler`, the anchor is beat's own send time for the last firing (`task_runs.beat_sent_at`), so the next occurrence shown is the one beat will stamp. Without it, the anchor is the newest `task_runs.started_at` with that `schedule_name` (including skipped runs, excluding dashboard retries), which is off by queue latency. Once the schedule has run at least once while celery-manager was recording, the times shown are stable and a skip or cancel matches the real run.

Limitations:
- Before the first observed run, occurrences are only estimates ("now + interval") and shift on every page load. A skip saved then may not match the real fire. Wait for one run before pausing interval schedules.
- Without the stamping scheduler only: ad-hoc calls (`.delay()`/`apply_async` of the same `@track`ed task outside beat) are recorded under the same schedule name and re-anchor the projection, and a task that calls `self.retry()` re-stamps the run's start time.
- Beat restarts: beat may fire an overdue entry immediately when it comes back up after downtime, which is off the projected grid until that run re-anchors it. The stamped occurrence of such a firing is the latest scheduled time that had passed.
- Each firing moves the following interval occurrences by beat's scheduling jitter (milliseconds), so occurrences further ahead are matched within `eta_tolerance_seconds`, not exactly. crontab occurrences match exactly.
- `relative=True` interval schedules aren't modelled.
- The `@track(schedule_name=…)` value must equal the `beat_schedule` key. This was already required for skips to work.

## Workers


Every worker that answers the broker, refreshed every 10 seconds while the
tab is visible, with controls to shut a worker down, resize its pool and
change its queues, plus a table for changing task rate limits at runtime.
Runtime rate limits are not saved: they reset when a worker restarts. See
[Workers and rate limits](workers.md).

## Audit log


`/audit`. A read-only table of every manually-triggered control action, with
**When**, **User**, **Action**, and **Target**
(`{target_type}:{target_id}`, e.g. `task:abc123`) columns, newest first,
backed by `GET /api/audit`.

What you will actually see here, given what the dashboard itself can do:
task retries (single and bulk), per-occurrence schedule pauses, and
[branding changes](#branding--deployment-wide) (one row per changed key).
The API also audits `start` and `cancel`, but **no dashboard control
triggers either** — there is no "run now" and no "cancel" button in the UI
today — so those rows only appear if something calls
`POST /api/tasks/start` or `POST /api/tasks/{id}/cancel` directly. There's no filtering or
pagination control in the UI beyond the API's default 50-row limit
(`limit` is a raw query param on `GET /api/audit` but the screen doesn't
currently expose a control for it). An empty state ("No manual actions
recorded yet.") is shown until the first control action is taken through
the dashboard. A failed load shows the server's own message with a **Try
again** button — the same treatment the task list and both schedule screens
use, so an error screen is never a dead end.

This is the audit trail that answers "who did what, to what, and when" for
anything the dashboard itself performed on a user's behalf — it does not
record automatic system behavior (task status transitions recorded by the
events listener, or automatic skip/cancel outcomes recorded by `@track`);
those show up in the task list and detail screens instead, not here.

## Appearance and branding

`/settings`. Two groups of settings that look similar and are deliberately
scoped very differently — the screen says so on each panel, because users
otherwise assume both are personal.

### Branding — deployment-wide

Stored on the server, so one operator sets it and everyone sees it,
including on the sign-in screen before anyone has logged in.

- **Brand name** — up to 64 characters. Replaces the wordmark in the nav,
  on the sign-in card, on each page's eyebrow, and in the browser tab
  title. Leave it empty to go back to `celery-manager`.
- **Accent colour** — one hex value. The hover, pressed, link and tint
  variants are *derived* from it rather than picked by hand, and the text
  colour on an accent-filled button is chosen by measuring contrast
  against your colour, so a light brand colour gets black text and a dark
  one gets white. Link-coloured text is derived separately, because a
  colour that works as a button fill often fails as small text on a pale
  surface.
- **Logo URL** — an `https://` URL, a `/path` served by this deployment,
  or a `data:image/…` URI. Replaces the brand dot; if the image fails to
  load, the dot comes back rather than leaving a broken-image icon.

A live preview shows the result before you save. Invalid values are
rejected by the API with a message that lands on the offending field (see
[REST API: settings](rest-api.md#settings-branding) for the exact rules and why
they are strict — the accent goes into a CSS custom property and the logo
URL into an `<img src>`). **Reset to defaults** clears all three.

Every change is written to the [audit log](#audit-log), one entry per
changed key, with the old and new values. Note there is no role system in
v1: any signed-in user can rebrand the deployment, and the audit trail is
what tells you who did.

### Theme — this browser only

**Auto / Light / Dark**, available both here and in the nav bar. Auto
follows the operating system; Light and Dark override it in both
directions, so choosing Light on a dark-mode machine works. The choice is
kept in the browser's local storage, applies immediately, and is applied
before the page paints — a dark preference doesn't flash a white screen
first. Your colleagues, and your own other browsers, keep their own
choice.


<!-- docs/insights.md -->

# Insights

The **Insights** page answers "how are my tasks doing?" without leaving the
dashboard. Everything is computed when you open the page from the existing run
history; nothing extra is stored.

## Trends


Pick a range (1h, 24h, 7d, 30d). The page shows:

- **KPIs**: runs, success rate, p95 runtime and failures.
- **Runs by status**: stacked bars per interval, in the same colours as the
  task list.
- **Runtime**: p95 (solid) and median (dashed) per interval.
- **Busiest tasks** and **Highest failure rate** (tasks with at least 3 runs).
  Each name links to that task's page.

Every chart has a written summary and a "View as a table" fallback.

| Range | Interval |
|---|---|
| 1h | 5 minutes |
| 24h | 1 hour |
| 7d | 6 hours |
| 30d | 1 day |

Definitions:

- A run is placed by `started_at`, or `finished_at` if it never started.
  Queued runs with neither timestamp are not counted.
- **Success rate** is succeeded divided by (succeeded + failed). Skipped,
  revoked, retried and in-flight runs are excluded from the ratio.
- **Runtime** percentiles use finished runs (succeeded or failed) with a
  recorded runtime, linearly interpolated, and are calculated in Python so
  they behave the same on SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL.
- A query scans at most 50,000 runs (newest first). If a range holds more, the
  page says the figures cover the newest runs only (`truncated: true`).

## Task page


Open `/task-types/<task name>` from the task name on a run's detail page or
from the Insights lists. It shows totals, success rate, median/p95/slowest
runtime, the last success and failure, the same charts filtered to the task,
the 10 most recent runs, and its top errors.

## Failures


The **Failures** tab groups failed runs by signature: exception type, message
with volatile parts masked (numbers, UUIDs, hex ids, memory addresses, quoted
values) and the last traceback frame (`file.py:function`). So
`ConnectionError('relay 10.0.0.1:587 refused')` and `...10.0.0.2:25...` fall
into one group. Groups are sorted by count and show first and last seen,
affected tasks and an example exception.

Actions per group:

- **Open latest run** opens the most recent failed run in the group.
- **Show runs** opens the task list on the Failed tab (and the task, when only
  one is affected).
- **Retry all in group** asks for confirmation showing the number of runs,
  then retries them through `POST /api/tasks/retry-bulk`, writing one audit
  row per run. A group retries at most its 100 most recent runs.

See [REST API](rest-api.md#analytics) for the endpoints.


<!-- docs/workers.md -->

# Workers and rate limits

The **Workers** page shows every Celery worker that answers the broker right
now, and lets you act on them: shut one down, resize its pool, change which
queues it consumes, and change a task's rate limit at runtime.

None of this is stored by celery-manager. Each refresh asks the workers
directly through Celery's remote-control API (`app.control.inspect()` and
friends), so what you see is only as fresh as the last answer, and every
change you make lives in the worker's memory only.

## What you need

- A worker running against **the same broker** as the dashboard's
  `celery_app`.
- Remote control enabled on that worker. It is on by default; the
  `worker_enable_remote_control = False` setting (or a broker without
  broadcast support) turns it off, and then the worker never appears here.

Task events (`-E`) are not needed for this page. They are needed for the
task list, which is fed by the events listener.

## The worker list


The page refreshes every 10 seconds while its tab is visible and stops while
the tab is hidden. "Updated 5s ago" shows how old the current answer is.

Each refresh sends one `ping` broadcast and waits up to
[`inspect_timeout_seconds`](configuration.md) (1 s by default) for replies.
It then asks the workers that answered for `stats`, `active`, `reserved`,
`scheduled` and `active_queues`, and stops waiting as soon as all of them have
replied. With no workers a refresh therefore costs about one timeout; with
healthy workers, a little more.

For each worker the card shows:

| Field | Source |
|---|---|
| Online | answered `ping` |
| PID, uptime | `stats` |
| Pool | `stats.pool.implementation`, shortened (`prefork`, `threads`, `gevent`, `solo`, ...), with the live process count (prefork) or the configured concurrency |
| Processed | sum of `stats.total`, the per-task counts since the worker started |
| Active / Reserved / Scheduled | lengths of `active()`, `reserved()` and `scheduled()`. Active tasks link to their run in the task list |
| Queues | `active_queues()` |

**"No workers answered"** means nothing replied within the timeout. Either no
worker is running, it uses a different broker, remote control is off, or the
broker is slow. On a slow or distant broker, raise `inspect_timeout_seconds`.

**"Couldn't reach the Celery broker"** means the broadcast itself failed: the
API answers `503` with the broker's error. If an earlier refresh worked, the
page keeps showing that answer and says how old it is.

## Controls

Every control is a `POST`, requires a signed-in user and writes an
[audit log](rest-api.md#audit-log) row.

| Control | Celery call | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Shut down** | `control.shutdown(destination=[worker])` | Asks you to confirm first. A warm shutdown: the worker stops taking new tasks, finishes its running ones, then exits. Celery sends no reply, so the page can only say the command was sent. If a process supervisor (systemd, Kubernetes, supervisord) manages the worker, it will probably start it again. |
| **Add process** / **Remove process** | `control.pool_grow(1)` / `control.pool_shrink(1)` | Only pools that can be resized (prefork, eventlet, gevent) accept these. Other pools reply with an error, which the page shows. |
| **Consume queue** / the **×** on a queue | `control.add_consumer(queue)` / `control.cancel_consumer(queue)` | Lasts until the worker restarts. After a restart its `-Q` option applies again. |

A control reply lists which workers confirmed (`acknowledged`) and which
refused, with the reason (`errors`). A worker that is in neither list didn't
reply within the timeout. The command may still have reached it, so check on
the next refresh.

## Runtime rate limits

The **Rate limits** section lists every task registered on the dashboard's
`celery_app` (Celery's own `celery.*` tasks are left out) with the rate limit
declared in code, `@app.task(rate_limit="10/m")`. **Change limit** sends
`control.rate_limit(task_name, rate)` to every running worker.

A rate is a number of tasks per second, minute or hour: `10/s`, `10/m`,
`100/h`, or a bare number meaning per second. An empty value removes the
limit. The API rejects anything else with `422` before broadcasting.

!!! warning "Runtime rate limits are not saved"
    Each worker keeps the new limit in memory only. When a worker restarts,
    and for any worker started after the change, the limit declared in code
    applies again. To make a limit permanent, set it in code.

Celery has no inspect call that reports the limit a worker is enforcing, so
the table shows the declared default. After a change, the row also shows the
value you applied in this browser session ("Runtime: 30/m").

The list only contains tasks registered in the process that serves the
dashboard. If it is empty or missing tasks, import your task modules (or call
`app.autodiscover_tasks()`) in that process.

## Delayed tasks

A task sent with `countdown=` or `eta=` doesn't wait on the broker. The first
worker to see it takes it off the queue straight away and keeps it in memory
until it is due. Queue depth no longer counts it, and nothing runs it until the
ETA, so the only place it can be seen is the worker holding it.

**Held tasks → Delayed** in the sidebar lists every such task the workers
report (`inspect().scheduled()`), soonest first: task, a countdown to its ETA,
the worker holding it, queue, priority, its arguments and the status
celery-manager has recorded for the run. It refreshes every 5 seconds while the
tab is visible. Like the worker list, it only shows what workers that answer
within `inspect_timeout_seconds` report.

**Arguments are masked.** The list shows each argument's type and the keyword
names (`(str, int) {user_id: int}`), never the values. Operators can tick
**Show argument values** (`?reveal_args=true` on the API); viewers can't.

Below the list, runs celery-manager recorded as `queued` with an ETA still in
the future that no answering worker holds are listed separately. Such a run is
still waiting on the queue (nothing consumes it yet), held by a worker that
didn't answer, or lost. On Redis, check
[Stuck and lost tasks](queues.md#stuck-and-lost-tasks-redis).

### Cancelling

Operators can cancel one delayed task or a selection. This sends the same
`control.revoke` broadcast as the Tasks page's cancel, and also marks the
recorded run `revoked` immediately. A worker only drops a revoked ETA task, and
only then emits `task-revoked`, when the ETA arrives, so without this a task
cancelled today with a week-long countdown would show `queued` for a week. A
cancelled task stays in the list, marked "dropped at the ETA", until then.
Task ids with no recorded run are revoked too. Each cancel writes a `cancel`
(one task) or `cancel_bulk` (several) audit row with `"delayed": true`.

!!! warning "Revokes live in worker memory"
    A worker keeps its list of revoked task ids in memory. If it restarts
    before the ETA, it forgets the cancel, gets the task back from the broker
    and runs it. To make revokes survive restarts, run workers with
    `--statedb` (for example `celery worker --statedb=/var/run/celery/worker.state`).

## API

See [REST API → Workers](rest-api.md#workers) for the endpoints, request
bodies and responses.

## Recorded heartbeat history (0.3)

The events listener stores one heartbeat observation per worker per UTC minute.
An observation includes state (online/offline), the sender's event timestamp,
active tasks and processed count when supplied. Repeated heartbeats in a minute
update its bucket rather than appending unbounded rows. Recording is serialized
under the same locked `WorkerState` row used for last-seen state, so concurrent
listeners do not create duplicate minute samples.

Events older than the worker's latest observation are ignored; late delivery does
not rewind current state or rewrite history. If offline and online observations
share a timestamp, offline wins. An ordinary later heartbeat can bring the worker
online again. Missing samples mean missing observations, not proven downtime.

`worker_heartbeat_retention_days=7` bounds retained history by default. `0` disables
new history collection while continuing last-seen tracking; it does not immediately
purge previously stored history. Positive values are limited to 3,650 days.
Old samples are deleted hourly during collection and through the normal retention
prune command. Keep this setting consistent between listener and API processes.
Prune previews include `heartbeats_deleted` and do not delete samples in dry-run mode.

Open **Recorded heartbeat history** on a worker card to load its active-task trend
and observed-state table. Paging reads 60 samples at a time. This is the event
listener's durable history, separate from the worker's current inspect reply.

`GET /api/workers/{worker}/heartbeats` accepts `since` and `until` ISO timestamps,
`limit` (1–1,000, default 120), and `offset` (0–1,000,000). Any authenticated role
may read it. Naive input timestamps mean UTC; reversed ranges return 422. The
response is `{items, total, limit, offset, retention_days}`. Items carry UTC
`bucket_at`, `observed_at`, `state`, `active`, and `processed`. Unknown workers
return an empty page. History is not a work-completion or availability guarantee.


<!-- docs/queues.md -->

# Queues, purge and bulk cancel

The dashboard's **Queues** page shows how much work is waiting on the broker
for each queue, lets you look at the messages waiting in one, delete or move
a single message, and purge a queue; the task list can cancel many runs at
once. All of these are thin wrappers over Celery/kombu primitives; this
page is about what they actually do, and where they can't see.

## Which queues are listed


A queue appears if celery-manager knows its name from any of:

| Source (shown under the name) | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| default | `celery_app.conf.task_default_queue` (`"celery"` if unset) |
| configured | `celery_app.conf.task_queues` |
| routed | `celery_app.conf.task_routes` — dicts and lists of dicts. Router *functions* are skipped, since reading them would mean calling your code. |
| seen in runs | any `task_runs.queue` value (written by the events listener) |
| consumed by workers | `inspect().active_queues()` from live workers, 1s timeout, cached for 30s |

A queue that none of these mention isn't listed. If your workers consume a
queue nothing else names and no worker answered the inspect, it is missing
until one does; the page says so when no worker replied.

## Two numbers that disagree

Each queue shows two counts:

- **Broker depth**: messages the broker is holding right now, read with a
  passive `queue_declare` on a short-lived connection. Nothing is created
  by looking.
- **Recorded queued**: `task_runs` rows in this queue whose status is still
  `queued`, which is what celery-manager has *seen*.

They routinely differ, and neither is wrong:

- tasks sent while the events listener was down never got a row;
- the listener lags the broker by however long event delivery takes;
- a worker pulls ETA/countdown tasks off the queue right away and holds them
  until they're due. Broker depth drops, but the run is still `queued`;
- runs written by the decorator or a retry don't know their queue until the
  listener fills it in. Those are counted separately ("no recorded queue
  yet") rather than guessed into the default queue.

**Consumers** is the broker's consumer count. Redis, SQS and the other
kombu *virtual* transports always report zero, so on those it is shown as
unknown (`null`), not `0`.

The sparkline is the depth recorded over the last 24 hours (see
[Depth history](#depth-history)); select it for a larger chart. Until two
samples exist (the sampler is off, or just started) it falls back to the
depth over this browser session, which is scaled to the session's own low
and high and starts empty every time the page opens.

## Wait time

The **Wait p50 / p95** column is how long runs sat in the queue before a
worker started them, over the last 15 minutes:

    wait = started_at - max(sent_at, eta)

- `sent_at` is the timestamp of the `task-sent` event, which the events
  listener stores on the run (`received_at`, from `task-received`, is stored
  beside it). The earliest value seen wins: a duplicate or late event can
  never push it later and shrink the wait. A run that never had a send time
  recorded (the client doesn't emit `task-sent`, the listener was down) is
  left out, not guessed at. The producer must emit `task-sent`
  (`task_send_sent_event = True`, see the [quickstart](quickstart.md)).
- **ETA and countdown time is not waiting.** A task sent with
  `countdown=300` is meant to sit for five minutes; its wait is measured from
  the moment it was due. The listener stores `eta` from the same events.
- A retry reuses the task id, so a retried run forgets its first attempt's
  `sent_at`/`eta` and is left out of wait statistics unless the new attempt's
  events refill them.
- Negative results (the producer's clock ahead of the worker's) count as 0.
- Only runs that *started* inside the window count, and a queue with none
  shows `—`.

The worker-side decorator does not write `received_at`: Celery does not hand
the receive time to the task, and approximating it would be wrong more often
than it is right. The listener's event is the one source.

**How the percentiles are computed.** Not in SQL: `percentile_cont` exists
on PostgreSQL only, and celery-manager also runs on SQLite and MySQL. The
window's raw send/ETA/start values are read (newest 50,000 runs at most) and
p50, p95 and the maximum are computed in Python with linear interpolation.
Under the cap the numbers are exact; above it they describe the newest runs
(the API says so with `truncated`). The cost is that one request reads up to
that many narrow rows; the window is short, and the same figure feeds
[metrics](metrics.md), the [task Insights page](insights.md) (over its
chosen range), the task's detail page ("waited 2.3s before starting") and the
`queue_wait` [alert](alerts.md#rule-kinds).

## Depth history

The events listener (`celery-manager events`) runs a small sampler thread
that, every `queue_sample_interval_seconds` (60 by default, `0` turns it
off), lists every known queue exactly as the Queues page does (same
connection timeout and 3 s deadline, so a dead broker costs a skipped tick,
never a hang) and stores one row per queue in `queue_depth_samples(sampled_at,
queue, depth)`, indexed by `(queue, sampled_at)`.

- **Only depths the broker reported are stored.** An unreachable broker, a
  transport that can't report depth (`memory://`) and a RabbitMQ queue nobody
  has declared are skipped, not stored as `0`: a `0` would read as "empty" and
  hide the outage. A Redis queue that is simply empty is a true `0` and is
  stored.
- **Several listener processes.** The sampler dedupes per interval on a
  best-effort basis: before sampling it looks at the newest sample row, and if
  that is younger than 60% of the interval another process just sampled and
  it skips the tick. It is a read, not a lock, so two processes ticking in the
  same instant can both write. That costs one extra point per queue, which the
  chart and the growth rule tolerate, so correctness never depends on
  exactly-once.
- **Retention.** Samples older than `queue_sample_retention_days` (14 by
  default, `0` keeps them) are deleted by the [retention](retention.md) prune
  (`celery-manager prune`, the `prune` Celery task) and, at most once an hour,
  by the sampler itself, so a deployment that never schedules the prune still
  stays bounded. A prune's summary reports `samples_deleted`.
  `celery-manager prune` has no config, so it uses the 14-day default.
- **The chart.** `GET /api/queues/{name}/history?hours=24` returns the window
  cut into at most 240 buckets (never narrower than a minute), each holding
  the *highest* depth sampled in it so a spike is not averaged away. Gaps in
  sampling are gaps in the line. The dashboard offers 1 hour, 6 hours, 24
  hours and 7 days.

### The `queue_growing` alert

It fires per queue when the samples of the last `minutes` (default 15) show
the queue **rising monotonically-ish**. All of these must hold:

1. at least three samples, spanning at least half the window, the newest not
   older than half the window;
2. the depth rose by at least `min_increase` (default 50) from the first
   sample to the last;
3. at most 20% of the steps between consecutive samples go down (flat steps
   are neutral);
4. no single step down is larger than half the net rise.

So noise and a short dip are tolerated, a sawtooth or a queue that climbs and
then drains is not, and a queue that jumped once and then stays high still
counts (nothing is draining it). With too few or too old samples the queue is
*unknown*: an open incident stays open instead of being resolved by a gap in
sampling. If no sample exists at all the rule says so ("couldn't check").

## When the broker can't be asked

`GET /api/queues` always answers `200`. Broker trouble shows up as
`broker.error` and `depth: null` per queue, with the recorded counts still
filled in:

- **unreachable / auth failure**: one connection attempt with a 2s connect
  timeout, no retry loop;
- **slow**: the whole broker round-trip has a 3s deadline. A broker that
  accepts the connection and then hangs can't hang the request; the stuck
  call finishes in a small background pool;
- **`memory://` and `filesystem://`**: reported as unsupported. The
  in-memory transport is private to each process, so the API process would
  only ever see its own empty queues, and the filesystem transport can't
  count the messages in its directory (it would answer `0` for a full one).
  A confident `0` would be a lie, so the page says "queue depth isn't
  available" instead;
- **queue not declared**: depth `0`, `exists: false`. On Redis that just
  means empty (Redis deletes a list when it drains); on RabbitMQ the reason
  says nobody has declared it yet.

The page refreshes every 5 seconds and stops while the browser tab is
hidden.

## Broker health

The **Broker** panel at the top of the Queues page, and `GET /api/broker/health`
(any signed-in user), answer a different question from queue depth: is the
broker itself up, and is it in trouble? What can be shown depends on what the
broker lets a client see.

| Transport | What you get |
|---|---|
| **Redis** (including Sentinel) | Reachable, latency, version, memory used against `maxmemory` (a bar; `maxmemory` of 0 means unlimited, so no bar), eviction policy, connected and blocked clients, evicted keys, refused connections, RDB/AOF status, uptime. |
| **RabbitMQ** (AMQP) | Reachable, latency, product and version. Memory and disk alarms need the RabbitMQ management API, which celery-manager doesn't talk to yet, so the panel says `management: not configured` instead of implying there are none. |
| **Anything else** | Reachable, latency, and "details not available for <transport>". |

**The eviction policy is the one to watch.** A queued task is a key in a Redis
list. If `maxmemory-policy` is anything other than `noeviction`
(`allkeys-lru`, `volatile-ttl`, ...), Redis deletes keys when it runs out of
memory, and it can delete queued tasks, which then never run and leave no
error. The panel shows a warning for any other policy (and for a nonzero
`evicted_keys`). Set `maxmemory-policy noeviction`: a full Redis then refuses
new tasks, which you can see, instead of losing old ones, which you can't.
With no `maxmemory` set nothing is evicted today, and the warning says so.

The check opens one connection with the same 2s connect timeout and 3s
deadline as the queue list and never raises: an unreachable broker is
`reachable: false` with the error. The broker URL is shown with its password
masked, and the same masking is applied to error text. The panel refreshes
with the page. The numbers are also in [`/metrics`](metrics.md) and drive the
`broker_unreachable` and `broker_memory` [alert kinds](alerts.md).

## Looking inside a queue

Click a queue's name on the **Queues** page to see the messages waiting in
it, next to run first: position, task name and id (linked to the run when
celery-manager has recorded it), priority, age, ETA, retries, size and the
arguments. `GET /api/queues/{name}/messages?limit=50&offset=0` returns the
same list. Any role can look.

### Redis: exact, and nothing is taken

Kombu keeps a Redis queue as plain lists, one per priority step (`0`, `3`,
`6`, `9` by default; the queue's own name for `0` and `<name>\x06\x163` and so
on for the others, under any `global_keyprefix`). Producers push at the head
and workers pop from the tail, step `0` first. **On Redis a lower priority
number runs sooner**, the opposite of RabbitMQ. celery-manager reads the
lists in that same order with `LRANGE`, which takes nothing off the queue,
so the order shown is the order workers will take them, as of that moment.

### RabbitMQ: approximate, off by default

RabbitMQ has no way to read a message without handing it out. The only way
to look is to take messages without acknowledging them (`basic_get`) and
reject them back onto the queue. That has side effects:

- while they are being read (milliseconds), workers can't take them;
- RabbitMQ marks every message read as **redelivered**;
- a message put back may land at a different place, usually the front, so
  the order shown can change just by looking.

So browsing RabbitMQ is off until you set `queue_browser_amqp=True`. With it
on, the dashboard says the view is approximate and lists these side effects,
the API returns `approximate: true` and `side_effects`, and at most 20
messages are read per look, whatever page size is asked for. Queue depth is
unchanged afterwards. With it off, and on any transport other than Redis and
RabbitMQ, the answer is `supported: false` with the reason.

### Arguments

Arguments follow the same rule as task runs: every role sees them (see
[Roles](roles.md#what-viewers-can-see)). They come from the `argsrepr` and
`kwargsrepr` headers the producer wrote (already shortened by Celery's
`argsrepr_maxsize`), or, for messages without them, from the body if it is
JSON and under 64 KB. Pickled bodies are never decoded: unpickling would run
whatever code the message names inside the dashboard process. Long arguments
are cut to 2,000 characters, and the raw body is never sent to the browser.

If your task arguments carry secrets, set `queue_browser_show_args=False`.
The arguments are then left out of the response for every role, not just
hidden on the page.

**Age** is only known for some messages: Celery doesn't put a send time on a
message. It is shown for messages beat sent through celery-manager's
stamping scheduler (`cm_sent_at` header) and for runs that record when they
were sent.

### Deleting or moving one message (Redis)

Admins get **Delete** and **Move** on each message, each with a confirmation.

- **Delete** removes that one message for good. If celery-manager recorded
  its run as `queued`, the run is marked `revoked`, as a purge does, because
  no worker will ever report on it. Audited as `delete_message`.
- **Move** sends it to the end of another queue, keeping its priority, and
  records the run's new queue. The target must be a queue celery-manager
  knows (configured, routed, seen on a run, or consumed by a worker), so a
  typo can't create a queue nobody reads. The message's own routing fields
  are updated too, so if a worker takes it and then dies, Redis puts it back
  on the new queue, not the old one. Audited as `move_message`.

Both find the exact stored message by task id and remove that exact entry
in one Redis transaction (`WATCH` on the list, then `LREM` and, for a move,
`LPUSH`). If a worker takes the message in between, the transaction does
nothing and the answer is `409` "already taken by a worker": the message is
never both run and moved, and a delete is never reported for a message that
ran. A message that isn't waiting there at all is a `404`.

These need Redis. On RabbitMQ a single message can't be taken out of the
middle of a queue, so delete and move answer `409`.

## Stuck and lost tasks (Redis)

Redis has no acknowledgements of its own, so kombu emulates them. When a worker
takes a message off a queue, kombu copies it into a hash (`unacked`) and records
the time in a sorted set (`unacked_index`). Acknowledging the message deletes
both. If the worker dies first (`kill -9`, the OOM killer, a lost host), the
message stays there. It is no longer on the queue and no worker has it, so it
isn't in the queue depth or the worker list.

kombu puts such messages back on their queue once they are older than the
**visibility timeout** (`visibility_timeout` in `broker_transport_options`,
3600 seconds by default), but only while some worker on that broker is running
to do it. Until then the task is lost from view.

**Held tasks → Stuck (Redis)** lists every unacknowledged message, oldest first
(at most 500, with the total), each with its task, queue, how long it has been
held, its ETA if it has one, and the status recorded for the run. Each message
is checked against what live workers report (`inspect` active, reserved and
scheduled):

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Running** | A live worker is executing it. That is normal for `acks_late` tasks, which are acknowledged when they finish. |
| **Held by a worker** | A live worker has it prefetched or is holding it until its ETA. Normal. |
| **Orphaned** | No worker that answered has it: its worker most likely died. |
| **Unknown** | The workers couldn't be asked, so nothing can be classified. |

The **Redelivery** column says when kombu will put an orphaned message back
(the visibility timeout minus its age), or that it is already past it. A
*held* ETA task whose countdown is longer than the visibility timeout is a
known Celery pitfall: kombu redelivers it while the first worker still holds
it, and the task runs twice.

celery-manager reads the key names, the `global_keyprefix` and the visibility
timeout from kombu's own Redis channel, so custom settings are picked up.

### Restoring a message

Operators can put chosen messages back at the front of their queue now instead
of waiting for the visibility timeout. Restore does exactly what kombu does
after the timeout: in one `WATCH`/`MULTI` transaction it removes the entry from
`unacked` and `unacked_index` and pushes the stored message back with kombu's
own `_do_restore_message` (same format, marked `redelivered`). The workers are
asked again just before restoring:

- a message a live worker is **running** is always refused;
- a message a live worker **holds** (prefetched or scheduled) is refused
  unless you also tick the force option, because that worker will still run it;
- if the workers can't be asked at all, nothing is restored (`409`).

!!! warning "Restoring can run a task twice"
    A worker that is alive but slow to answer looks the same as a dead one.
    And a task whose worker died partway through runs again from the start.
    Only restore tasks that are safe to repeat. The dashboard asks you to
    confirm with this warning.

Each restore that put anything back writes a `restore_unacked` audit row.
Messages that were acknowledged or restored by kombu in the meantime are
reported as missing.

### Other brokers

RabbitMQ tracks unacknowledged messages itself and redelivers them as soon as
the consumer's connection closes, so nothing gets stuck the way it can on
Redis. On RabbitMQ (and other non-Redis transports) the endpoint answers
`{"supported": false, "reason": ...}`. The RabbitMQ management UI shows
unacknowledged counts per queue, and the planned RabbitMQ management
integration ([roadmap](roadmap.md)) will show them here.

## Purging a queue

`POST /api/queues/{name}/purge` calls `queue_purge` on that one queue and
returns how many messages the broker removed. The dashboard asks you to type
the queue name first. There is no "purge every queue" action.

Only *ready* messages are removed. Messages a worker has already reserved
(prefetched, or ETA/countdown tasks it is holding) are not in the queue any
more and still run.

### What happens to the recorded runs

A purged message never reaches a worker, so no `task-revoked` event will
ever arrive for it, and its run would read `queued` forever. So after a
purge that removed **at least one** message, celery-manager marks every run
recorded as `queued` **in that queue** and **without an ETA** as `revoked`
(with `finished_at` set to now). The audit row records both numbers and the
ids it marked.

This is a best guess, because the broker returns a count, not ids:

- ETA runs are left alone because the worker holds them, so the purge didn't
  touch them;
- if the purge removed nothing, nothing is marked. A stale `queued` row is
  then some other problem, not this purge;
- it corrects itself: if a run marked here does execute after all, its
  succeeded/failed event overwrites `revoked`, because a later terminal
  status wins in the listener.

Errors: `404` if the broker says the queue doesn't exist (RabbitMQ), `503`
if the broker is unreachable, timed out, or is `memory://`. Nothing is
marked or audited on failure.

## Bulk cancel

`POST /api/tasks/cancel-bulk` revokes many runs in one call. It takes either
explicit `task_ids` or a `filter` with the same fields as `GET /api/tasks`
(`status`, `task_name`, `q`, `date_from`, `date_to`), never both. An empty
body is a `400`, not "everything".

- Only runs that can still be stopped are revoked: `queued`, `started` and
  `retried`. Finished ones (`succeeded`, `failed`, `revoked`, `skipped`) are
  counted as `skipped_finished`. Ids with no row are counted as `unknown`
  and not revoked, because bulk actions only touch runs you could see.
- **Cap: 1,000.** More than that is refused with a `400` and nothing is
  revoked. Cancelling an arbitrary first 1,000 of a bigger set isn't a
  scope you chose, so narrow the filter instead.
- `dry_run: true` returns the counts without revoking or auditing. That is
  how the dashboard's "Cancel all matching" shows the number before you
  confirm.
- `terminate: true` also kills runs already executing (the same flag as the
  single cancel). It's off by default and an explicit checkbox in the
  dashboard.
- Revokes go out as `control.revoke([...])` broadcasts of up to 100 ids
  each, followed by one `cancel_bulk` audit row listing every id revoked.

Like the single cancel, this only *asks* workers to revoke. A run's status
changes to `revoked` when the worker's `task-revoked` event comes back
through the listener, not at the moment you click.

In the dashboard, selecting runs on the **Queued**, **Started** or
**Retried** tab offers **Cancel N selected**. **Cancel all matching…**, on
those tabs and on **All**, counts the cancellable runs under the current
filters and asks you to confirm.


<!-- docs/rabbitmq.md -->

# RabbitMQ

On RabbitMQ, celery-manager can read the
[management API](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/management) for what a plain
AMQP connection can't tell it:

- per queue: consumers, unacknowledged messages, publish and deliver rates,
  queue type (classic, quorum or stream), maximum priority, dead-letter
  exchange and routing key, and how long it has been idle;
- per node: memory and disk use against their limits, memory and disk
  **alarms**, file descriptors and sockets;
- **dead-letter queues**: what RabbitMQ dead-lettered, why, and a way to send
  it back where it came from.

All of it is off until you configure the management API, and stays off when
the broker isn't RabbitMQ.

## Setup

### Enable the management plugin

```bash
rabbitmq-plugins enable rabbitmq_management
```

The `rabbitmq:3-management` Docker images have it already. It listens on port
15672.

### The management user

Give celery-manager its own user. Reading needs only the `monitoring` tag:

```bash
rabbitmqctl add_user celery-manager 'a-long-random-password'
rabbitmqctl set_user_tags celery-manager monitoring
rabbitmqctl set_permissions -p / celery-manager '' '' ''
```

That covers the Queues page panel, metrics, the `rabbitmq_alarm` alert and the
list of dead-letter queues. Two things need more:

| To | The management user also needs |
|---|---|
| Browse a dead-letter queue's messages | `read` permission on that queue in the vhost. RabbitMQ can only show a message by handing it out and taking it back, which is a read. |
| Requeue dead-lettered messages | Nothing more on the management user: requeue runs over AMQP with **the broker URL's user** (your Celery user), which needs `read` on the dead-letter queue and `write` on the exchanges the messages came from. It already has both if your workers use it. |

For example, to let the management user browse queues ending in `.dlq`
without touching anything else:

```bash
rabbitmqctl set_permissions -p / celery-manager '' '' '^.*\.dlq$'
```

### Configuration

```python
from celery_manager import CeleryManagerConfig

config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=app,
    rabbitmq_management_url="http://rabbit:15672",
    rabbitmq_management_username="celery-manager",
    rabbitmq_management_password=os.environ["RABBITMQ_MANAGEMENT_PASSWORD"],
)
```

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `rabbitmq_management_url` | `None` | The management API. `https://` works; redirects are never followed, because following one would send the credentials somewhere else. Put the address it redirects to here instead. |
| `rabbitmq_management_username` / `_password` | `None` | Sent as a Basic auth header. The password is never stored in the database, returned by the API, logged, or shown in the config's `repr()`. Don't put credentials in the URL. |
| `rabbitmq_management_verify_tls` | `True` | Turn off only for a test broker with a self-signed certificate. |
| `rabbitmq_management_timeout_seconds` | `3.0` | Time limit for one operation (all its HTTP calls together). |
| `rabbitmq_dlq_patterns` | `["*.dlq", "*.dead", "dlq.*"]` | Queue names that count as dead-letter queues even if nothing dead-letters to them. |

The vhost comes from the broker URL (`amqp://user:pass@rabbit:5672/prod`
uses the vhost `prod`; `//` at the end is the default vhost `/`).

## On the Queues page

A **RabbitMQ** panel shows the version, each node's memory against its
high-watermark, free disk against its limit, file descriptors and sockets. A
red banner names any node with a memory or disk alarm: while it lasts,
RabbitMQ blocks every publisher, so new tasks can't be sent.

Under each queue's name: its type, unacknowledged messages, publish (in) and
deliver (out) rates, priority range, where it dead-letters to, and how long
it has been idle. Rates are what the management API samples (every 5 seconds
by default) and show `—` until it has a sample.

If the management API can't be reached, the panel says why (`401` means check
the credentials) and the rest of the page works as before.

Without a management URL on a RabbitMQ broker, the panel explains how to set
it up. On other brokers it isn't shown.

## Dead-letter queues

RabbitMQ *dead-letters* a message when a consumer rejects it without requeue,
its TTL expires, the queue is over its length limit, or a quorum queue's
delivery limit is hit. It goes to the queue's dead-letter exchange
(`x-dead-letter-exchange`, as a queue argument or a policy), and from there
to whatever queue is bound to it.

**Which queues count.** A queue is a dead-letter queue if:

- some queue's dead-letter exchange and routing key route to it (read from
  queue arguments and policies, through the exchange's bindings: direct,
  topic, fanout and the default exchange); or
- its name matches one of `rabbitmq_dlq_patterns`.

The page also warns when a queue dead-letters to an exchange with nothing
bound, because RabbitMQ then drops those messages.

Open **Queues → Dead-letter queues** (`#/rabbitmq/dead-letters`).

### Browsing

The first 20 messages of the selected queue, with the task name and id, and
each `x-death` entry: the reason (`rejected`, `expired`, `maxlen`,
`delivery_limit`), the queue and routing key it died in, how many times, and
when.

Browsing is **approximate and has side effects**. RabbitMQ has no way to look
at a message without handing it out, so celery-manager asks the management
API to take each one and put it straight back (`ack_requeue_true`). The
messages come back marked *redelivered* and may change order, and a consumer
on the dead-letter queue could take one meanwhile. For that reason the page
reads only when you open a queue or press Refresh; it doesn't poll.

**Arguments are hidden by default**, for every role, and shown when you tick
