**Show arguments** (`reveal_args=true`). This is the same policy as task runs,
where every role can see arguments (see [Roles](roles.md#what-viewers-can-see));
it only keeps them off the screen until someone asks. Celery's own
`argsrepr`/`kwargsrepr` headers are shown when present, so an app that already
masks arguments in them stays masked.

### Requeue

Admins can requeue the selected messages, or the first 100. Each message goes
back to the **exchange and routing key of its newest `x-death` entry**: where
it was published before it died.

Nothing is lost on failure. Requeue runs over AMQP and, for each message:

1. takes it from the dead-letter queue **without acknowledging it**;
2. publishes a copy to the original exchange and routing key, *mandatory* and
   with **publisher confirms**;
3. waits for RabbitMQ to confirm the copy, and checks it wasn't returned as
   unroutable (for example because the original queue is gone);
4. only then acknowledges the original, removing it from the dead-letter queue.

The first failure stops the run. The message being moved is put back, later
ones are never taken, and the result says how many moved and why it
stopped. The worst case is a duplicate: if the connection drops after the
confirm but before the acknowledgement, the message is both requeued and
still in the dead-letter queue.

Every requeue is in the [audit log](rest-api.md#audit-log) as
`requeue_dead_letters`, with the task ids moved.

**The copy keeps its headers, `x-death` included**, and gets an
`x-celery-manager-requeues` header counting how often celery-manager has
requeued it. Keeping `x-death` keeps the message's history visible if it dies
again. The counter matters on RabbitMQ 4, which ignores `x-death` on messages
a client publishes and starts its count again.

**Loop protection.** A message that has died more than 3 times, by its
`x-death` counts or by that requeue counter, is refused and stays in the
dead-letter queue. Something keeps rejecting it, and sending it round again
just repeats that. Tick **Also send messages that have died more than 3
times** (`force`) to send it anyway. A message without an `x-death` header is
also refused, since where it came from is unknown.

## Metrics and alerts

With management configured, `/metrics` adds
`celery_manager_rabbitmq_queue_unacked`, `_queue_consumers`,
`_queue_publish_rate`, `_queue_deliver_rate` per queue and
`celery_manager_rabbitmq_mem_alarm` / `_disk_alarm` per node
(see [Metrics](metrics.md)).

The `rabbitmq_alarm` [alert kind](alerts.md#rule-kinds) fires while a node
matching its target reports a memory or disk alarm.

## REST API

`GET /api/rabbitmq/overview`, `GET /api/rabbitmq/dlqs`,
`GET /api/rabbitmq/dlqs/{name}/messages` and
`POST /api/rabbitmq/dlqs/{name}/requeue`; see the
[REST API reference](rest-api.md#rabbitmq).


<!-- docs/dead-letters.md -->

# Dead letters

The **Dead letters** page lists runs that failed for good, in one place, and
lets you fix their arguments and run them again, one at a time or many at once.

## What counts as a dead letter

A run is a dead letter when both of these are true:

- Its status is `failed`. While Celery is still retrying a task the run reads
  `retried`; it only becomes `failed` once Celery has given up, so every
  retry a task was allowed has been used.
- Nothing was run again from it. When you run a dead letter again (here, or
  with **Retry** on its page) the new run records which run it came from, and
  the original leaves the list straight away, whether the new run succeeds,
  is still queued, or fails again.

A new run that fails again is a dead letter in its own right. Its **Earlier
runs** column counts the runs that came before it in the chain, so a task that
keeps failing is easy to spot.

Nothing extra is stored: the list is a query over the run history, so there
is no new table and no migration. Celery's own retries reuse the task id and
are not separate rows, so **Earlier runs** counts re-runs made through
celery-manager, not Celery's automatic retries.

## The page

- **Summary.** Dead letters counted by task and exception type, biggest first.
  Click a group to filter the list to it.
- **Filters.** Task, exception type, and how recently the run failed.
- **The list.** Each row shows the task, the exception type, the last line of
  the traceback, how many earlier runs led to it, and when it failed. The task
  links to the run's own page.

Viewers see the page and the list but not the buttons.

## Running them again

Operators (see [Roles](roles.md)) can:

- **Edit arguments and run again** on a row: opens the editor prefilled with
  the run's arguments and keyword arguments. The new run goes to the same
  queue as the original.
- **Run N again, same arguments** for the selected rows. Tasks can be mixed.
- **Run again with new arguments** for the selected rows: one set of
  arguments for all of them, so every selected run must be of the same task.
  The button is disabled otherwise.

At most 500 runs can be run again in one go. Selection survives paging and
filtering, so you can pick runs across pages.

Reruns preserve the original tenant, correlation ID, operation key and approved
metadata under the current metadata policy. The new initiator identifies the
acting operator. External observations stay visible for diagnosis but cannot be
rerun through Celery controls.

Everything is checked before anything is sent. If a selected run is no longer
a dead letter (someone else ran it again first), or its stored arguments cannot
be read back, nothing is dispatched and the message says why. For stored
arguments that cannot be read, supply them yourself with the editor. If the
broker refuses one run part-way, the others still go, and the refused ones stay
in the list.

After a run the page shows links to the new runs. Each run is written to the
[audit log](rest-api.md#audit-log) as `rerun_dead_letter`, with whether the
arguments were changed (and the arguments sent, when they were).

## Reviewing without rerunning

Use acknowledge or ignore to remove a failure from the active inbox without
changing its execution result. Reopen restores an otherwise eligible failure;
see the review API below.

## REST API

| Method | Path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/api/dead-letters` | any signed-in user |
| `POST` | `/api/dead-letters/rerun` | `operator` |

See the [REST API reference](rest-api.md#dead-letters).

## Acknowledge, ignore and reopen (0.3)

The failure inbox excludes failed runs whose current resolution is acknowledged
or ignored. Their task rows, logs and traceback remain readable; acknowledgement
is a workflow decision, not a change to Celery's execution result. Reopening makes
a still-unretried failure appear in the inbox again.

Use **Review failure** next to a run, or enter its full task ID in the failure
history panel. Operators can acknowledge, ignore or reopen with an optional note
(up to 2,000 characters). Viewers can inspect the history. Each transition records
actor, stable subject when available, note and timestamp, and writes an audit
entry. Repeating the same state and note is idempotent. History has no foreign key
to task runs so run-retention pruning does not delete it.

| Route | Minimum role |
|---|---|
| `POST /api/dead-letters/{task_id}/acknowledge` | operator |
| `POST /api/dead-letters/{task_id}/ignore` | operator |
| `POST /api/dead-letters/{task_id}/reopen` | operator |
| `GET /api/dead-letters/{task_id}/history` | viewer |

POST bodies are optional `{ "note": "Investigating upstream timeout" }` objects.
Only failed runs can be resolved (409 otherwise), and unknown task IDs return
404 on writes. History is ordered oldest first and can be read after the original
run is pruned. Reopening an already retried failure does not undo its retry lineage
or put it back in the unretried inbox.


<!-- docs/retention.md -->

# Data retention

Every task run is stored, with its arguments, traceback and captured logs.
On a busy system that grows without limit. Data retention deletes runs older
than a number of days you choose, per task if you like.

**It is off by default.** Until an admin sets a number of days, nothing is
ever deleted, so upgrading changes nothing.

## Setting the rules

In the dashboard, an admin opens **Settings**, then **Data retention**:

- **Keep runs for (days)** is the default for every task. Empty keeps runs
  forever.
- **Keep failed runs for (days)** is optional. It can only keep failed runs
  *longer* than the rule that applies to their task, so it must be at least
  the default. Empty means failed runs follow the normal rule.
- **Keep the audit log for (days)** also deletes old [audit log](dashboard.md#audit-log)
  entries. Empty, the default, keeps them all.
- **Per-task rules** override the default for one task. Pick the task from
  the list of tasks celery-manager knows, then give a number of days, or tick
  **Keep forever** to exempt that task from the default.

**Preview what would be deleted** counts, without deleting anything, what a
prune would remove if the form were saved. Anyone signed in can preview;
saving needs the `admin` [role](roles.md).

The rules are stored in the `app_settings` table, so there is no migration
for this feature.

From Python:

```python
from celery_manager.control.retention import update_retention

update_retention(session, {
    "default_days": 30,
    "failed_days": 90,
    "tasks": {"reports.nightly": 7, "billing.invoice": None},  # None: keep forever
}, username="admin")
```

## What is deleted, and what never is

A run's age is when it **finished**. A run that never finished (the worker
died, an event was lost) is judged by when it was last updated instead.

Never deleted:

- A **queued or started** run is only deleted after it has gone the whole
  period with no update. A run that is waiting or still working is safe.
  Progress reports count as an update.
- A run with an **ETA in the future**, however old its row is.
- With failed runs kept longer, a **retry of a failed run** is kept for as
  long as the failed run is. Otherwise the original would show up again under
  [Dead letters](dead-letters.md) once its retry was deleted.

Deleting a run also deletes its captured logs and progress, which live on the
same row. Retry and workflow links store task ids rather than database
references, so a run whose parent was pruned still displays normally; the
parent is simply not shown.

The [Insights](insights.md) pages and [metrics](metrics.md) are computed from
stored runs, so history shorter than your retention period disappears from
them as well.

## Queue depth samples

The [depth history](queues.md#depth-history) samples are not governed by
these rules. They have no task name and are tiny, so one setting covers
them: `queue_sample_retention_days` (14 by default, `0` keeps them). A prune
deletes older samples along with the runs and audit rows, and reports them as
`samples_deleted`.

## Running a prune

Nothing prunes on its own. Pick one of these.

**From the command line** (use cron or a Kubernetes CronJob):

```bash
celery-manager prune --db-url postgresql://... --dry-run   # see what would go
celery-manager prune --db-url postgresql://...             # do it
```

`--batch-size` (default 1000) sets how many rows each transaction deletes.

**From Celery beat**, with the optional built-in task:

```python
from celery_manager.tasks import register_prune_task

register_prune_task(app, config, schedule=3600.0)   # hourly
```

Put it in the module your workers import. It registers the task
`celery_manager.tasks.prune` and, because `schedule` is given, a beat entry
named `celery-manager-prune`. Leave `schedule` out to add the entry yourself
or to call the task by hand. Nothing is registered unless you call it.

Large first prunes are safe: rows go in batches, one short transaction per
batch, so the table is never locked for the whole run.

## What gets recorded

A prune that deleted something writes one [audit log](dashboard.md#audit-log)
row, `prune` on `retention`, with the counts (the 25 busiest tasks, if more
were touched). The user is `cli` for the command line and `system` for the
Celery task. A prune that finds nothing writes no row, so an hourly schedule
does not fill the log. Changing the rules is audited as an `update` on
`retention`. The **Last prune** line on the Settings page shows the most
recent real prune.


<!-- docs/metrics.md -->

# Prometheus and OpenTelemetry metrics

celery-manager serves run counts, durations, failure ratios, queue depth,
online workers and missed runs at `GET /metrics`, in the Prometheus text
format. For teams that already watch Grafana.

## Turn it on

The endpoint is **off by default** and answers `404` until you set a token:

```python
config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=app,
    db_url="...",
    secret_key="...",
    metrics_token="<a long random value>",   # python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"
    metrics_cache_seconds=5.0,               # default
)
```

Scrapers send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A missing or wrong token is a
`401`. Prometheus cannot use the dashboard's session cookie, so the token is
the only credential: treat it like a password and serve `/metrics` over
HTTPS. It is a read-only `GET`, so no role applies. When the dashboard is
mounted under a prefix, so is the endpoint (`/celery-manager/metrics`).

## Prometheus scrape config

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: celery-manager
    metrics_path: /metrics            # or /celery-manager/metrics
    scheme: https
    authorization:
      type: Bearer
      credentials_file: /etc/prometheus/celery-manager.token
    scrape_interval: 30s
    scrape_timeout: 10s
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["dashboard.example.com"]
```

## What you get

Everything is computed from celery-manager's database and the broker at
scrape time, and every metric is a gauge.

| Metric | Labels | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `celery_manager_task_runs` | `task`, `status` | Runs **currently stored**. A gauge of rows, not a counter: it falls when [retention](retention.md) prunes and when a run changes status, so do not `rate()` it. |
| `celery_manager_task_runs_finished_window` | `task`, `status` | Runs that finished in the last 15 minutes. |
| `celery_manager_task_failure_ratio_window` | `task` | failed / (succeeded + failed) over the last 15 minutes. Absent for a task with nothing finished in it. |
| `celery_manager_task_runtime_window_seconds_bucket` | `task`, `le` | Runtime buckets for runs finished in the last 15 minutes (cumulative). |
| `celery_manager_task_runtime_window_seconds_sum` / `_count` | `task` | Total runtime and number of runs behind those buckets. |
| `celery_manager_queue_depth` | `queue` | Messages waiting in the broker. Omitted when the broker cannot say (a down broker, or `memory://`). |
| `celery_manager_queue_recorded_queued` | `queue` | Runs recorded as `queued` (from the database). |
| `celery_manager_queue_wait_seconds` | `queue`, `quantile` | How long runs that started in the last 15 minutes waited in the queue, excluding ETA/countdown time ([how](queues.md#wait-time)). `quantile` is `0.5`, `0.95` or `1` (the maximum). A windowed gauge, like the runtime buckets; absent for a queue with no run that has a recorded send time. |
| `celery_manager_workers_online` | none | Workers that answered a ping within `inspect_timeout_seconds`. Omitted if the broker cannot be reached. |
| `celery_manager_schedule_missed_runs_24h` | `schedule` | Scheduled firings that never arrived in the last 24 hours (needs the [stamping beat scheduler](decorator.md#missed-run-detection)). |
| `celery_manager_broker_up` | `transport` | `1` if the broker accepted a connection, `0` if not. An outage shows here, not in `collector_up`. |
| `celery_manager_broker_latency_seconds` | `transport` | Time to connect to the broker (and ping it, on Redis). Omitted while the broker is down. |
| `celery_manager_broker_memory_used_bytes` | `transport` | Redis `used_memory`. Redis only. |
| `celery_manager_broker_memory_max_bytes` | `transport` | Redis `maxmemory`; `0` means no limit. Redis only. |
| `celery_manager_broker_evicted_keys` | `transport` | Keys Redis has evicted since it started. Redis only. Above zero can mean queued tasks were lost (see [Broker health](queues.md#broker-health)). |
| `celery_manager_broker_connected_clients` | `transport` | Clients connected to Redis. Redis only. |
| `celery_manager_rabbitmq_queue_unacked` | `queue` | Messages delivered to consumers but not yet acknowledged. Every queue in the vhost (at most 200). Only with [RabbitMQ management](rabbitmq.md) configured, as are the next five. |
| `celery_manager_rabbitmq_queue_consumers` | `queue` | Consumers attached to the queue. |
| `celery_manager_rabbitmq_queue_publish_rate` | `queue` | Messages published into the queue per second, as sampled by the management API. Absent until it has a sample. |
| `celery_manager_rabbitmq_queue_deliver_rate` | `queue` | Messages delivered or fetched from the queue per second. Absent until sampled. |
| `celery_manager_rabbitmq_mem_alarm` | `node` | `1` while the node has a memory alarm (RabbitMQ blocks every publisher), else `0`. |
| `celery_manager_rabbitmq_disk_alarm` | `node` | `1` while the node has a disk-space alarm, else `0`. |
| `celery_manager_window_seconds` | none | The length of the window above: 900. |
| `celery_manager_collector_up` | `collector` | `1` or `0` for `runs`, `queues`, `queue_wait`, `workers`, `missed`, `broker`, and `rabbitmq` when RabbitMQ management is configured. `0` means that part failed and its metrics are left out of the response. |

The "histogram" is windowed, so it is exposed as gauges named
`_bucket`/`_sum`/`_count`, not as a Prometheus histogram. Use
`histogram_quantile` on it; `rate()` does not apply.

**Label cardinality is bounded.** `task` is the name of a task Celery has
registered or celery-manager has recorded, at most 200 of them; the rest are
summed into `task="other"`. Queue and schedule labels are capped at 200 too.

**Caching.** The computed snapshot is reused for `metrics_cache_seconds`
(default 5), so several scrapers, or a scrape storm, cost one database pass
and one broker round trip per interval. Set it to `0` to compute on every
request. If the broker is unreachable, a scrape still succeeds and takes up to
about three seconds per broker call; queue depth and worker count are simply
missing.

## Grafana tips

```promql
# Failure ratio per task, worst first
topk(10, celery_manager_task_failure_ratio_window)

# p95 runtime per task, over the last 15 minutes
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (task, le) (celery_manager_task_runtime_window_seconds_bucket))

# Backlog
sum(celery_manager_queue_depth)

# Alert: no workers
celery_manager_workers_online == 0

# Alert: a periodic task is not firing
celery_manager_schedule_missed_runs_24h > 0
```

`celery_manager_collector_up == 0` is worth an alert of its own: it is how
you tell a missing metric from a healthy zero.

## Grafana dashboard and alert rules

Two ready-made files ship in the repository (and the sdist) under
`examples/monitoring/`:

- `grafana-dashboard.json`: import it in Grafana (**Dashboards → New →
  Import**) and pick your Prometheus data source. Panels: broker up, workers
  online, backlog, failing collectors, failure ratio and p95 runtime per
  task, finished runs by status, queue depth and wait, missed scheduled runs,
  broker latency and Redis memory.
- `prometheus-rules.yml`: ten alerting rules (collector down, broker down, no
  workers, high failure ratio with a minimum of 10 runs, slow p95, backlog,
  queue wait, missed schedule firings, Redis evictions, RabbitMQ resource
  alarms). Add it under `rule_files:`; it passes `promtool check rules`.

The thresholds are starting points. Both files are checked in CI against the
metric names this exporter really emits, so they do not drift from it.

## OpenTelemetry

Install the extra, then register the same numbers as observable gauges:

```bash
pip install "celery-manager[otel]"
```

```python
from celery_manager.api.app import create_app
from celery_manager.metrics import otel

app, session_factory = create_app(config)
otel.register(meter_provider, app=app)   # meter_provider: your SDK MeterProvider
                                         # (omit it to use the global one)
```

Each metric above becomes an observable gauge of the same name, read from the
same cached snapshot every time your exporter collects. Only the API is
needed to import the module; configure the SDK and exporter yourself. Without
`opentelemetry-api`, `register` raises an `ImportError` that says which extra
to install. The OpenTelemetry path does not need `metrics_token`.


## Alongside an event exporter

The package's metrics summarize stored observations and manager-specific state.
For continuously accumulating event counters and a wider Grafana/Prometheus
alerting stack, deploy an independent Celery event exporter alongside it.
Keep exporter metric names and collection semantics separate from these
windowed gauges; do not apply `rate()` to a DB-derived windowed gauge.
Configure events on workers and authenticate network access to both scrape
endpoints. Existing Prometheus/Alertmanager deployments can remain the
notification authority while the dashboard supplies run links and manager
controls. The manager does not install or operate that external stack.


<!-- docs/alerts.md -->

# Alerts

Alerts send a message to Slack, a webhook or email when something goes wrong:

- a task's **failure rate** goes over a threshold,
- a **queue backs up**,
- a **worker goes offline**,
- a periodic task **misses its run**.

You set up **rules** (what to watch) and **channels** (where messages go) on
the **Alerts** page. A separate process, the **evaluator**, checks the rules
every minute and sends the messages. Each problem is an **incident**: it sends
one message when it starts and, if you want, one when it is over.

## Run the evaluator

Rules are only checked while an evaluator is running. Start one next to the
events listener:

```bash
celery-manager alerts --celery-app your_module:your_celery_app --db-url postgresql://...
```

Or run it inside the events listener process, on its own thread:

```bash
celery-manager events --celery-app your_module:your_celery_app --db-url postgresql://... --with-alerts
```

Options:

- `--interval 60`: seconds between checks (default `alert_interval_seconds`, 60).
- `--once`: check every rule once, print what was sent, and exit. Handy in a
  cron job or to try a rule out.
- `--config your_module:config`: import a whole `CeleryManagerConfig` instead
  of building one from `--celery-app` and `--db-url`. This is how the
  evaluator gets the [SMTP settings](#email) and `dashboard_url`, which have
  no command-line flags (a password on the command line is visible to every
  user on the machine in `ps`). `--celery-app` and `--db-url` given as well
  override the config's values.

From Python, `celery_manager.alerts.run_forever(session_factory, celery_app,
config)` runs the same loop, and `start_in_background(...)` runs it on a
daemon thread; `evaluate_once(...)` is one check.

The Alerts page warns when a rule has never been checked, which usually means
no evaluator is running.

### Running more than one

You can run several evaluators against the same database, for example one per
events listener, for redundancy. They don't send duplicate messages: every
decision that leads to a message is a database write only one process can win
(a unique key on the open incident, and a compare-and-set update before each
message). Nothing that decides a message is kept in memory between checks, so restarting an evaluator
loses nothing (the one exception, `broker_unreachable`'s down-since time, only delays its alert).

## Rule kinds

Every rule has a **target**: a task, queue, worker or schedule name, a
pattern such as `reports.*` or `celery@web-*`, or `*` for all. Each name that
matches is judged on its own and gets its own incident, so one rule on `*` can
tell you about three failing tasks separately.

| Kind | Target | Fires when | Parameters (default) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `failure_rate` | task name | At least `min_runs` runs of the task finished in the last `window_minutes`, and at least `rate` of them failed. Only finished runs count (succeeded and failed), as on the Insights page. | `rate` (0.2, a fraction: 0.2 is 20%), `min_runs` (10), `window_minutes` (15) |
| `queue_backlog` | queue name | The broker holds at least `depth` messages in the queue. | `depth` (1000) |
| `worker_offline` | worker name | A worker the evaluator has seen before hasn't answered a ping for `minutes`. | `minutes` (5) |
| `missed_run` | schedule name | A run of the schedule that was due in the last `window_minutes` never arrived. | `window_minutes` (60) |
| `broker_unreachable` | `*` (one broker) | The broker has not accepted a connection for `minutes`. | `minutes` (2) |
| `broker_memory` | `*` (one broker) | Redis uses at least `ratio` of its `maxmemory`. Redis only. | `ratio` (0.8, a fraction: 0.8 is 80%) |
| `queue_wait` | queue name | At least `min_runs` runs started from the queue in the last `window_minutes`, and their `quantile`-th percentile queue wait is at least `seconds`. | `seconds` (60), `quantile` (95, meaning p95; 1 to 100), `window_minutes` (15), `min_runs` (5) |
| `queue_growing` | queue name | The queue's sampled depth rose by at least `min_increase` over the last `minutes` without draining on the way. | `minutes` (15), `min_increase` (50) |
| `llm_cost` | task name or glob (`*` for all) | The task's recorded [LLM cost](llm-usage.md) in the last `window_minutes` is at least `usd`. Calls without a cost are ignored. | `usd` (10), `window_minutes` (60) |
| `rabbitmq_alarm` | RabbitMQ node name, e.g. `rabbit@node-1` | A RabbitMQ node reports a memory or disk alarm. Needs [RabbitMQ management](rabbitmq.md). | none |

An incident **resolves** when its condition no longer holds: the failures
leave the window, the queue drains, the worker answers again, or the missed
run is older than the window.

Some details per kind:

- **`failure_rate`** needs `min_runs` so one failure out of one run (100%)
  doesn't wake anyone up. A task that stops running resolves once its failures
  leave the window.
- **`queue_backlog`** reads the broker's own count, the same number as the
  [Queues page](queues.md), with the same limits: brokers that can't report a
  queue's depth (see [Queues](queues.md)) never fire. If the broker can't be
  reached the rule is marked *couldn't check* and nothing opens or resolves
  until it can.
- **`worker_offline`** remembers every worker that has answered a ping
  while a `worker_offline` rule existed. A worker that hasn't answered for 24
  hours is forgotten, which resolves its incident: it was probably scaled
  down or renamed on purpose. If the ping itself fails (broker down), the rule
  is marked *couldn't check* instead of reporting every worker offline. Uses
  `inspect_timeout_seconds` as the ping timeout.
- **`queue_wait`** measures `started_at - max(sent_at, eta)`, so ETA and
  countdown time never counts, and only runs whose send time was recorded
  (see [Wait time](queues.md#wait-time)). `min_runs` keeps three slow runs
  from paging anyone. It resolves when the slow runs leave the window.
- **`queue_growing`** reads the [depth samples](queues.md#depth-history) the
  events listener records, so it needs the listener running with
  `queue_sample_interval_seconds` above 0; the exact growth rule is defined
  there. Gaps in sampling neither fire nor resolve it.
- **`rabbitmq_alarm`** reads `/api/nodes` from the RabbitMQ management API.
  While a node has an alarm RabbitMQ blocks every publisher, so no task can
  be sent. Each node is its own incident; it resolves when the alarm clears.
  If the management API isn't configured or can't be reached the rule is
  marked *couldn't check*. The message names the alarm (memory, disk or both).
- **`missed_run`** uses the same detection as the Schedules page, so it needs
  beat to run the stamping scheduler and respects `missed_run_grace_seconds`
  (see [Missed-run detection](decorator.md#missed-run-detection)).

- **`broker_unreachable`** checks the same way as the
  [Broker panel](queues.md#broker-health) (one connection, 3s deadline). The
  target is always `*`: there is one broker, and any other target is replaced
  with `*`. To know *how long* the broker has been down, the evaluator keeps
  the time it first saw it down **in memory**, so unlike the other kinds a
  restart of the evaluator restarts that clock (a down broker alerts up to
  `minutes` late, never early). The first successful check resolves it.
- **`broker_memory`** reads Redis `used_memory` against `maxmemory`. **It
  never fires when `maxmemory` is 0** (Redis's default: no limit), because
  there is no ceiling to be near; set a `maxmemory` if you want this alert.
  On a broker that isn't Redis the rule is marked *couldn't check* with the
  reason, and an unreachable broker does the same (use `broker_unreachable`
  for that).

## Quiet period, and what gets sent

- **One incident, one message.** A rule sends a message when an incident
  opens. While the problem lasts, nothing more is sent.
- **Resolved message.** When the incident closes, the rule sends a
  "resolved" message, unless you turned **Also send a message when it
  resolves** off.
- **Quiet period** (default 60 minutes). If the same problem comes back
  within the quiet period after its last message, the new incident is
  recorded but not announced. If it is still going when the quiet period
  ends, the message is sent then; if it clears first, nobody is told, not
  even that it resolved. This keeps a flapping queue from sending a message
  every minute.
- Disabling a rule, or changing its kind or target, closes its open incidents
  without a message.

The Alerts page lists recent incidents, with "Not sent yet" on an incident the
quiet period is holding back.

## Channels

Every rule sends to any number of channels. A rule with no channels still
shows its state on the Alerts page.

Each delivery has a time limit (`alert_send_timeout_seconds`, 10 seconds). A
channel that fails or times out doesn't stop the others; its error is shown
on the channel on the Alerts page. If *every* channel of a rule fails, the
message is tried again on the next check; if only some fail, it isn't (that
would send it twice to the ones that worked).

**Send test** on a channel sends a test message straight away and shows the
channel's answer.

### Slack

Create an [incoming webhook](https://api.slack.com/messaging/webhooks) in
Slack and paste its URL. Messages have a one-line summary, the details, and an
**Open in the dashboard** link when `dashboard_url` is set.

### Webhook

Any URL that accepts a JSON `POST`. The body:

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "event": "alert.firing",
  "summary": "reports.build: 6 of 10 runs failed in the last 15 min (60%)",
  "rule": {"id": 3, "name": "Report failures", "kind": "failure_rate", "target": "reports.*"},
  "key": "reports.build",
  "details": {"failed": 6, "runs": 10, "failure_rate": 0.6, "threshold": 0.5, "window_minutes": 15},
  "opened_at": "2026-10-28T12:00:00+00:00",
  "resolved_at": null,
  "url": "https://ops.example.com/celery/#/task-types/reports.build",
  "sent_at": "2026-10-28T12:00:00+00:00"
}
```

- `event` is `alert.firing`, `alert.resolved` or `alert.test` (a test has
  `rule` and `key` set to `null`).
- `key` is the task, queue, worker or schedule name (`broker` for the broker kinds).
- `details` depends on the kind: `failed`, `runs`, `failure_rate`,
  `threshold`, `window_minutes` for `failure_rate`; `depth`, `threshold` for
  `queue_backlog`; `last_seen_at`, `offline_minutes`, `threshold_minutes` for
  `worker_offline`; `missed`, `last_due_at`, `window_minutes` for
  `missed_run`; `unreachable_minutes`, `threshold_minutes`, `error` for
  `broker_unreachable`; `used_memory`, `maxmemory`, `ratio`, `threshold` for
  `broker_memory`; `wait_seconds`, `quantile`, `runs`, `threshold`,
  `window_minutes` for `queue_wait`; `from`, `to`, `increase`, `samples`,
  `minutes`, `threshold` for `queue_growing`.
- `url` is `null` without `dashboard_url`.

Any `2xx` answer counts as delivered. Redirects are not followed and count as
a failure.

**Signing.** Give the channel a secret and every request carries two headers:

- `X-Celery-Manager-Timestamp`: Unix time in seconds.
- `X-Celery-Manager-Signature`: `sha256=` and the hex HMAC-SHA256 of
  `"<timestamp>." + body`, keyed with the secret.

To verify, recompute it over the raw body and compare in constant time, and
reject old timestamps so a captured request can't be replayed:

```python
import hashlib, hmac, time

def verify(secret: str, headers, body: bytes, max_age: int = 300) -> bool:
    timestamp = headers["X-Celery-Manager-Timestamp"]
    if abs(time.time() - int(timestamp)) > max_age:
        return False
    expected = "sha256=" + hmac.new(secret.encode(), timestamp.encode() + b"." + body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, headers["X-Celery-Manager-Signature"])
```

### Email

An email channel is a list of addresses (up to 20). The mail server is set on
`CeleryManagerConfig`, not in the dashboard:

```python
config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=app,
    db_url="postgresql://...",
    dashboard_url="https://ops.example.com/celery/",
    smtp_host="smtp.example.com",
    smtp_port=587,
    smtp_username="alerts@example.com",
    smtp_password=os.environ["SMTP_PASSWORD"],
    smtp_use_tls=True,            # STARTTLS
    alert_email_from="alerts@example.com",
)
```

Give the evaluator this config with `--config`, and the dashboard the same
settings if you want **Send test** to work for email (the test is sent from
the API process). Without `smtp_host`, email channels fail with a message
saying so.

### PagerDuty

A PagerDuty channel sends Events API v2 events. Give it the **integration
key** of a PagerDuty service (Service → Integrations → Events API v2). The URL
defaults to `https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue`; set it only for the EU
endpoint (`https://events.eu.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue`) or a proxy. The key is
stored like a webhook secret: never returned by the API, only
`routing_key_set: true`.

Each incident uses the dedup key `celery-manager:<rule id>:<key>`, so the
resolve event closes the PagerDuty incident the trigger opened, and a repeated
trigger for the same open incident does not page twice. `summary`, `source`
(`environment_name`), `component` (the task, queue or schedule), `group` (the
rule kind), the rule's details and a link to the dashboard page are included.
**Send test** triggers an `info`-severity event with the dedup key
`celery-manager:test:-`; resolve it in PagerDuty afterwards.

```json
{"name": "On call", "kind": "pagerduty", "config": {"routing_key": "<32-character integration key>"}}
```

## Security

- **Only admins** can add, change, test or delete rules and channels. Every
  signed-in role can see them and the incidents. See [Roles](roles.md).
- **Secrets are write-only.** A Slack webhook URL is itself a credential:
  whoever has it can post to your channel. The API never returns channel URLs
  in full (only scheme and host, `https://hooks.slack.com/…`) or webhook
  secrets (only whether one is set). Editing a channel without retyping the
  URL keeps the stored one. The audit log records which fields changed, not
  their values.
- **SMTP credentials never touch the database.** They live only in
  `CeleryManagerConfig`.
- **Outbound requests.** Webhook and Slack URLs are entered by an admin and
  requested by the evaluator (and by the API process for **Send test**). Only
  `http://` and `https://` URLs are accepted, redirects are not followed, and
  every request has a time limit. celery-manager does not block private or
  internal addresses: an admin could point a webhook at a service inside your
  network. Of the answer, only the status and the first 200 characters of
  an error response are kept, as the channel's last error (which every
  signed-in role can see). If that matters in your environment,
  restrict where the evaluator and API processes can connect with your
  network policy or an egress proxy (the standard `HTTPS_PROXY` variables
  are honoured).
- Every change and every test message is in the [audit log](dashboard.md#audit-log).

## Production rule kinds (0.3)

All new kinds use the existing incident, quiet-period and channel-delivery
machinery. They are available in the alert-rule editor. A missing observation,
insufficient sample or an excessive scan is **unknown**, not a recovery: existing
incidents remain open and `last_check_error` explains checks that cannot be judged.
Candidate queries are bounded to matching task names and relevant reporting or
baseline windows, with a 20,000-row ceiling. If a required candidate scan exceeds
its ceiling, the check refuses to judge rather than silently reporting a healthy
system; narrow the target/window or use external metrics for larger populations.

| Kind | Target and parameters | Firing and recovery |
|---|---|---|
| `task_failed` | task glob; `window_minutes=60` | One incident per failed task ID in the window. Clears after leaving the window or when the recorded status changes. |
| `consecutive_failures` | task glob; `count=3`, `window_minutes=1440` | Most recent completed runs (ordered by finish time then ID) all failed. A later success recovers. Fewer than `count` completed runs is unknown. |
| `run_stuck` | task glob; `seconds=3600`, `p95_multiplier=3`, `min_runs=10` | A started run exceeds the greater of the configured floor and its task's successful-run p95 over 30 days times the multiplier. With insufficient baseline, uses the explicit floor. Completion recovers; a missing start time is unknown. |
| `worker_lost` | task glob; `seconds=120` | A started run's observed worker is explicitly offline or its heartbeat is stale. A current online heartbeat/completion recovers. A worker never observed is unknown. |
| `beat_stale` | target should be `*`; `seconds=120` | Stored beat heartbeat exceeds the threshold. A fresh tick recovers. No heartbeat or malformed stored heartbeat is unknown. |
| `task_sla` | task glob; `seconds=3600`, `window_minutes=60` | A completed run's recorded runtime exceeds its configured SLA. Clears when that run leaves the lookback window or its runtime is corrected. |
| `duration_regression` | task glob; `multiplier=2`, `baseline_days=30`, `recent_minutes=60`, `min_runs=10` | Recent successful-run p95 exceeds historical successful-run p95 by the multiplier. Baseline ends where the recent window begins: a slow new run cannot inflate its own baseline. Both windows require minimum samples; insufficient samples or zero baseline is unknown. |
| `run_late` | task glob; `seconds=300`, `window_minutes=60` | A scheduled occurrence (stamped by the beat mixin) due in the window started more than `seconds` after it was due, or still has not started that long after. One incident per run. Leaving the window recovers. A finished run with no recorded start is unknown. Firings that never arrived at all are `missed_run`'s job. |
| `daily_digest` | task glob; `hour_utc=8` | One dated incident summarizing the preceding 24-hour UTC reporting window. Details include total runs, status counts and task-by-task status totals. Set `notify_resolved=False` to avoid a resolved notification when the next day's bucket replaces it. |

Daily digest incident keys contain the reporting-window end timestamp. This is a
persisted watermark: evaluator restarts reuse the incident and do not resend a
successfully recorded delivery. Every day is a distinct bucket, including empty
reporting windows once there are retained task observations. It is not an
exactly-once delivery guarantee: a recipient may accept a message before the
sender sees a timeout or before the database records success. Retries can then
produce a duplicate; webhook recipients should deduplicate by rule and incident
key. Tasks with no `finished_at` do not contribute to completed-run digests.

Stuck/lost findings never rewrite execution status or automatically retry work.
A missing heartbeat cannot prove the worker stopped executing; an automatic retry
could duplicate external side effects.


### Deep links in notifications

With `dashboard_url` set, every message links to the page that explains it:
the run itself for `task_failed`, `task_sla`, `run_stuck`, `worker_lost` and
`run_late`; the task overview for `failure_rate`, `consecutive_failures` and
`duration_regression`; the schedule's occurrences for `missed_run`; the queues
or workers page for broker, queue and worker rules. A retry is one click from
the run page; notifications never carry an action that changes state.

## Host probes and independent schedulers

`custom_probe` targets stored probe-name globs with `stale_seconds=120` by default
(1–86400). `scheduler_stale` targets registered scheduler-instance globs with
`seconds=120` (1–86400). Both are available in the alert editor. Degraded evidence
fires, healthy evidence recovers, and unknown/missing/stale probe evidence never
resolves an existing incident. Scheduler state can be degraded by heartbeat age
or an overdue expected command, including its first due occurrence.

The evaluator reads stored observations only; it never invokes a host provider
or scheduler. Configure and collect them through the
[host health APIs](real-world-operations.md#custom-health-probes-and-outbox-diagnostics).
Annotations do not automatically suppress these alerts. Global alert/probe views
remain unavailable in tenant history mode.


<!-- docs/roles.md -->

# Roles

Every dashboard account has one of three roles. Each role can do everything
the role before it can.

| Role | For | Can |
|---|---|---|
| `viewer` | People who watch: support, on-call shadowing, managers | Read operational data, subject to log access policy; manage own browser sessions. No operational writes. |
| `operator` | People who run things day to day | Everything a viewer can, plus retry (including dead letters), cancel and terminate tasks, start a task, pause, resume and edit schedules, manage maintenance windows, skip single runs, review failure inbox entries, and the worker controls you can undo from the dashboard. |
| `admin` | People who own the deployment | Everything, including purging queues, deleting or moving single queued messages, shutting down workers, changing branding and setting up alerts. |

With `tenant_resolver` enabled, [tenant history mode](tenancy.md) adds a stricter
boundary: all operational writes and global views are denied even for admin.
Only scoped history reads are admitted; the role table below describes the
normal manager-wide deployment.

External (`source="external"`) observations remain under host execution control:
Celery retry/cancel/rerun is refused regardless of role. With
`operator_safeguards=True`, the documented sensitive actions also need audited
reason/environment headers after passing role checks; see
[operator preconditions](real-world-operations.md#reasons-and-environment-confirmation-for-sensitive-actions).

The server checks the role on every request that changes something. A
request the role doesn't allow gets `403` and does nothing. The dashboard
also hides the buttons a role can't use, but that's only for convenience.
The server check is the real one. Task dispatch also applies registered-task,
allowlist, argument-schema and queue/edit policy checks; having `operator` is
necessary but does not override those restrictions. `log_view_role` may require
operator or admin for captured logs. See [production policies](production.md#safe-dispatch).

## What each role can do

| Action | Endpoint | Role needed |
|---|---|---|
| Read task lists/details, schedules, workers, queues, broker health, Insights, audit log and live stream | corresponding `GET` routes; exceptions below | `viewer` (logs may require `log_view_role`) |
| See a queue's depth history | `GET /api/queues/{name}/history` | `viewer` |
| Export tasks to CSV or JSON | `GET /api/tasks/export` | `viewer` |
| Create a backend schedule | `POST /api/schedules` | `admin` |
| Update a backend schedule | `PATCH /api/schedules/{name}` | `operator` |
| Delete a backend schedule | `DELETE /api/schedules/{name}` | `admin` |
| Preview a new schedule | `POST /api/schedules/preview` | `viewer` |
| Skip next or run a schedule now | `POST /api/schedules/{name}/skip-next`, `.../run-now` | `operator` |
| Read related operation/correlation attempts | `GET /api/tasks/{task_id}/related` | `viewer`; same tenant as selected run |
| Read stored custom probe/scheduler health | `GET /api/health/probes`, `.../schedulers` | `viewer` |
| Retire an independent scheduler's monitoring expectations | `DELETE /api/health/schedulers/{instance_id}` | `admin` |
| Read deployment/maintenance annotations | `GET /api/operations/annotations` | `viewer`; configured environment |
| Record a deployment/maintenance annotation | `POST /api/operations/annotations` | `admin` |
| Run local/configuration preflight | `GET /api/operations/preflight` | `admin` |
| Read worker heartbeat samples | `GET /api/workers/{worker}/heartbeats` | `viewer` |
| Inspect singleton leases | `GET /api/locks` | `viewer` |
| Conditionally release a singleton lease | `POST /api/locks/release` | `admin`; current lease ID and durable audit required |
| Read failure review history | `GET /api/dead-letters/{task_id}/history` | `viewer` |
| Acknowledge, ignore or reopen a failure | `POST /api/dead-letters/{task_id}/acknowledge`, `.../ignore`, `.../reopen` | `operator` |
| Export scheduler definitions | `GET /api/schedule-reconciliation/export` | `viewer` |
| Generate or apply an adoption/repair plan | `POST /api/schedule-reconciliation/plan`, `.../apply` | `admin` |
| Import legacy schedule pauses (including dry-run) | `POST /api/schedules/pause-import` | `admin` |
| Inspect beat owners and definition/consumer drift | `GET /api/health/beat`, `GET /api/schedules/health` | `viewer` |
| Retire a recorded beat owner | `DELETE /api/health/beat/owner?owner_id=...` | `admin` |
| List own tracked browser sessions | `GET /api/auth/sessions` | any signed-in role; own identity only |
| Revoke own tracked browser session | `POST /api/auth/sessions/{session_id}/revoke` | any signed-in role; own identity only |
| Bridge external authentication | `POST /api/auth/bridge` | `viewer` with fresh external authentication; opt-in |
| Force cancellation of an unknown task ID | `POST /api/tasks/{id}/cancel?force=true` | `admin` |
| Start a task | `POST /api/tasks/start` | `operator` |
| Cancel or terminate a task | `POST /api/tasks/{id}/cancel` | `operator` |
| Retry a task (with or without edited arguments) | `POST /api/tasks/{id}/retry` | `operator` |
| Retry many tasks | `POST /api/tasks/retry-bulk` | `operator` |
| Cancel many tasks | `POST /api/tasks/cancel-bulk` | `operator` |
| Run dead letters again (with or without edited arguments) | `POST /api/dead-letters/rerun` | `operator` |
| Skip or cancel one schedule run | `POST /api/schedules/{name}/occurrences/pause` | `operator` |
| Pause or resume a schedule | `POST /api/schedules/{name}/pause`, `.../resume` | `operator` |
| Preview a schedule change (the next five runs; saves nothing) | `POST /api/schedules/{name}/preview` | `viewer` |
| Change when a schedule runs, or revert it to the code's | `PUT /api/schedules/{name}/schedule`, `DELETE .../schedule` | `operator` |
| List maintenance windows | `GET /api/maintenance-windows` | `viewer` |
| Preview a maintenance window (the next five spans; saves nothing) | `POST /api/maintenance-windows/preview` | `viewer` |
| Create, edit or delete a maintenance window | `POST /api/maintenance-windows`, `PUT`/`DELETE .../{id}` | `operator` |
| Add or remove a worker pool process | `POST /api/workers/{worker}/pool/grow`, `.../shrink` | `operator` |
| Make a worker start or stop consuming a queue | `POST /api/workers/{worker}/queues/add`, `.../cancel` | `operator` |
| Set a task rate limit | `POST /api/tasks/rate-limit` | `operator` |
| Shut down a worker | `POST /api/workers/{worker}/shutdown` | `admin` |
| Purge a queue | `POST /api/queues/{name}/purge` | `admin` |
| See delayed (ETA/countdown) tasks, arguments masked | `GET /api/delayed` | `viewer` |
| See delayed tasks' argument values | `GET /api/delayed?reveal_args=true` | `operator` |
| Cancel delayed tasks | `POST /api/delayed/cancel` | `operator` |
| See stuck and lost (unacknowledged) messages (Redis) | `GET /api/queues/unacked` | `viewer` |
| Put unacknowledged messages back on their queue (Redis) | `POST /api/queues/unacked/restore` | `operator` |
| Browse the messages waiting in a queue | `GET /api/queues/{name}/messages` | `viewer` |
| Delete one waiting message (Redis) | `DELETE /api/queues/{name}/messages/{task_id}` | `admin` |
| Move one waiting message to another queue (Redis) | `POST /api/queues/{name}/messages/{task_id}/move` | `admin` |
| See RabbitMQ nodes, alarms and dead-letter queues, and browse a dead-letter queue | `GET /api/rabbitmq/overview`, `.../dlqs`, `.../dlqs/{name}/messages` | `viewer` |
| Requeue messages from a RabbitMQ dead-letter queue | `POST /api/rabbitmq/dlqs/{name}/requeue` | `admin` |
| Change branding | `PUT /api/settings` | `admin` |
| Change data retention | `PUT /api/settings/retention` | `admin` |
| Preview what retention would delete (deletes nothing) | `POST /api/settings/retention/preview` | `viewer` |
| List users | `GET /api/users` | `admin` |
| Add a user | `POST /api/users` | `admin` |
| Change a user's role | `PATCH /api/users/{username}` | `admin` |
| Reset a user's password | `POST /api/users/{username}/password` | `admin` |
| Delete a user | `DELETE /api/users/{username}` | `admin` |
| Change your own password | `POST /api/me/password` | `viewer` (any signed-in account) |
| See alert rules, channels (URLs masked) and incidents | `GET /api/alerts/rules`, `.../channels`, `.../incidents` | `viewer` |
| Add, edit or delete an alert rule | `POST /api/alerts/rules`, `PATCH`/`DELETE /api/alerts/rules/{id}` | `admin` |
| Add, edit or delete an alert channel | `POST /api/alerts/channels`, `PATCH`/`DELETE /api/alerts/channels/{id}` | `admin` |
| Send a test message to a channel | `POST /api/alerts/channels/{id}/test` | `admin` |

Why the line falls where it does:

- **Operator** controls are the ones you use in an incident and can undo.
  A paused schedule can be resumed, an edited schedule reverted to the
  code's, a pool can grow back, a rate limit can be cleared. Cancel and
  terminate are here too, because stopping a runaway task is a normal
  on-call job, and so is cancelling a delayed task. Putting a stuck Redis
  message back on its queue is here too: it deletes nothing and does what
  kombu itself does after the visibility timeout, and the server refuses it
  for anything a live worker reports holding. Seeing a delayed task's
  argument values also needs operator; viewers see their types only.
  Previewing a schedule change is a `POST` only because it
  sends a body; it changes nothing, so viewers may do it.
- **Admin** controls either lose data (a purge deletes messages for good,
  and so does deleting one waiting message; moving one changes where and
  whether it runs),
  can't be undone from the dashboard (a shut-down worker needs someone to
  start it again), or affect everyone (branding; data retention, which
  decides what is deleted for good; and alerts: a rule or channel decides
  who gets woken up, and a channel holds a webhook URL that is itself a
  credential).

`GET /metrics` is not role-based: it uses its own bearer token
([Metrics](metrics.md)), because Prometheus has no dashboard session.

### What viewers can see

Viewers see task arguments, keyword arguments, captured logs and
tracebacks, and they can export. The same goes for the arguments of
messages still waiting in a queue ([Looking inside a queue](queues.md#looking-inside-a-queue));
`queue_browser_show_args=False` leaves those out of the response for every
role. That's on purpose: a read-only role is
mostly used for debugging, and the list and detail pages already show this
data, so blocking export would only make it slower to get. If your task
arguments hold secrets, don't give that person a dashboard account at all.

## Managing accounts

### From the dashboard

Admins get a **Users** page in the sidebar. It lists every local account (see
[Roles from your own app](#roles-from-your-own-app) for users signed in by your
app) and lets
you add a user, change a role, reset a password (type one, or have a random
one generated and shown once) and delete a user. Every change is recorded in
the [audit log](dashboard.md) as `create_user`, `set_role`, `reset_password`
or `delete_user`. Passwords are never logged. Everyone, whatever their role,
can change their own password from **Change password** in the sidebar; that
needs the current password.

Rules the server enforces, with the reason shown in the dashboard:

- **There is always at least one admin.** The last admin can't be demoted
  or deleted. Make another account an admin first.
- **You can't delete your own account.** Ask another admin. (Deleting
  yourself would end your session mid-request, and another admin can do it
  just as well.)
- **You reset your own password with Change password**, not the admin reset,
  because that asks for the current one.
- Passwords are at least 8 characters and at most 72 bytes. Usernames are
  1-64 characters: letters, digits and `. _ @ + -`, starting with a letter
  or digit (so an email address works). These limits apply to accounts made
  in the dashboard; the CLI and `create_user()` accept shorter passwords as
  before.

**A password change signs the account out everywhere.** The session cookie
carries a fingerprint of the account's password hash, checked on every
request, so a reset or change ends every session issued before it. When you
change your own password, the browser you did it in stays signed in. Very old cookies without a password fingerprint fail that check. Cookies from
before tracked sessions that do have a valid fingerprint remain stateless until
expiry, password reset or signing-key rotation; they cannot be individually
revoked. Newly issued cookies also carry a registered session ID. See
[browser session compatibility](auth-sessions.md#upgrade-compatibility).

Own-session list/revocation, singleton release, beat-owner retirement and CSV
imports are documented API/CLI operations; this release does not add dedicated
dashboard screens for them. Failure review and schedule adoption/repair do have
dashboard controls. See [0.3 release scope](release-0.3.md).

### From the command line

Use the CLI. It works on the same database as the dashboard (`--db-url`):

```bash
# First account: make it an admin.
celery-manager create-user alice --role admin --db-url sqlite:///celery_manager.db

# Read-only by default.
celery-manager create-user bob --db-url sqlite:///celery_manager.db

# Change a role. It applies from that person's next request.
celery-manager set-role bob operator --db-url sqlite:///celery_manager.db

celery-manager list-users --db-url sqlite:///celery_manager.db
```

`create-user` asks for the password twice. To script it, pipe it in with
`--password-stdin`. There's no `--password` flag, because a password on the
command line ends up in shell history and in `ps`. Like the dashboard's user
admin, it requires at least 8 characters and a valid username.

From Python:

```python
from celery_manager.auth.users import create_user, set_user_role

create_user(session, "carol", "a-real-password", role="operator")
set_user_role(session, "carol", "viewer")
```

### Default roles

- **`celery-manager create-user` defaults to `viewer`.** A new account starts
  with the least access. Pass `--role` to give more.
- **`create_user()` in Python defaults to `admin`.** Setup scripts written
  before roles existed call `create_user(session, name, password)` and
  expect a working account. Changing that default would quietly give those
  scripts read-only users.
- **Upgrading makes every existing account `admin`.** Before roles, every
  account could do everything, so nobody loses access on upgrade. Demote
  people afterwards with `set-role`.
- A row added to the `users` table by hand, without a role, gets `viewer`.

A role change, or a deleted account, takes effect on the next request. The
role is read from the database every time, not stored in the session cookie.

## Checking the role from the API

`GET /api/whoami` and `POST /api/auth/login` both return the role:

```json
{"username": "bob", "role": "operator"}
```

A refused request looks like this:

```text
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
{"detail": "Not allowed: this action needs the admin role (you are operator)."}
```

The dashboard shows that message as is.

## Roles from your own app

When celery-manager is mounted in (or next to) a Django, Flask or FastAPI app,
people can sign in with that app's users instead of dashboard accounts (see
[Sign in with your app's users](integrations.md#sign-in-with-your-apps-users)).
Your app then decides each person's role, on every request, through a
`role_for(user)` function that returns `"viewer"`, `"operator"`, `"admin"`, or
`None` for no access:

| Your app | Default mapping | Other options |
|---|---|---|
| Django | superuser → `admin`, staff → `operator`, everyone else → no access | `permission_roles(admin="app.perm", operator=..., viewer=...)` (highest permission held, directly or through a group), or any function of the user (groups, a profile field) |
| Flask | none: you pass `role_for` | any function of your user object |
| FastAPI | none: your function returns the role | anything your token or user record carries |

The same three roles and the table above apply to both `/api` and `/api/v1`; only where the role is
stored changes. Things to know:

- **Changes apply on the next request**, as for local accounts: demote or
  deactivate someone in your app and their next dashboard request has the
  new role, or none.
- **`None` means no access**, shown as a "No access" page naming the account.
  It never falls back to a local account in the same browser.
- **A role that isn't one of the three is refused** with a server error
  (`500`) and a log line, not guessed. A typo like `"Admin"` locks people out
  loudly rather than letting them in quietly.
- **The Users page manages local accounts only**, and is titled "Local
  accounts" while your app signs people in. Users of your app aren't listed:
  their roles live in your app. They have no password here, so **Change
  password** is hidden for them.
- **The audit log names them by the username your app returns.**

Local accounts keep working alongside unless you set
`local_login_enabled=False`. Keeping one local admin is a sensible way back in
if your app's sign-in is ever broken.

## For contributors: adding a route

Any route that changes state must declare a role:

```python
from celery_manager.api.deps import require_admin, require_operator, require_role

@router.post("/{name}/something")
def something(name: str, username: str = Depends(require_operator)):
    ...
```

`require_role(...)` returns the username, like `get_current_user`, so audit
entries still record who did it. `create_app()` refuses to start if any
`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` route doesn't declare a role (login and
logout are the only exceptions). So a forgotten check fails the first test
run, not production. `tests/unit/test_roles.py` also pins the whole table
above, so moving an action to a different role means updating this page too.


<!-- docs/llm-usage.md -->

# LLM usage

Tasks that call a language model can record each call: model, token counts,
cost and latency. celery-manager attaches the calls to the run, shows totals on
the **Insights** page and the run's detail page, exposes them through the REST
API and MCP, and can alert on spend. **Prompts and completions are never
stored**, only counts.

## Recording calls

```python
from celery_manager import record_llm_usage, track

@app.task(bind=True)
@track()
def summarize(self, text):
    response = client.messages.create(model="...", max_tokens=512, messages=[...])
    record_llm_usage(response=response)      # model and tokens come from the response
    return response.content[0].text
```

`response` may be an Anthropic- or OpenAI-style object or its dict form. Model,
token counts (including cached input) and the number of tool calls are read from
it. Pass values yourself to override, or when you have no response object:

```python
record_llm_usage("my-model", input_tokens=812, output_tokens=140, cost_usd=0.0021)
```

To time a call and record failures too:

```python
from celery_manager.llm import llm_call

with llm_call("my-model") as call:
    call.response = client.chat.completions.create(...)
```

If the block raises, the call is recorded with status `error` and the exception
propagates. Recording never raises into your task: a failed write is logged and
the task carries on. The process needs `celery_manager.setup(config)`, like
`@track`.

## Cost

Cost is the `cost_usd` you pass, otherwise it is computed from `llm_prices` in
your config (USD per million tokens). Nothing is built in, because prices
change:

```python
CeleryManagerConfig(
    ...,
    llm_prices={
        "claude-sonnet-4": {"input": 3.0, "output": 15.0, "cache_read": 0.3},
    },
)
```

The longest matching model-id prefix wins. A model with no price has no cost;
the dashboard counts those calls as unpriced rather than showing $0.

## Where it shows up

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| Insights, Trends tab | Calls, tokens, cost, errors, cost over time, by model, by task |
| Run detail | The run's calls and totals |
| `GET /api/llm/usage?range=24h&task_name=...` | The same summary as JSON |
| `GET /api/llm/runs/{task_id}` | One run's calls |
| MCP | `llm_usage`, `run_llm_usage` |
| Alerts | The `llm_cost` rule |

### Alert on spend

The `llm_cost` rule fires per task name when its recorded cost in the last
`window_minutes` reaches `usd` (defaults 10 USD, 60 minutes). The rule's target
is a task name or glob, `*` for all. Calls without a cost are ignored.

## Retention

`llm_call_retention_days` (default 90, `0` keeps everything) controls how long
rows are kept; `celery-manager prune` and the dashboard's retention prune apply
it.


<!-- docs/agents.md -->

# Building with AI agents

celery-manager gives agents three things: a **Model Context Protocol (MCP)
server** that lets them look at and, if you allow it, operate your Celery
system; **machine-readable docs** (`llms.txt`) so a coding agent can wire the
package into your project correctly; and **LLM-usage tracking** for the agent
workloads your tasks run ([LLM usage](llm-usage.md)).

## The MCP server

```bash
celery-manager mcp --app myproject.celery:app --db-url postgresql+psycopg://... --role viewer
```

It speaks MCP over stdio (newline-delimited JSON-RPC) and needs no extra
dependency. Register it with any MCP client, for example:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "celery-manager": {
      "command": "celery-manager",
      "args": ["mcp", "--app", "myproject.celery:app", "--db-url", "postgresql+psycopg://...",
               "--role", "viewer", "--agent-name", "triage-bot"]
    }
  }
}
```

`--config module:attr` works too, for settings with no flag (`environment_name`,
`operator_safeguards`, `llm_prices`, SMTP). The server runs next to your
database, like the other CLI commands, and shares nothing with a running
dashboard.

### Roles decide what the agent can do

The agent acts as one fixed principal, `mcp:<agent-name>`, at the role you pass
to `--role`. Tools above that role are **not listed and cannot be called**.

| Role | Adds |
|---|---|
| `viewer` (default) | Read-only: runs, failure groups, workers, queues, schedules, alerts, LLM usage |
| `operator` | `retry_run`, `retry_runs`, `cancel_run`, `start_task`, `pause_schedule`, `resume_schedule`, `set_rate_limit`, `acknowledge_dead_letter` |
| `admin` | `preview_queue_purge`, `purge_queue`, `run_doctor` (broker and worker probes) |

Start with `viewer`. Every tool calls the same REST route the dashboard uses, so
validation, role checks, [operator safeguards](configuration.md) and the
[audit log](rest-api.md#audit-log) behave exactly as for a person. Audit rows
show the actor as `mcp:<agent-name>`.

### Guard rails built into the tools

- `retry_runs` defaults to `dry_run=true`. A real bulk retry needs
  `dry_run=false` and `confirm_count` equal to the number of ids (max 500).
- `purge_queue` needs `confirm` equal to the queue name.
- Write tools accept a `reason`. It is sent as the `X-CM-Action-Reason` header,
  so `operator_safeguards` deployments accept it, and it lands in the audit
  details. With `operator_safeguards` the environment confirmation is sent
  automatically (an agent has no other way to give it), so only the reason is
  a real gate. Write tools that can change state are marked `destructiveHint`
  (except `preview_queue_purge`).
- A real `retry_runs` (`dry_run=false`) is refused unless `confirm_count`
  equals the number of ids.
- Identifiers used in a URL path (task id, schedule or queue name) may not be
  empty or contain `/`, `\`, `?`, `#` or control characters.
- The stdio loop answers malformed input with JSON-RPC errors instead of
  stopping: invalid JSON, NaN/Infinity, empty batches, non-object `params`,
  and lines over 1 MiB.
- Arguments are checked against each tool's schema before any call; unknown or
  mistyped arguments come back as an error naming the field.
- Results over 40,000 characters are cut with a note to narrow the filters.

### Treat task data as untrusted

Task arguments, exceptions, tracebacks, logs and results come from your
application and can contain text written by outsiders. The server says so in its
instructions and in each tool's description, but the safest setup is also the
simplest: give an agent the `viewer` role unless it needs to act, and review
what an `operator` agent does through the audit log.

### Tools

| Tool | Role | What it returns |
|---|---|---|
| `list_runs`, `get_run`, `get_related_runs`, `get_workflow` | viewer | Run history and detail |
| `failure_groups`, `analytics_overview`, `task_stats` | viewer | Where things are failing, success rate, runtimes |
| `llm_usage`, `run_llm_usage` | viewer | LLM calls, tokens, cost |
| `list_dead_letters` | viewer | Runs that exhausted retries |
| `list_workers`, `list_rate_limits` | viewer | Live worker state, rate limits |
| `list_queues`, `queue_history`, `broker_health` | viewer | Depth, history, broker state |
| `list_schedules`, `schedule_health`, `beat_health` | viewer | Periodic schedules and whether they fire |
| `list_alert_incidents`, `list_alert_rules` | viewer | Alerting state |
| `list_registered_tasks`, `whoami` | viewer | Task names and signatures, identity |
| `run_doctor` | admin | Preflight of the configuration you started the server with |

## Machine-readable docs

- [`llms.txt`](llms.txt) is a short index of the documentation for agents.
- [`llms-full.txt`](llms-full.txt) is the whole documentation in one file, for
  loading into a coding agent's context. It is generated by
  `python scripts/build_llms_txt.py` and checked in CI.
- `celery-manager openapi -o openapi.json` writes the REST API's OpenAPI
  document offline, for generating a typed client.
- `celery-manager doctor --json` prints the preflight as JSON (`ok` and a list
  of checks with `name`, `state` and `detail`); `--fix-suggestions` prints a
  Markdown checklist with a fix for each open item.

### Teach your own coding agent

Paste this into your project's `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` so an agent that edits
your code uses celery-manager correctly:

```markdown
## celery-manager
- Docs for agents: https://pythondeveloper6.github.io/celery-manager/llms-full.txt
- Call `celery_manager.setup(config)` once per process, including the Celery worker.
- Decorate tasks with `@app.task` first, then `@track()` directly below it.
- Record LLM calls inside tasks with `record_llm_usage(response=...)`.
- Run `celery-manager doctor --fix-suggestions` after changing Celery settings.
```

## Not included

Authenticated remote access (an HTTP transport with API tokens) is not part of
this release: the MCP server runs where the database is. Idempotency keys on
write routes are not implemented either; the bulk tools' dry run and
confirmation counts are the protection against repeated calls.


<!-- docs/sql-schedules.md -->

# Durable SQL schedules and explicit ownership

Install `celery-manager[sqlalchemy-beat]` to store schedule definitions in
sqlalchemy-celery-beat's SQL tables. This is separate from celery-manager's
monitoring tables and separate from Celery's result backend. Importing
celery-manager does not require the optional scheduler package.

## Deployment

Use the same URL and schema in the dashboard process and the beat process:

```python
from celery_manager import CeleryManagerConfig
from celery_manager.schedulers import SQLAlchemyBeatBackend

app.conf.beat_dburi = "postgresql+psycopg://user:password@db/tasks"
app.conf.beat_schema = "celery_schedules"  # optional; provision it first
backend = SQLAlchemyBeatBackend(app)
# Run this once as a deployment step, with DDL privileges:
backend.initialize()
config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=app,
    db_url="postgresql+psycopg://user:password@db/monitoring",
    secret_key="load-a-secret-from-your-environment",
    scheduler_backend=backend,
)
```

Start one beat process for this schedule namespace:

```shell
celery -A myproject.celery_app beat -S celery_manager.beat:SQLAlchemyDatabaseScheduler
```

The shipped scheduler stamps scheduled messages with their schedule and occurrence
identity, so occurrence pauses and monitoring use the same identity as other
celery-manager schedulers. It retains upstream reserve/sync behavior and persists
run counters. Initialization is explicit: beat does not silently create tables.
Upstream table upgrades remain the deployment operator's responsibility when
upgrading the optional package; celery-manager migrations manage monitoring tables.

Each backend and scheduler instance has an independent engine and schema mapping.
Different projects can use different URLs or schemas in one process. Projects
sharing a URL and schema intentionally share a namespace; schedule names must then
be unique. Named schemas must already exist. SQLite uses no schema by default.
`backend.close()` releases its pool when the host shuts down. Do not run several
beat owners against one namespace without external leader election.

CRUD supports intervals in whole seconds (1–2147483647; the upstream column is
a portable 32-bit integer), crontab (including its timezone), and solar schedules.
Arguments, keyword arguments, enabled state, queue, exchange, routing key,
priority, headers and expiry are persisted. Relative expiry is nonnegative whole
seconds; absolute expiry accepts a timezone-aware datetime or ISO timestamp. Unsupported delivery
options fail rather than being dropped. Existing upstream rows using `one_off`
or `start_time` fail with an explicit error: this adapter cannot yet export or edit
those semantics safely. Clocked schedules and intervals with `relative=True` rounding are not supported. Solar schedules also need Celery's solar
dependencies. The HTTP schedule editor currently accepts interval/crontab specs;
solar definitions can be supplied through Python or an exported document.

## Choose which side owns definitions

SQL is authoritative when using the shipped SQL scheduler. It deliberately does
not import `app.conf.beat_schedule` at every startup: doing so would overwrite
operator edits after a restart. Existing code definitions enter SQL through an
explicit adoption plan. Keep a single owner policy per deployment:

- `backend`: observe differences only. SQL, Redis, or Django Beat remains the
  source of truth and the plan applies no changes.
- `code`: compare code definitions with a writable backend and explicitly adopt
  missing definitions. Existing changes require `allow_updates=True`.
- `sql`: use the same explicit adoption/repair workflow, requiring the SQL backend.
  After adoption, SQL edits survive deployment and beat restart.

This ownership choice controls each reconciliation operation; it is not a second
background sync process. Existing Redis/Django scheduler startup behavior is
unchanged. If a backend's own scheduler imports code definitions at startup,
configure that scheduler consistently with your chosen policy.

## Dry run, adoption and repair from Python

```python
from celery_manager.schedulers.base import StaticBeatBackend
from celery_manager.schedulers.reconcile import (
    export_backend, load_export, plan_reconcile, apply_reconcile,
)

# Dry run: no writes, default backend ownership means observation only.
comparison = plan_reconcile(backend, StaticBeatBackend(app).list())

# Review and persist this JSON plan before applying it.
plan = plan_reconcile(backend, StaticBeatBackend(app).list(), ownership="sql")
result = apply_reconcile(backend, plan, app=app)

# Back up all backend definitions as JSON-serializable data.
backup = export_backend(backend)

# Repair missing entries from a reviewed backup. Existing differences remain
# unapplied until explicitly opting into updates.
desired = load_export(backup, app)
repair = plan_reconcile(backend, desired, ownership="sql", allow_updates=True)
result = apply_reconcile(backend, repair, app=app)
```

A plan lists `create`, `update`, and `extra` changes with complete before/after
values and an `apply` flag. No reconciliation operation deletes schedules;
`extra` always remains unapplied. Individual schedule deletion is a separate,
explicit CRUD operation. A backup contains definitions, not last-run counters,
execution history, monitoring overrides or broker messages. Restoring it does not
replay past tasks. Unsupported schedule objects or non-JSON arguments cause export
to fail, rather than returning a misleading backup.

Apply validates all definitions before its first write, rejects duplicate plan
names, checks a fingerprint of the reviewed backend, then rechecks each target
before changing it. Runtime last-run counters do not invalidate a plan. A definition
change after review raises `ReconcileConflict`; generate and review a fresh plan.
Reconciliation across the supported backends is not one database transaction:
a connection failure or concurrent writer can leave partial progress. Review a
fresh diff after failure. Pause other administrative writers for a consistent
repair; the snapshot check is not a distributed lock.

## Moving from RedBeat or code to SQL

`celery-manager copy-schedules` copies every definition from one backend into
another in one reviewed step. It prints the plan as JSON and writes nothing
unless you pass `--apply`:

```shell
# Review: what would be created in the SQL scheduler from RedBeat?
celery-manager copy-schedules --config myproject.cm:config --from redbeat --to sql
# Apply the same plan.
celery-manager copy-schedules --config myproject.cm:config --from redbeat --to sql --apply
```

`--from` is `code` (the app's `beat_schedule`), `redbeat` or `sql`; `--to` is
`sql` or `redbeat`. The SQL side uses the app's `beat_dburi`/`beat_schema`
unless `--beat-db-url`/`--beat-schema` are given. Entries present only in the
target are reported as `extra` and left alone; entries whose definition differs
are only overwritten with `--allow-updates`. Run-state (last run time, total run
count) is not copied, so each schedule starts fresh in the target.

A safe cut-over: stop beat, run the dry run and review it, apply, switch beat to
`celery_manager.beat:SQLAlchemyDatabaseScheduler`, start
beat, and keep the old RedBeat keys until the new scheduler has fired each
schedule once. The same function is available from Python as
`celery_manager.schedulers.reconcile.copy_schedules(source, target, app=app,
apply=False)`.

Monitoring-side pauses and per-occurrence overrides live in celery-manager's
own tables, not in the scheduler backend, so they survive the move unchanged.
Pauses kept in a legacy table of your own can be imported with
[`celery-manager import-pauses`](release-0.3.md#legacy-pause-csv-import).

## HTTP workflow

Authenticated viewers can download `GET /api/schedule-reconciliation/export`.
Administrators can generate a plan with
`POST /api/schedule-reconciliation/plan`:

```json
{"ownership":"sql","allow_updates":false}
```

Omit `document` to compare code's `beat_schedule`. To restore a backup, pass its
complete export object as `document`. Send the reviewed plan object itself to
`POST /api/schedule-reconciliation/apply`. The response lists `applied` names and
an always-empty `deleted` list. An audit intent is persisted before backend changes, so an unavailable audit
database prevents application. Successful applications also write an outcome and
refresh the dashboard's backend snapshot. The API validates task registration and
reserved occurrence headers before applying. A stale plan returns 409, invalid
definitions return 422. These endpoints obey the same authentication and CSRF
rules as other administrative endpoints. Equivalent `/api/v1` aliases are included by the shipped application.

## Verification limits

The adapter's integration tests exercise the real optional package with SQLite,
including restart durability and the shipped scheduler's stamp/counter contract.
Connection drivers and deployment permissions are supplied by the host. Run the
same deployment smoke test against your PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server version
before enabling production writes; SQLite verification alone does not establish
that every server and isolation configuration behaves identically.

## Dashboard adoption and repair

Administrators can open **Schedules → Schedule backup and reconciliation**.

1. Choose **Export backend JSON** to download the current definitions as a
   version-1 backup. Exports may contain arguments and headers; store them as
   carefully as your scheduler configuration.
2. Leave **Desired export JSON** blank to compare code's current `beat_schedule`,
   or paste a complete exported document to adopt or restore those definitions.
3. Choose **Backend** for observation only, **Code** to adopt desired definitions,
   or **SQL** to adopt into the `sqlalchemy-beat` backend. These are explicit
   reconciliation modes for this operation; applying a plan does not install a
   continuous code-to-backend synchronization job.
4. Enable **Include repairs of differing existing entries** only when existing
   definitions should be updated. New missing definitions can be adopted without
   enabling repairs. Extra backend entries are displayed and never deleted.
5. Choose **Generate review plan**. Expand each difference to inspect its complete
   before/after definition, including task, timezone, arguments and options. A
   selected write can be unchecked; regenerate the plan to select it again.
6. Check the explicit approval statement, then choose **Apply reviewed changes**.
   This is unavailable on a read-only backend or an observation-only plan. Any
   change to inputs invalidates the old plan. Each apply attempt consumes the
   displayed plan and approval, including failures: inspect the backend and
   generate a fresh plan before retrying.

A backend definition changed after review yields a conflict, so the operator must
