| `pause_schedule` | `schedule` | the schedule name | `POST /api/schedules/{name}/pause` — only when it actually pauses (not on an idempotent repeat); `details` is `null` |
| `resume_schedule` | `schedule` | the schedule name | `POST /api/schedules/{name}/resume` — only when it actually resumes; `details={"paused_at", "paused_by"}` of the pause it ended |
| `edit_schedule` | `schedule` | the schedule name | `PUT /api/schedules/{name}/schedule` — only when the spec changes; `details={"before", "after", "code", "unmatched_overrides"}` (`before` is `null` when it ran as the code said) |
| `revert_schedule` | `schedule` | the schedule name | `DELETE /api/schedules/{name}/schedule` — only when there was an edit; `details={"before", "code", "edited_by", "edited_at"}` |
| `cancel_bulk` | `task` | `selection` (by ids), `filter`, or `delayed` (`POST /api/delayed/cancel` with several ids) | `POST /api/tasks/cancel-bulk` (not on `dry_run`, nor when nothing matched) — `details={"terminate", "revoked", "skipped_finished", "unknown", "filter", "task_ids"}` |
| `purge` | `queue` | the queue name | `POST /api/queues/{name}/purge` — `details={"messages_removed", "runs_marked_revoked", "task_ids"}` (the runs marked `revoked`) |
| `restore_unacked` | `queue` | the queue name, or `selection` when messages from several queues were restored | `POST /api/queues/unacked/restore` — `details={"restored", "missing", "refused", "force"}` |
| `delete_message` | `queue` | the queue name | `DELETE /api/queues/{name}/messages/{task_id}` — `details={"task_id", "task_name", "run_marked_revoked"}` |
| `move_message` | `queue` | the queue it left | `POST /api/queues/{name}/messages/{task_id}/move` — `details={"task_id", "task_name", "from", "to"}` |
| `requeue_dead_letters` | `rabbitmq_queue` | the dead-letter queue | `POST /api/rabbitmq/dlqs/{name}/requeue` — `details={"moved", "task_ids", "refused", "forced", "error"}` |
| `update` | `setting` | the setting key (`brand_name`, `brand_accent`, `brand_logo_url`) | `PUT /api/settings` — one row per *changed* key, `details={"old", "new"}` (each truncated to 200 characters, so a data-URI logo doesn't turn the audit log into an image store) |
| `update` | `retention` | `retention` | `PUT /api/settings/retention` — only when the rules changed, `details={"old", "new"}` |
| `prune` | `retention` | `task_runs` | `celery-manager prune` (user `cli`), the `celery_manager.tasks.prune` task (user `system`) — only when something was deleted, `details={"runs_deleted", "audit_deleted", "samples_deleted", "by_task"}` |

A retry records only `retry`, never an additional `start`, even though it
dispatches through the same `start_task` call underneath.

## Live updates (SSE)

| Method | Path | Auth | Response |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/api/stream` | required | `text/event-stream`. Opens with a `: connected` comment frame, then sends one `data: {"type": "task-updated", "task_id": str, "status": str, "updated_at": str}\n\n` event (default `message` event name, no custom `event:` field) per changed `task_runs` row, and a `: keepalive` comment every 15 seconds while idle. Connection stays open indefinitely; the client (dashboard) reconnects with the browser's native `EventSource` retry behavior. |

Like every other endpoint on this page, it returns `401` without a valid
session cookie. (Development builds before 0.1.0a1 had no auth on it at all.) The browser's
`EventSource` sends the cookie when opened with `withCredentials: true`,
which is what the dashboard does.

The dashboard's task list subscribes to this stream and refetches
`/api/tasks` when events arrive (coalesced to at most one refetch a second)
rather than applying them to its local state directly; a task's detail page
refetches that one run when an event names it — see
[Dashboard](dashboard.md).

### How changes reach the stream

Most writes worth announcing happen outside the API process: the events
listener (`celery-manager events`) and the workers (`@track`,
`report_progress()`) are separate OS processes. They don't publish anything
themselves. Instead every write to a run bumps its `task_runs.updated_at`
column, and each API process polls the database for rows whose
`updated_at` moved on since it last looked, then pushes one event per row
to its own connected browsers. So the stream works with the listener in its
own process, with several API processes behind a load balancer, and without
any broker or extra infrastructure. The database is the only shared piece.

- **Interval.** The poll runs every
  [`live_poll_interval_seconds`](configuration.md) (default 1.0), so an
  event reaches the browser up to about a second after the write commits.
- **Only while someone is watching.** One poller thread per API process
  starts with the first `/api/stream` connection and stops when the last
  one closes. No lifespan hooks are involved, so this works the same when
  the app is mounted inside a host application.
- **Cost.** Each poll is one or two small queries on the indexed
  `updated_at` column (a bounded batch, `(updated_at, id)` keyset paging).
- **Ordering and duplicates.** A row written several times between two
  polls produces one event carrying its latest status. Each poll also
  re-reads the last few seconds, which catches transactions that commit
  later than their timestamp and writers whose clocks are slightly skewed,
  and drops anything it has already sent.
- **No replay.** A connection gets changes from the moment it opens, not
  the ones it missed while disconnected. Clients should refetch on
  (re)connect, as the dashboard does.


## Production API additions (0.2)

See [production adoption](production.md) for identity setup, optional extras,
scheduler ownership, dispatch validation and the deployment checklist.

| Method | Path | Minimum role | Contract |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/api/auth/bridge` | viewer, external authentication | Disabled unless explicitly enabled. Issues a short cookie after fresh external authentication; cannot renew from the bridge cookie alone. |
| `GET` | `/api/schedules/backend` | viewer | Backend `name`, `writable`, and recommended `beat_scheduler` class. |
| `POST` | `/api/schedules/preview` | viewer | A schedule spec or `{schedule: spec}`; returns validated `schedule`, description, timezone and ten UTC ISO `occurrences`. Text specs use `{type:"text", text:"weekdays at 06:30"}`. Saves nothing. |
| `POST` | `/api/schedules` | admin | `{name, task, schedule, args?, kwargs?, options?, enabled?}`. Registered user task required. Returns definition; duplicate 409, read-only backend 409, invalid input 422. |
| `PATCH` | `/api/schedules/{name}` | operator | Partial schedule/args/kwargs/options/enabled update; explicit null fields are refused. Backend must be writable. |
| `DELETE` | `/api/schedules/{name}` | admin | Deletes the backend definition; run and override history remain. |
| `POST` | `/api/schedules/{name}/skip-next` | operator | Records the next enabled occurrence as a one-off skip. Repeated calls use existing tolerance-based idempotence. No available occurrence returns 409. |
| `POST` | `/api/schedules/{name}/run-now` | operator | Dispatches the entry arguments through the task policy. Returns `{task_id}`; carries no occurrence header and consumes no scheduled skip. |
| `GET` | `/api/schedules/health` | viewer | Backend/definition drift, unregistered tasks and historical entries missing from the backend. Optional `inspect_consumers=true` adds bounded observed-consumer diagnostics; unknown replies do not prove absent workers. |
| `GET` | `/api/health/beat` | viewer | Healthy/stale/unknown beat state, last tick and age. Optional `stale_seconds` threshold. |
| `GET` | `/api/health/workers` | viewer | Durable last-seen worker online/offline observations. |
| `GET` | `/api/health/runs` | viewer | Advisory `worker_lost`/`suspect_stuck` findings; optional `stuck_seconds`. Never changes execution status. |

Task detail adds `result_repr`, `result_truncated`, `log_output_truncated`,
`logs_restricted` and `initiator`. Restricted log output is `null`; a result can be
`null` because collection is disabled or no result was recorded. Truncated results
are display text, not guaranteed valid JSON. Audit entries add `actor_subject`.
Schedule summaries add `source`, `backend_writable` and a stored `definition`.
Auth options additionally expose `live_stream`, `allow_queue_override` and
`retry_edit_args`; `external` also covers configured principal providers.

Task dispatch defaults to registered user tasks only and additionally applies
`startable_tasks`, argument schemas and edit/queue restrictions. These checks
cover retry, bulk retry, failed-run reruns and schedule run-now too. Denials are
audited as `start_denied`. An unknown single cancel returns 404; an admin may
explicitly request `?force=true` (other roles receive 403).

With `live_stream="poll"`, `/api/stream` is absent and the SPA polls. Teams is an
additional alert-channel kind with `{url}` configuration; the URL is write-only.


## Native observations and operator context (0.3)

[Real-world operations](real-world-operations.md) documents Python `RunObserver`,
probe collection, scheduler registration, metadata/privacy and preflight.
Observation writes belong to trusted host code; there is no anonymous HTTP
endpoint for inventing observations or assigning tenants.

Task list/detail responses add `source`, `tenant_id`, `correlation_id`,
`operation_key` and bounded `context_json`. `source="external"` identifies work
whose execution remains owned by the host; Celery retry/cancel/rerun refuses it
with 409. External lifecycle states include `interrupted`; an unreported hard
crash can still leave a started row. Related-run matching is visibility only.
Manager retries, bulk retries and failed-run reruns preserve original
tenant/correlation/operation metadata under the current metadata policy, while
recording the acting operator as initiator. Invalid stored context fails before
publication, including full-scope validation before a bulk batch is sent.

| Method | Endpoint | Role | Request/response contract |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/api/tasks/{task_id}/related` | viewer | `kind=operation` (default) or `correlation`; `limit=100`, 1–500. Same-tenant matches from either source, newest first; `{items,has_more,kind}`. No key returns an empty list, unknown run 404. |
| `GET` | `/api/health/probes` | viewer | Stored latest sanitized measurements and freshness; no provider invocation. `{items}` with name/state/metrics/reason/observation age. More than 1,000 persisted names returns 503 instead of a partial inventory. |
| `GET` | `/api/health/schedulers` | viewer | Stored independent scheduler heartbeats and command expectations, including first-run due state; `{items}`. Does not contact or start the host scheduler. More than 1,000 instances returns 503. |
| `DELETE` | `/api/health/schedulers/{instance_id}` | admin | Audit and retire monitoring expectations; `{removed}`. Does not stop execution. |
| `GET` | `/api/operations/annotations` | viewer | Configured environment only; optional start-time `date_from`/`date_to`, `limit=50` (1–200), `offset=0`. `{items,has_more,environment}`. |
| `GET` | `/api/operations/context` | viewer | Required `at` timestamp. Latest deployment at/before it and maintenance active at it, scoped to configured environment. `{at,environment,deployment,maintenance,has_more}`; maintenance capped at 200. No suppression or causal inference. |
| `POST` | `/api/operations/annotations` | admin | `{kind,label,revision?,note?,starts_at?,ends_at?}`; `kind` deployment/maintenance. Maintenance requires a later end. Returns stored annotation with ID/environment/actor; creation is audited. No edit/delete endpoint. |
| `GET` | `/api/operations/preflight` | admin | Read-only storage/configuration diagnostic report `{ok,environment,checked_at,checks}`. Outbound broker/worker checks require CLI/Python opt-in. |

All have equivalent `/api/v1` aliases. Monitoring-only deployments
(`celery_app=None`) refuse Celery broker/worker/scheduler execution controls with
409. [Tenant history mode](tenancy.md) is more restrictive: SQL-scoped task reads
only, all global views and operational writes denied even for admin, including
metrics/events/annotations/preflight. Newly added endpoints are denied until
explicitly admitted to its reviewed allowlist.

Auth options add `monitoring_only`, `tenant_scoped`, `read_only`, `environment`
and `sensitive_actions`. The latter is the enabled sensitive-action pattern list;
with safeguards disabled it is empty. Tenant mode forces `live_stream="poll"`.
`whoami` includes its resolved tenant when scoped. These flags help the dashboard
hide controls; server enforcement does not depend on the flags reaching a client.

With `operator_safeguards=True`, protected HTTP requests must send UTF-8
percent-encoded `X-CM-Action-Reason` (decoded printable 1–500 characters) and
`X-CM-Confirm-Environment` (exact configured environment). Missing/invalid
preconditions return 428, unavailable intent audit returns 503, and neither
performs the action. Authentication, role and task-policy restrictions still
apply. Accepted intent does not imply successful completion. The complete
[action list and audit semantics](real-world-operations.md#reasons-and-environment-confirmation-for-sensitive-actions)
apply equally to mounted and versioned routes.


<!-- docs/configuration.md -->

# Configuration reference

Every celery-manager process — the API app, the `celery-manager events`
listener and the `celery-manager alerts` evaluator — is configured through a single dataclass,
`celery_manager.config.CeleryManagerConfig`:

```python
from celery_manager.config import CeleryManagerConfig

config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=your_celery_app,
    db_url="sqlite:///celery_manager.db",
    # Placeholder — replace with your own private random value, e.g. from
    # python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"
    secret_key="<your-generated-secret>",
    eta_tolerance_seconds=60,
    missed_run_grace_seconds=300,
    cookie_secure=True,
    auto_migrate=True,
    inspect_timeout_seconds=1.0,
    schedule_editing=False,
)
```

| Field | Type | Default | What it affects |
|---|---|---|---|
| `celery_app` | `celery.Celery \| None` | `None` | `None` enables monitoring-only host-job observations; Celery execution/broker/schedule controls return 409. Supply your application's Celery instance for task introspection (dispatching tasks via `send_task`, reading `beat_schedule` to compute upcoming occurrences) and control calls (`revoke`/`terminate`). The API app and the events listener must both be given the *same* Celery app configuration (same broker, same `beat_schedule`) or their views of the world will disagree. |
| `db_url` | `str` | `"sqlite:///celery_manager.db"` | SQLAlchemy connection URL for celery-manager's own storage (task runs, schedules, overrides, users, audit log — see `celery_manager.db.models`). Any SQLAlchemy-supported backend works; swap to Postgres/MySQL/etc. for production. For `sqlite:///:memory:` specifically, the engine is built with `StaticPool` so every connection shares one in-memory database — needed for it to behave sensibly under FastAPI's threadpool (as used in the test suite); other SQLite URLs use `check_same_thread=False` instead. Every process that needs to see the same data (API app + events listener) must point at the same `db_url`. |
| `secret_key` | `str` | `"change-me"` (a placeholder) | Signs session cookies for the built-in cookie-based auth (`itsdangerous.URLSafeTimedSerializer`, sessions valid for `session_max_age_seconds`, default 7 days). Anyone who knows the key can forge a valid session cookie for any username, so **`create_app()` raises `ValueError` and refuses to start if it is empty or still `"change-me"`** — set a private random value in every process that serves the dashboard, local development included. Processes that don't serve HTTP (Celery workers calling `celery_manager.setup()`, the events listener) never sign sessions and may leave the default. Rotating it invalidates every existing session (users are signed out). See [`secret_key` in production](#secret_key-in-production). |
| `eta_tolerance_seconds` | `int` | `60` | How far apart two timestamps of the same occurrence may be: an interval-schedule occurrence stamped by beat vs. a saved `target_time` (in `@track`, capped at half the interval), and a saved `target_time` vs. a recomputed occurrence (in `GET /api/schedules/{name}/occurrences`). It is compared with "now" only for messages without occurrence headers while beat has never stamped any (see [How the skip/cancel check works](decorator.md#how-the-skipcancel-check-works)). See the trade-off below. |
| `missed_run_grace_seconds` | `int` | `300` | How long after a scheduled run was due it may still arrive before it is reported as missed (`GET /api/schedules/{name}/missed`, the `missed_count` on `GET /api/schedules`). Detection needs beat to run the stamping scheduler (see [Missed-run detection](decorator.md#missed-run-detection)). Raise it if your broker or workers are routinely slow to start a run. |
| `cookie_secure` | `bool` | `True` | Sets the `Secure` flag on the session cookie, so browsers only ever send it back over HTTPS. See below for why the default is `True` and when to change it. |
| `export_max_rows` | `int` | `50000` | Hard cap on rows in one `GET /api/tasks/export` download. Larger results are cut to the newest rows and flagged with `X-Export-Truncated: true`. |
| `live_poll_interval_seconds` | `float` | `1.0` | How often each API process polls `task_runs` for changes to push down `/api/stream` while at least one dashboard has it open. Each poll is a small query on an indexed column; nothing is polled while nobody is connected. Lower means quicker live updates and more queries. See [REST API: how changes reach the stream](rest-api.md#how-changes-reach-the-stream). |
| `auto_migrate` | `bool` | `True` | Whether `init_db()` upgrades the database schema to the latest revision at startup. Set it to `False` to run `celery-manager migrate` as a deploy step instead; `init_db()` then leaves the database untouched and logs a warning if the schema isn't current. See [Schema and upgrades](#schema-and-upgrades). |
| `metrics_token` | `str \| None` | `None` | Bearer token for `GET /metrics`. `None` disables the endpoint (it answers `404`). When set, scrapers must send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. See [Metrics](metrics.md). |
| `metrics_cache_seconds` | `float` | `5.0` | How long the computed metrics snapshot is reused, so many scrapers cost one database pass and one broker round trip per interval. `0` disables the cache. |
| `inspect_timeout_seconds` | `float` | `1.0` | How long the [Workers page](workers.md) and the worker control endpoints wait for workers to reply to a broadcast (`inspect()`, `pool_grow`, `rate_limit`, ...). The HTTP request blocks for it, so keep it short; raise it only if workers on a slow or distant broker show as missing when they are running. |
| `schedule_editing` | `bool` | `False` | Lets operators change a schedule's crontab or interval from the dashboard. Leave it off unless beat runs `celery_manager.beat:DatabaseScheduler`: no other scheduler reads the edits, so the dashboard would list runs that never happen. While it's off, `PUT /api/schedules/{name}/schedule` answers `409`, saved edits are ignored when listing upcoming runs, and the dashboard's editor can only preview and revert. See [Editing schedules](schedules.md). |
| `dashboard_url` | `str \| None` | `None` | The dashboard's public address, e.g. `https://ops.example.com/celery/`. [Alert](alerts.md) messages link to the page about the problem (the task, queue, worker or schedule) under it. Without it, messages carry no link: the alerts evaluator runs outside the web server and can't know the address people use. |
| `smtp_host` | `str \| None` | `None` | SMTP server for [email alert channels](alerts.md#email). `None` disables email: an email channel's messages fail with that explanation, shown on the channel. |
| `smtp_port` | `int` | `587` | SMTP port. |
| `smtp_username` | `str \| None` | `None` | SMTP login. `None` sends without authenticating. |
| `smtp_password` | `str \| None` | `None` | SMTP password, used with `smtp_username`. Only ever lives here: never in the database, never in an API response, and not in the config's `repr()`. |
| `smtp_use_tls` | `bool` | `True` | Upgrade the SMTP connection with STARTTLS before logging in. Turn off only for a local relay. |
| `alert_email_from` | `str \| None` | `None` | From address of alert emails. Required for email channels. |
| `alert_send_timeout_seconds` | `float` | `10.0` | Time limit for each outbound alert delivery: one Slack post, one webhook call, one SMTP session. A channel that doesn't answer in time is recorded as failed and the other channels are still tried. |
| `alert_interval_seconds` | `float` | `60.0` | How often the alerts evaluator checks every rule (`celery-manager alerts`, or `events --with-alerts`; `--interval` overrides it). |
| `queue_sample_interval_seconds` | `float` | `60.0` | How often the events listener records every queue's broker depth, for the [depth charts](queues.md#depth-history) and the `queue_growing` alert. `0` turns sampling off. |
| `queue_sample_retention_days` | `int` | `14` | How long depth samples are kept. The retention prune and the sampler itself (hourly) delete older ones. `0` keeps them forever. |
| `authenticate_request` | callable or `None` | `None` | Sign people in with your Django, Flask or FastAPI app's users. Takes the Starlette `Request`, returns `ExternalUser(username, role)` or `None` (not signed in to your app). Asked first on every request; `None` falls back to local accounts. `role=None` is a `403`; an unknown role, a wrong return type or an exception is a `500`, never access. Ready-made: `celery_manager.integrations.django.django_authenticator()` and `celery_manager.integrations.flask.flask_authenticator(...)`. See [Sign in with your app's users](integrations.md#sign-in-with-your-apps-users). |
| `local_login_enabled` | `bool` | `True` | Whether celery-manager's own accounts can sign in. `False` (only with `authenticate_request`) replaces the password form with "Sign in with ...", refuses `POST /api/auth/login` and ignores existing `cm_session` cookies. `create_app()` refuses `False` without an authenticator. |
| `login_url` | `str` or `None` | `None` | Your app's login page, for the "Sign in with ..." link. `{next}` is replaced with the dashboard's address. A path or an `http(s)` URL; anything else makes `create_app()` refuse to start. |
| `logout_url` | `str` or `None` | `None` | Your app's sign-out page, linked from "Sign out" for people your app signed in. Without it they get no sign-out item. Same rules as `login_url`. |
| `login_provider_name` | `str` | `"your app"` | What the sign-in screen and sidebar call your app ("Sign in with Acme"). |
| `queue_browser_show_args` | `bool` | `True` | Show task arguments when [browsing a queue's waiting messages](queues.md#looking-inside-a-queue). Every role sees them, as on task runs (see [Roles](roles.md#what-viewers-can-see)). `False` leaves `args`/`kwargs` out of the response for everyone, for deployments whose task arguments carry secrets. |
| `queue_browser_amqp` | `bool` | `False` | Allow browsing RabbitMQ queues. Off by default because RabbitMQ can only show a message by handing it out: each one looked at is taken without acknowledgement and put back, which marks it redelivered and may move it to the front. While off, browsing a RabbitMQ queue answers `supported: false` with the reason. Redis browsing is read-only and needs no switch. |
| `rabbitmq_management_url` | `str \| None` | `None` | The [RabbitMQ management API](rabbitmq.md), e.g. `http://rabbit:15672`. Turns on the RabbitMQ panel on the Queues page, the `rabbitmq_*` metrics, the `rabbitmq_alarm` alert kind and the dead-letter queue page. Off while `None`, and always off when the broker isn't RabbitMQ. The vhost is taken from the broker URL. Redirects are never followed. |
| `rabbitmq_management_username` | `str \| None` | `None` | Management API login. The `monitoring` tag is enough to read; browsing a dead-letter queue also needs read permission on it; requeue uses the broker URL's user ([permissions](rabbitmq.md#the-management-user)). |
| `rabbitmq_management_password` | `str \| None` | `None` | Its password. Only ever lives here: never in the database, an API response, a log line or the config's `repr()`. |
| `rabbitmq_management_verify_tls` | `bool` | `True` | Verify the management API's certificate on `https` URLs. Turn off only for a test broker with a self-signed certificate. |
| `rabbitmq_management_timeout_seconds` | `float` | `3.0` | Time limit for one management API operation, all its HTTP calls together. |
| `rabbitmq_dlq_patterns` | `list[str]` | `["*.dlq", "*.dead", "dlq.*"]` | Queue-name patterns that count as [dead-letter queues](rabbitmq.md#dead-letter-queues) even when no queue's dead-letter exchange routes to them. |

The fields above are the whole dataclass — `CeleryManagerConfig` has no
other options, and nothing else in celery-manager reads configuration from
the environment.

The beat process doesn't use `CeleryManagerConfig`. When beat runs
`celery_manager.beat:DatabaseScheduler`, that scheduler reads two keys from
your Celery app's own config:

| Celery setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `celery_manager_db_url` | *required* | celery-manager's database, the same URL as `db_url`. Beat only reads the saved schedule edits from it. |
| `celery_manager_schedule_refresh` | `10` | Seconds between reads of the saved edits. An edit reaches beat within this time. |

See [Editing schedules](schedules.md).

[Data retention](retention.md) is deliberately not a config field: it is
changed at runtime from the Settings page and stored in the database.

## Tunables that are *not* config fields

Two limits that operators reasonably go looking for on `CeleryManagerConfig`
are not there. They are module-level constants, deliberately: both are
implementation limits with one sensible value, and threading them through the
config would imply a per-deployment decision that neither really is.

| Constant | Module | Value | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MIN_WRITE_INTERVAL_SECONDS` | `celery_manager.progress` | `0.5` | Minimum seconds between database writes for one run's [live progress](progress.md). The completing call ignores it. |
| `MAX_PAGE_SIZE` | `celery_manager.control.tasks` | `500` | Ceiling that `GET /api/tasks` clamps a caller-supplied `limit` to. Applied at the HTTP boundary only — a Python caller of `list_task_runs` is trusted and may ask for more. |

Both are plain module attributes read at call time, so a deployment with an
unusually loaded database can raise the throttle by assigning to it before
any task runs:

```python
from celery_manager import progress

progress.MIN_WRITE_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 2.0
```

That is a supported escape hatch rather than a documented API — if you find
yourself needing it in production, say so on the issue tracker and it can
become a real setting.

## Choosing `eta_tolerance_seconds`

Both the read side (matching a paused occurrence back to its row when the
dashboard recomputes upcoming occurrences) and the write side (the
decorator deciding whether *this* run corresponds to a paused occurrence)
match by "close enough" rather than exact timestamp equality, because
occurrence timestamps are computed independently each time rather than
stored once. That means the tolerance window is a genuine trade-off, not
just a fudge factor:

- **Too small** (e.g. under a second) risks an interval-schedule skip not
  matching beat's real firing. With beat running
  `celery_manager.beat:Scheduler`, queue delay no longer matters: the
  decorator compares the occurrence beat stamped, not the start time.
  Without it (old beat), the window is still compared with "now", and a
  task picked up outside it runs instead of being skipped.
- **Too large** (e.g. tens of minutes) on a tightly-spaced periodic
  schedule (interval shorter than `2 * eta_tolerance_seconds`) makes a
  single override ambiguous between two neighboring occurrences. The
  read-side matching in `list_upcoming_with_overrides` handles this by
  claiming each override for at most one occurrence (closest match, removed
  from the pool before matching the next occurrence), but a tolerance
  window comparable to or larger than the schedule's own interval is a
  sign it should be tightened.

The default of 60 seconds is a reasonable middle ground for schedules on
the order of minutes or longer. If you have periodic tasks firing more
than once a minute, consider a smaller value.

## `db_url` backend notes

- **SQLite** (`sqlite:///path.db` or `sqlite:///:memory:`) — zero setup,
  fine for local development, demos, and single-process deployments. Not
  recommended if the API app and events listener (or multiple API worker
  processes) need concurrent write access at any real volume.
- **Postgres/MySQL/etc.** — any URL SQLAlchemy's `create_engine` accepts
  works unmodified; celery-manager doesn't use any SQLite-specific SQL
  beyond the connection-pooling adjustments described above. Recommended
  for anything beyond local development, and required if you're running
  more than one API process behind a load balancer.

## `cookie_secure` and why it defaults to `True`

The session cookie is a bearer credential: anyone who obtains it *is* the
signed-in user for the remainder of that session, with full access to every
control action the dashboard exposes (start, cancel/terminate, retry, pause a
schedule occurrence). Without the `Secure` flag, a browser will happily send
that cookie over plain HTTP, where anything on the network path can read it.

celery-manager therefore sets `Secure` by default. This is a deliberate
"safe unless you say otherwise" choice: a default of `False` would silently
ship every deployment that never thought about the setting with a leakable
credential, and nothing about the running system would look wrong.

**Set `cookie_secure=False` only for local HTTP development.** Its failure
mode is loud rather than dangerous, which is the point: over plain HTTP with
the default left on, you will log in successfully and then immediately appear
logged out, because the browser accepts the `Secure` cookie but refuses to
send it back over an insecure connection. If that is what you are seeing on
`http://localhost`, this setting is the cause:

```python
config = CeleryManagerConfig(
    celery_app=your_celery_app,
    secret_key="dev-only",
    cookie_secure=False,  # local plain-HTTP development only
)
```

The bundled Django demo (`examples/django_demo`) does exactly this — it runs
over `http://localhost:8001` — via `CELERY_MANAGER_COOKIE_SECURE = False` in
its `settings.py`. Do not carry that line into a real deployment.

Terminating TLS at a proxy in front of celery-manager still counts as HTTPS
from the browser's point of view, so keep the default on in that setup; the
flag describes the browser-to-edge connection, not the edge-to-app hop.

## Schema and upgrades

celery-manager's tables are versioned with [Alembic](https://alembic.sqlalchemy.org/).
The migrations ship inside the package (`celery_manager/db/migrations/`) and
are configured in code, so you don't need an `alembic.ini` or the `alembic`
command.

### Automatic upgrades (the default)

`init_db()`, which the API app, `celery_manager.setup()` in workers and the
`celery-manager events` listener all call, upgrades the database to the latest
revision at startup. Upgrading celery-manager is just: install the new
version, restart. That works from any starting point:

| Database | What happens |
|---|---|
| Empty | Every revision runs, creating all tables. |
| Created by 0.1.0a1–0.1.0a3 (no version table) | Adopted: the baseline revision finds the tables already there and only records the version, then later revisions run. Your data is kept. |
| Created by a pre-release 0.1.0a4 build that already added `paused_at`/`paused_by` itself | Recorded at the revision that adds those columns, so they aren't added twice. Then any later revisions run. |
| Already versioned | Pending revisions run. Nothing happens if it's current. |

Several processes often start at once. The upgrade holds a lock while it
checks and migrates (a PostgreSQL advisory lock, MySQL `GET_LOCK`, or SQLite's
write lock via `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`), so the first process does the work and the
others wait for it, then find nothing to do.

The version is stored in a table called `celery_manager_alembic_version`, not
Alembic's default `alembic_version`. That way celery-manager can share a
database with an application that runs its own Alembic migrations.

The database user needs DDL permissions (`CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`,
`CREATE INDEX`) whenever a release includes a new revision. Release notes call
out every schema change. Back up the database before upgrading if its history
matters to you.

### Migrating as a deploy step

If your deploys run migrations separately, or the app's database user
shouldn't have DDL rights, turn automatic upgrades off in every process:

```python
config = CeleryManagerConfig(celery_app=app, ..., auto_migrate=False)
```

Then migrate with the CLI, using a database URL that has DDL rights:

```bash
celery-manager migrate --db-url postgresql://admin@db/celery_manager          # upgrade to latest
celery-manager migrate --db-url postgresql://admin@db/celery_manager --check  # report only
```

`--check` prints the current and latest revision and exits with status 1 if an
upgrade is needed, which makes it usable as a deploy gate. With
`auto_migrate=False`, `init_db()` doesn't touch the database at all. If the
schema isn't current it logs a warning, and queries against the new columns or
tables fail until you run `migrate`.

From Python, the same operations are
`celery_manager.db.migrate.upgrade_database(engine)` and
`migration_status(engine)`.

### Downgrades

Each revision has a `downgrade()`, but celery-manager doesn't wrap downgrades
in a command, and running an older celery-manager against a newer schema
isn't supported. To roll back, restore the backup you took before upgrading.

## `secret_key` in production

Generate a long random value once:

```bash
python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"
```

and set it via your normal secrets-management path (environment variable, a
secrets manager, etc.) — never commit a real value to source control. Every
API process behind the same load balancer needs the *same* key, or a cookie
signed by one is rejected by the next. There is no signing key for the
events listener, which doesn't serve HTTP; its CLI takes no `--secret-key`.

## Security model

Know what celery-manager does and doesn't defend against before you expose
it:

- **Operators are powerful.** Accounts have a [role](roles.md): `viewer`
  (read-only), `operator` or `admin`. Operators can dispatch registered user
  tasks subject to `startable_tasks` and optional strict argument schemas,
  cancel or terminate known tasks, retry runs and pause schedules. Queue
  overrides are disabled by default. Forced cancellation of an unknown ID
  requires an admin and explicit `force=true`. Give `operator` and `admin` only to people you'd
  trust with that, use `viewer` for everyone else, and treat the dashboard
  as an admin surface, ideally reachable only from a private network or VPN.
  Viewers can see task arguments and tracebacks; `log_view_role` can restrict logs.
- **Upgrading makes every existing account `admin`**, because before roles
  every account could do everything. Demote accounts afterwards with
  `celery-manager set-role`.
- **With `authenticate_request`, your app's session is a dashboard
  credential.** Whoever is signed in to your app gets the role your
  `role_for` gives them, so map roles deliberately (the Django default admits
  staff only) and treat an XSS hole anywhere on the same host as a dashboard
  hole. The `Origin` check below still blocks cross-site writes made with your
  app's cookie, whatever its `SameSite` setting; see
  [Security notes](integrations.md#security-notes).
- **Local password login has shared database backoff.** Account and direct-peer
  budgets apply across API instances sharing the database and secret. Configure
  `login_backoff_threshold`, `login_backoff_max_seconds` and
  `login_backoff_reset_seconds`; refused attempts return 429 with `Retry-After`.
  Proxy peer identity must be configured deliberately. External logins retain
  the host's controls. See [login backoff](auth-sessions.md#shared-login-backoff).
- **New browser sessions are individually revocable, valid for 7 days by default.**
  `session_max_age_seconds` controls local-cookie lifetime. HTTP login and bridge
  issuance register a random session ID in the database; logout revokes it before
  removing the cookie. Users can list and revoke their own sessions through the
  API. Live local-role lookup and password fingerprints still apply. Cookies
  issued before this upgrade, or signed manually without a session ID, remain
  stateless until expiry; logout cannot revoke a stolen copy of those older
  cookies. Rotate `secret_key` to invalidate all cookies, or reset a local
  account's password to invalidate its old cookies. See
  [session upgrade compatibility](auth-sessions.md#upgrade-compatibility).
- **`brand_logo_url` may point at an external host.** It lands in an
  `<img src>` on every page, including the login screen, so whoever controls
  that host sees a request (IP address, user agent) from each visitor, and
  can change the image. Prefer a same-origin path (`/logo.png`) or a
  raster `data:` URI; otherwise use a host you control.

What *is* in place: `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=lax`, `Secure`-by-default session
cookies; refusal of cross-origin `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` requests by
`Origin` check (with explicit `trusted_origins` and a bearer-only exception);
`X-Frame-Options: DENY` and `frame-ancestors 'none'` by default against
clickjacking; bcrypt password hashes, with login timing that doesn't reveal
whether a username exists. See the [REST API auth notes](rest-api.md#auth)
for the exact behaviour, including what a proxy in front of the app must
forward.


## Production options introduced in 0.2

The [production adoption guide](production.md) gives working examples, migration
instructions, adapter installation and operational limitations. These options
compose with the existing configuration and retention UI.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `startable_tasks` | `None` | Registered user tasks only. A collection restricts names; an empty collection disables dispatch. A callable receives `(name, principal)`. |
| `allow_queue_override` | `False` | Permit explicit task-start queue overrides. |
| `retry_edit_args` | `True` | Permit changed arguments when retrying a recorded run. |
| `args_schemas` | `{}` | Task-name to Pydantic model; strict validation of bound arguments before publishing. |
| `log_capture` / `log_capture_level` | `True` / `0` | Capture emitted records and filter by logging level; host logger levels remain authoritative. |
| `log_capture_max_bytes` | `256_000` | UTF-8 head/tail storage limit, including truncation marker. |
| `log_capture_loggers` | `()` | Optional logger-name prefixes; empty accepts all emitted task-context records. |
| `log_redactor` | `None` | Callable transforming a formatted log record. Failure withholds the raw record. |
| `log_view_role` | `"viewer"` | Minimum role that can retrieve captured logs. |
| `store_results` / `result_max_bytes` | `True` / `64_000` | Store bounded result representations in decorator and listener. |
| `principal_providers` | `()` | Ordered external providers, before the existing host callable and local-cookie fallback. |
| `session_max_age_seconds` | `604800` | Local-cookie lifetime; existing password fingerprints and live role lookup still apply. |
| `session_bridge_enabled` | `False` | Opt into a short external-authenticated dashboard cookie. |
| `bridge_max_age_seconds` | `300` | Bridge lifetime; fresh external authentication is required to renew. |
| `trusted_origins` | `()` | Explicit HTTP(S) origins for credentialed CORS and cross-origin cookie writes. |
| `frame_ancestors` | `()` | Explicit embedding origins. Empty denies framing; nonempty replaces deny-frame headers with the configured CSP. |
| `live_stream` | `"sse"` | `"poll"` omits the stream endpoint and disables EventSource in the SPA; use under WSGI. |
| `scheduler_backend` | `None` | Default static discovery, or a backend adapter such as RedBeat/Django Celery Beat. |
| `schedule_sync_interval_seconds` | `30.0` | Minimum interval between request-driven backend snapshot refreshes. |
| `cron_parser` | `None` | Deterministic rules by default, or a host parser/optional `LLMParser`. |
| `db_schema` | `None` | Provisioned SQL schema used by runtime models and migrations. SQLite uses a separate database file. |
| `engine_options` | `{}` | Additional SQLAlchemy engine options. |

Set worker, listener and API options consistently, particularly result/log
collection, storage namespace and scheduler configuration. The beat process uses
`app.conf.celery_manager_db_url` and `celery_manager_db_schema` when recording
optional liveness or reading package timing edits. Retention remains configured
through its existing persistent rules; it is not replaced by a new config flag.


## Operations options introduced in 0.3

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `tenant_resolver` | `None` | Trusted sync/async `(request, principal)` callable returning a tenant ID. Opts HTTP access into fail-closed, read-only task-history isolation; all global operational surfaces and writes are denied, including for admin. See [tenant scope](tenancy.md). |
| `lock_provider` | `None` | Explicit cross-process `LockProvider` for singleton execution. Redis brokers infer a Redis provider; other brokers require an explicit provider. There is no process-local production fallback. |
| `login_backoff_threshold` | `5` | Positive integer: initially admitted local login attempts before exponential backoff begins. Shared account and direct-peer budgets apply. |
| `login_backoff_max_seconds` | `300` | Positive integer: maximum local login backoff delay. |
| `login_backoff_reset_seconds` | `3600` | Positive integer: inactivity period after which a login budget resets. |
| `llm_call_retention_days` | `90` | Integer 0–3650: keep [LLM usage](llm-usage.md) rows this many days; `0` keeps them. |
| `llm_prices` | `{}` | Mapping of model-id prefix to `{"input": ..., "output": ..., "cache_read": ..., "cache_write": ...}` in USD per million tokens. Used to compute `cost_usd` when a call does not report one. `input` and `output` are required. |
| `worker_heartbeat_retention_days` | `7` | Integer 0–3650: retain minute-bucket worker observations for this many days. `0` disables collection and automatic history pruning, preserving existing samples and current WorkerState updates. |

The heartbeat history option supplements task-run retention rules; it does not
replace them. Keep it consistent in listener and API/maintenance processes. See
[worker history](workers.md#recorded-heartbeat-history-03),
[browser sessions](auth-sessions.md) and [singleton execution](singleton.md).
Use `scheduler_backend=SQLAlchemyBeatBackend(app)` for optional durable SQL
definitions; initialize the scheduler's own tables explicitly as documented in
[SQL schedules](sql-schedules.md).

Beat-process settings are Celery app configuration, **not**
`CeleryManagerConfig` constructor arguments:

| Celery app setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `celery_manager_db_url` | unset | Monitoring database for tick observations and package timing edits; not the optional scheduler definition database. |
| `celery_manager_db_schema` | unset | Provisioned monitoring schema. |
| `celery_manager_heartbeat_interval` | `30` | Tick observation interval, bounded to 5–86400 seconds. |
| `cm_beat_owner_id` | derived identity | Stable logical owner ID; set explicitly for independent production schedulers. |
| `cm_beat_healthcheck_url` | unset | Opt-in HTTP(S) dead-man monitor URL. No embedded credentials or redirects; paths/query tokens are withheld from logs. |
| `cm_beat_healthcheck_interval` | `30` | External ping interval, bounded to 5–86400 seconds. |
| `cm_beat_healthcheck_timeout` | `3` | Socket timeout, bounded to 0.1–10 seconds. DNS may take longer; single-flight requests bound thread growth. |

See [beat liveness](beat-liveness.md) for failure semantics, owner retirement and
external service configuration. A tick ping establishes scheduler liveness,
not task success or leader election.


## Native observation and operations options

See [real-world operations](real-world-operations.md) for working host-runner,
probe, scheduler and preflight examples. These features remain in the same 0.3
release; they do not require converting a host executor to Celery.

| Option | Default | Contract |
|---|---|---|
| `observer_fail_open` | `True` | Persistence failures report telemetry health without failing or retrying host work. A `RunObserver(..., fail_open=...)` can override this. Input validation still rejects invalid instrumentation. |
| `observer_context_max_bytes` | `16384` | Integer of at least 64; oversized sanitized metadata is replaced by an explicit truncation object. Also bounds publish-hook metadata. |
| `observer_metadata_keys` | `("integration", "request_id", "trace_id", "environment", "deployment_id", "resource_id")` | Metadata allowlist; a custom tuple restricts keys, `None` admits all keys before sanitation and limits. Identifiers such as tenant/correlation/operation remain separate fields. |
| `observer_error_callback` | `None` | Callable receiving sanitized observer health after telemetry failure. Callback errors are contained. |
| `observer_store_results` | `False` | Opt into sanitized, bounded results for external observations. Uses the existing result size policy; no automatic argument capture. |
| `environment_name` | `""` | Printable public deployment label, at most 100 characters. Namespaces operation annotations and labels the UI/action audit. It is not a tenant boundary. |
| `require_typed_confirmation` | `False` | HTTP purge must send `confirm` equal to the queue name, and bulk retry `confirm_count` equal to the number of ids. Clients sending either value are always checked; this makes them mandatory. The dashboard always sends them. |
| `operator_safeguards` | `False` | Require an audited reason and exact environment confirmation for the documented sensitive HTTP actions. Requires a nonblank `environment_name`. Role/task policies still apply. |
| `health_probes` | `()` | Up to 32 unique `ProbeDefinition(name, provider)` objects. Providers run only during explicit host collection, never on a health GET. |
| `probe_timeout_seconds` | `3.0` | Finite 0.01–30 seconds; bound collection waiting. A hung synchronous provider remains single-flight rather than being forcibly killed. |
| `probe_freshness_seconds` | `120.0` | Finite 1–86400 seconds; older probe observations become unknown on reads. Alert rules can set their own freshness threshold. |
| `health_observation_retention_days` | `7` | Integer 1–3650; explicit collection removes expired latest probe snapshots in bounded batches. This is not a metrics time series. |
| `max_request_body_bytes` | `4194304` | Requests to state-changing routes with a larger body get 413 before anything parses them, whether or not they send `Content-Length`. Keep your proxy's own limit at or below this. |

`tenant_resolver` is documented above and in [tenant security](tenancy.md).
Configure it at application construction; do not toggle it per request. Runtime
monitoring writes remain global, while HTTP reads are request-scoped. Provision
and migrate monitoring storage separately when using `auto_migrate=False`.


<!-- docs/contributing.md -->

# Working on celery-manager

Notes for changing celery-manager itself, rather than using it. The one that
catches people is the last section: **the dashboard bundle is committed, so a
frontend change is not done until you rebuild and commit it.**

## Set up

```bash
python -m venv venv
venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

The `dev` extra is `pytest`, `pytest-xdist`, `pytest-cov`, `httpx` (needed by
FastAPI's `TestClient`), `ruff`, and `uvicorn`. That is enough to run the unit
tier and the linter. Optional-adapter tests skip unless their extras are
installed.

Two more extras exist and are deliberately separate:

- `docs` — `mkdocs-material`, for building this site.
- `standalone` — `uvicorn`, for *serving* celery-manager rather than mounting
  it into an ASGI app you already run. Not a core dependency, because
  mounting needs no server of its own.

## Tests and linting

```bash
venv/bin/python -m pytest -m unit -n auto     # fast tier: no services, about a minute
venv/bin/python -m pytest -m integration      # live-service tier; skips what is not configured
venv/bin/python -m pytest -n auto             # everything
venv/bin/ruff check .
```

`tests/conftest.py` marks every test under `tests/integration/` as
`integration` and everything else as `unit`. The unit tier runs against
SQLite and an eager or stubbed Celery app: no broker, no worker, no Redis.
`-n auto` comes from `pytest-xdist` (in the `dev` extra); serially the unit
tier takes three to four minutes. The coverage job in CI runs the unit tier
with `--cov=celery_manager --cov-fail-under=...`; run the same command locally
before raising or lowering that floor.

Tests that need a live service skip themselves unless the matching variable is
set. CI sets them in the jobs named below, and pipes each selection through
`python -m tests.release_gate <junit.xml>`, which fails when any selected test
skipped, so a missing service cannot pass silently.

| Variable | Service | Example | CI job |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CM_STORAGE_DB_URL`, `CM_STORAGE_SCHEMA` | PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8.4, SQL Server 2022 | `postgresql+psycopg://postgres:pw@localhost:5432/cm_test` | Storage (matrix) |
| `CM_TEST_DB_URL` | same databases, race tests | as above | Storage, Race tests |
| `CM_TEST_REDIS_URL` | Redis 7 | `redis://localhost:6379/15` | Optional adapters, Live brokers |
| `CM_TEST_AMQP_URL` | RabbitMQ 3 | `amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672//` | Live brokers |
| `CM_TEST_RABBIT_MGMT_URL`, `_USER`, `_PASSWORD` | RabbitMQ management API | `http://localhost:15672` | Live brokers |

Disposable containers are enough to run every gate locally:

```bash
docker run -d --name cm-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw -e POSTGRES_DB=cm_test -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
docker run -d --name cm-redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7
docker run -d --name cm-rabbit -p 5672:5672 -p 15672:15672 rabbitmq:3-management
CM_STORAGE_DB_URL=postgresql+psycopg://postgres:pw@localhost:5432/cm_test CM_STORAGE_SCHEMA=cm_contract \
  venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/integration/test_storage_backends.py tests/integration/test_release_upgrade.py
```

SQL Server needs Microsoft's ODBC Driver 18 and `pip install pyodbc`. On
macOS with Homebrew, the driver may fail with "OpenSSL library could not be
loaded" when the default OpenSSL is newer than 3.x; point it at 3.x with
`DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH=$(brew --prefix openssl@3)/lib` on the Python command.

There is no `[tool.ruff]` section in `pyproject.toml`, so ruff runs with
whatever defaults (or user-level config) are in play; pin one there if you
want reproducible lint results across machines.

## Documentation

```bash
venv/bin/pip install -e ".[docs]"
venv/bin/mkdocs serve            # live preview on http://127.0.0.1:8000
venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict   # writes ./site (gitignored)
```

`--strict` turns warnings into failures, but note that a **broken in-page
anchor is reported at `INFO`, not as a warning** — so a build can exit `0`
while a `#some-heading` link is dead. Read the output, don't just check the
exit code.

The house rule for this documentation is that every claim is checked against
real source or real behaviour before it is written. If you document an
endpoint, call it. If you document a UI behaviour, read the component. Prior
review has found stale prose more than once, which is why the pages are
explicit about limitations and failure modes rather than tidy.

## Rebuilding the dashboard bundle

The React dashboard is committed **prebuilt** into
`src/celery_manager/dashboard/static/`, which is what lets an installed celery-manager (the wheel or a git install)
serve a UI with no Node toolchain. `frontend/dist/` is
gitignored; the copy under `src/` is the one that ships.

So a change under `frontend/src/` has no effect on the installed package
until you rebuild and copy:

```bash
cd frontend
npm install                      # first time only
npm run build                    # tsc -b && vite build -> frontend/dist
rm -rf ../src/celery_manager/dashboard/static
cp -r dist ../src/celery_manager/dashboard/static
```

Then commit `src/celery_manager/dashboard/static/` alongside your
`frontend/src/` change. Vite content-hashes the asset filenames, so the diff
will show a new `index-<hash>.js` / `index-<hash>.css` pair and a rewritten
`index.html` — that is expected, and a `frontend/src/` change with no bundle
change in the same commit is the bug to look for.

## Building the distributions

```bash
venv/bin/python -m build         # wheel + sdist into ./dist
```

Check two things in the result:

- The wheel contains `celery_manager/dashboard/static/` with the same asset
  hashes as your working tree — otherwise the installed package serves a
  stale UI.
- The sdist contains only what `[tool.hatch.build.targets.sdist]` allows.
  That list is an explicit allowlist rather than a denylist, because
  hatchling's default ("everything VCS doesn't ignore") happily ships
  whatever working files a tool has dropped in the repo root.

## Schema changes

celery-manager's schema is versioned with Alembic. Revisions live in
`src/celery_manager/db/migrations/versions/` and ship in the wheel, and
`init_db()` applies them at startup (see
[Configuration: schema and upgrades](configuration.md#schema-and-upgrades)).
Every change to `celery_manager.db.models` needs a new revision.
`tests/unit/test_migrations.py::test_models_and_migrations_agree` fails until
it has one.

The repo-root `alembic.ini` is for contributors only. It points at the
in-package migrations and a scratch SQLite database (`alembic-scratch.db`,
gitignored), and puts `src/` first on `sys.path`, so it always uses your
working tree. To add a revision, from the repo root:

```bash
rm -f alembic-scratch.db
venv/bin/alembic upgrade head          # scratch DB at the current latest revision
# ...edit src/celery_manager/db/models.py...
venv/bin/alembic revision --autogenerate --rev-id 0008 -m "add my_column"
venv/bin/alembic upgrade head && venv/bin/alembic check   # applies cleanly, no diff left
```

That writes `versions/0008_add_my_column.py`. Then:

- **Read the generated file.** Autogenerate misses some changes (renames
  become drop + add, and server defaults and some constraint changes
  aren't detected), so fix it by hand where needed. Tidy the
  `# ### commands auto generated` markers.
- **Revision IDs are sequential, four digits** (`0001`, `0002`, ...),
  and `down_revision` is the previous one. If two branches both add the same ID,
  whichever merges second renumbers its revision to the next free ID (file name,
  `revision`, `down_revision`). `test_revision_history_is_linear` fails while
  there are two heads.
- **Keep upgrades safe on a live table.** A new column on an existing table
  should be nullable, or have a `server_default` if it must be `NOT NULL`.
  Leave the `batch_alter_table` blocks that autogenerate writes (`env.py`
  sets `render_as_batch=True`): on SQLite they recreate the table for changes
  `ALTER TABLE` can't make, and on other backends they are plain `ALTER`s.
- **Write a working `downgrade()`.**
- **Never edit a revision that has shipped in a release.** Add a new one.
  Revisions `0001` and `0002` are special: they tolerate databases created
  before migrations existed. Later revisions don't need to, because every
  database that reaches them is versioned.
- **Add a test** if the revision transforms data, and mention the schema
  change in `CHANGELOG.md`.

To try a revision against PostgreSQL, pass a URL:
`venv/bin/alembic -x db_url=postgresql+psycopg://... upgrade head`.
The races and migration tests also run against a server database when
`CM_TEST_DB_URL` is set (CI does this for PostgreSQL).

<!-- docs/stability.md -->

# Stability and upgrade policy

celery-manager is released as beta (`0.x` with `bN` suffixes), but the
surfaces below are now treated as stable. A change that breaks one of them
needs a deprecation period, a CHANGELOG entry under **Breaking**, and a
migration note. Anything not listed may still change between minor releases.

## What is stable

| Surface | Stable contract |
|---|---|
| Package root | Every name in `celery_manager.__all__`: `CeleryManagerConfig`, `setup`, `track`, `report_progress`, `RunObserver`, `current_run`, `install_publish_hook`, `task_url`, `control`, `__version__`. |
| Configuration | Existing `CeleryManagerConfig` field names, their types and their defaults. New fields are added with defaults that keep current behaviour. |
| REST API | Every route under `/api/v1`, its request fields and the fields in its response. New optional request fields and new response fields can appear at any time; clients must ignore fields they do not know. The unversioned `/api/...` aliases follow the same rules. |
| CLI | The `celery-manager` subcommands (`events`, `alerts`, `migrate`, `create-user`, `set-role`, `list-users`, `prune`, `import-pauses`, `doctor`, and the ones added later) and their flags. |
| Metrics | Metric names and label names on `/metrics`. |
| Database schema | The tables are reached only through the Alembic revisions in `celery_manager/db/migrations`. Revisions that shipped are never edited; every schema change is a new revision with a working `downgrade()`. |
| Task headers | The `cm_*` message headers stamped by the scheduler mixins and the publish hook. |

Not stable: anything under a module or attribute whose name starts with `_`,
the dashboard's HTML and internal JSON shapes used only by the bundled UI,
log message text, and the exact wording of `doctor` checks.

## Deprecation

A stable name or route that is going away keeps working for at least one
minor release (for example `0.4` to `0.5`) after the release that deprecates
it. During that window it emits a `DeprecationWarning` (Python) or a
`Deprecation` response header (HTTP), and the CHANGELOG names the
replacement.

## Upgrades

- Upgrading from the **previous release** is supported directly; older
  releases upgrade through each intermediate release's migrations, which
  `celery-manager migrate` applies in order.
- Back up the monitoring tables, run `celery-manager migrate --db-url ...`
  with a DDL-capable credential, then confirm with `--check`. Run with
  `auto_migrate=False` in application processes when they must not issue DDL.
- Every revision has a `downgrade()`. Downgrading is for rolling back a
  failed deployment, not for long-term use: data in columns added by the
  newer revision is dropped.

## How the policy is enforced

- `tests/unit/test_stability_contract.py` pins the hashes of shipped
  migration revisions, the package-root names and the CLI command set.
  Changing a pinned value is a policy decision and needs this page and the
  CHANGELOG updated in the same change.
- `tests/unit/test_migrations.py` fails when models and migrations disagree
  or the revision history has two heads.
- `tests/integration/test_release_upgrade.py` seeds data at the previous
  release's schema, upgrades to head, checks the data survived, downgrades and
  upgrades again. CI runs it against PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8.4 and SQL Server
  2022 in the **Storage** job, through `tests.release_gate`, which fails if
  any selected check skipped.

## Towards 1.0

The `Development Status` classifier moved to Beta with `0.3.0b1` and moves
to Production/Stable at 1.0. The remaining blockers for 1.0 are tracked in
the [roadmap](roadmap.md): an independent security review, overhead numbers
from a production deployment, and a production trial.


<!-- docs/roadmap.md -->

# Production requirements and roadmap

Adoption requirements for existing Celery deployments are the baseline. The production
foundations shipped in **0.2.0a1**; **0.3.0b1** adds the operational features below
in one release. See [0.3 release scope](release-0.3.md) and
[production adoption](production.md) for contracts and limitations.

“Candidate” means implemented with local regression coverage, not certified in
every deployment. Live PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQL Server, optional scheduler and Redis
contracts, and a production rollout remain acceptance gates. A configured
CI job is not evidence that its live gate has run successfully for this release.

## Adoption requirements

| Review ID | Real-world requirement | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| P0-1 | Discover runtime schedules outside static Celery config | Candidate: backend protocol, static/RedBeat/Django adapters, request-driven refresh and preserved deletion history |
| P0-2 / F11 | Create, edit and delete schedules with attributable changes | Candidate: API, creation UI, timing editor, deletion confirmation and before/after audits; JSON argument, keyword-argument and delivery-option creation/editing in the dashboard |
| P0-3 | Several schedules of the same task remain independent | Candidate: stamping adapters, identity extractor and consumed identity kwargs |
| P0-4 | Host identity, SSO and stable audit identity | Existing host authenticators; candidate OIDC/JWKS, provider chain, subject, opt-in short session bridge, explicit CORS origins |
| P0-5 | Storage can safely share a production SQL database | Candidate schemas, engine options, UTC defaults and SQL Server locking; live database CI required; table prefixes remain open |
| P0-6 | A dashboard cannot freely dispatch sensitive tasks | Candidate shared dispatch allowlists, strict argument schemas, queue/edit policies, audited denials, explicit unknown-ID cancellation |
| P1-7 | Large or sensitive logs cannot exhaust storage | Candidate bounded head/tail capture, logger/level filters, redaction and role-based log reads |
| P1-8 | Inspect results and control history growth | Candidate bounded results and result opt-out; existing configurable batched retention/prune |
| P1-9 | Monitoring works when workers were not started with `-E` | Candidate periodic event-enabling broadcast and heartbeat warning; worker state reports observations, not a guessed enable flag |
| P1-10 / F9 | Host task links work immediately | Candidate link helper, after-publish seed, initiator header and waiting/recovery page |
| P1-11 | A WSGI deployment cannot dedicate workers to endless streams | Candidate explicit polling mode with no SSE endpoint |
| P1-12 | Embed the dashboard in a host application | Candidate explicit frame ancestors; independent from CORS |
| P2-13 | Scrape Prometheus/OpenTelemetry | Existing; preserve current metrics contract |
| P2-14 | Remember worker liveness beyond a current ping | Candidate minute-bucket heartbeat observations, bounded retention, authenticated range/paging API and worker-card trend/history; missing observations remain unknown |
| P2-15 | Limit local and bridged session lifetimes | Candidate configurable lifetimes, shared DB login backoff and revocable newly issued browser sessions; legacy stateless cookies require expiry, password reset or key rotation |
| P2-16 | Decorator placement is unambiguous | Candidate corrected docs and import-time rejection of reversed decorator order |
| P2-17 | Import a host's legacy cancellation table safely | Candidate validated, all-or-nothing CSV pause import through CLI/admin API; existing Python pause/occurrence controls remain |

## Broader product requirements

| Review ID | Capability | Coverage / remaining acceptance criteria |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | Natural-language scheduling | Candidate deterministic weekday lists/ranges, exact supported time windows, several same-minute daily times, per-entry IANA zones, ten-run create preview and optional AI adapter. Unsupported phrases, multiple expressions, holidays and custom DST policy are deferred. |
| F2 | Durable schedule authority and reconciliation | Candidate optional SQLAlchemy scheduler, explicit initialization, operation-scoped ownership, dry-run diff, adopt/export/repair API and dashboard, snapshot conflicts. Extra entries are never deleted; partial progress requires inspection and a fresh plan, not transactional crash recovery. |
| F3 | Skip next / run now | Candidate audited actions and UI. Manual runs must never consume a scheduled override. |
| F4 | Central alerts | Candidate individual/consecutive failure, stuck/lost, stale-beat, SLA, regression and digest rules in API/dashboard; existing incidents, durable dedup and delivery records. Network timeouts can still duplicate notifications. |
| F5 | Runtime regression, SLAs and digest | Candidate successful-run p95 baseline with minimum samples, per-task/glob runtime SLA, UTC daily per-task outcome totals and persisted incident-key delivery dedup. Insufficient evidence is unknown; candidate scans above 20,000 matching runs in the relevant windows are refused. |
| F6 | Stuck/lost runs | Candidate advisory health findings and matching alerts; stuck rules combine a fixed floor with task-specific successful-run p95, while lost-worker rules use observed offline/stale state. Unknown workers remain unknown; no execution is terminated. |
| F7 | Failure inbox | Candidate acknowledge/ignore/reopen with actor, note and durable review history in API/dashboard; existing grouped failures and selective reruns. Review state never changes the execution result. |
| F8 | Initiator identity | Candidate stored initiator, started-by-me and exact-identity filters across list/count/export/bulk cancel, dashboard saved filters, operator retry identity and instrumented chain/group publication inheritance. Uninstrumented producers cannot supply inferred identity. |
| F10 | Stable API and embedded status UI | Candidate /api/v1 aliases, OpenAPI and dependency-free authenticated task-status widget. Generated language-specific SDKs remain deferred. |
| F12 | Beat liveness and missed runs | Candidate durable per-owner tick observations, aggregate/owner health, stale-beat rule and external dead-man ping independent of DB writes; unknown owners remain unknown. Missed-run inference still starts from observed schedule identity. |
| F13 | Drift/orphan health | Candidate unregistered tasks, historical definitions missing from current backend, definition drift and opt-in observed queue consumers. Empty/failed worker inspection is unknown. Arbitrary orphan Redis-key discovery/deletion is deferred. |
| F14 | Singleton task execution | Candidate track(singleton=...) with explicit keys, Redis owner-token leases, renewal/expiry and skip/retry conflicts; bounded inspection and conditional audited release APIs. No process-local production fallback or fencing guarantee; the dashboard includes bounded inspection and explicit release confirmation. |

## Native operability

These ten capabilities are implemented in the same 0.3.0b1 candidate. Detailed
Python/API signatures, deployment requirements and limitations are in
[real-world operations](real-world-operations.md). “Candidate” remains a local
implementation status, not a completed live-rollout claim.

| Requirement | Candidate scope and boundary |
|---|---|
| 1. Observe non-Celery jobs | RunObserver sync/async contexts and decorators; monitoring-only config accepts no Celery app. Host retains its runner and controls. |
| 2. Tenant visibility/permissions | Trusted sync/async resolver, SQL scoping before paging/count/export, hidden foreign lineage and same-tenant related attempts. Read-only tenant mode denies all writes/global views/events even for admin. |
| 3. Durable background-work diagnostics | Queued, started and terminal observations; host-reported/cancellation interruption and telemetry health. No new delivery engine, hard-kill inference or automatic resume. |
| 4. Custom probes/outbox | Explicit host-collected bounded numeric snapshots, timeout/freshness unknown state, outbox depth/oldest age/exhaustion/latency helper and custom-probe alerts. No host-schema discovery or outbox draining. |
| 5. Scheduler instance expectations | Registered instances, monotonic heartbeat/command observations and first-due checks before first observation; advisory health/UI and alerts. No scheduler replacement or leader election. |
| 6. Request/business correlation | Tenant/correlation/operation IDs plus sanitized allowlisted metadata; trusted publish hook and observation context. Instrumentation must be installed in publishing processes. |
| 7. Duplicate visibility | Operation-key Python lookup and same-tenant operation/correlation related-run UI/API. Matching keys never suppress execution and do not provide exactly-once semantics. |
| 8. Preflight | Read-only doctor CLI/Python and admin Operations view; broker/worker checks are explicit opt-ins. A pass is not end-to-end certification or automatic repair. |
| 9. Deployment/maintenance context | Environment-scoped audited annotations in API/UI. Notes do not automatically pause jobs, suppress alerts or replace schedule maintenance windows. |
| 10. Sensitive action safeguards | Opt-in audited reason and exact environment confirmation on enumerated HTTP actions, after role checks. CLI/Python calls retain their own administrative boundary. |

## Remaining high-value work

- Dedicated calendar transition previews, holiday/business calendars and custom
  missing/repeated-local-time policy; current calendar semantics follow Celery.
- Listener resilience diagnostics beyond current observer health: cross-process
  collection lag, dropped-write counters and bounded event-queue instrumentation.
- Policy-aware task forms generated from argument schemas.
- Configurable monitoring table prefixes and generated language SDKs.
- Arbitrary orphan-key discovery/deletion, automatic transactional cross-backend
  repair and business-specific compensation remain outside this release.

## Release verification

- Existing database upgrades and model/migration agreement must pass.
- Policy denials must publish zero messages across every dispatch entry point.
- Large log/result tests must demonstrate byte limits without changing task outcomes.
- Backend contract and stamping tests must pass against supported optional packages.
- Live SQLite/PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQL Server contracts must cover concurrent migrations,
  task-run races, schema isolation, UTC defaults and batched pruning.
- Build, lint, docs, packaged static assets and local install smoke checks must pass.
- A production trial must verify SSO, deep links, queue routing, separate
  schedules for one task, one-off skips and rollback before retiring Flower or a
  host's existing scheduler layer.

CI runs on pushes to `main`, on pull requests and on manual dispatch. Publishing
runs only for a pushed `v*` tag that matches the package version: the tagged
commit re-runs the unit tier, builds, publishes to TestPyPI, installs from there,
then publishes to PyPI with PEP 740 attestations. Pushing to `main` never
publishes.
